उत्तर: (B) इलेक्ट्रॉन त्याग

प्रश्न 2: H₂SO₄ में सल्फर की ऑक्सीकरण संख्या कितनी है?

(A) +2

(B) +4

(C) +6

(D) −2

उत्तर: (C) +6

प्रश्न 3: ऑक्सीकारक स्वयं किस प्रक्रिया से गुजरता है?

(A) ऑक्सीकरण

(B) अपचयन

(C) उदासीनीकरण

(D) वाष्पीकरण

उत्तर: (B) अपचयन

प्रश्न 4: स्वतंत्र तत्व की ऑक्सीकरण संख्या कितनी होती है?

(A) +1

(B) −1

(C) 0

(D) +2

उत्तर: (C) 0

प्रश्न 5: H₂O₂ में ऑक्सीजन की ऑक्सीकरण संख्या कितनी होती है?

(A) −2

(B) −1

(C) 0

(D) +1

उत्तर: (B) −1

8.21 अध्याय का सारांश

  • रेडॉक्स अभिक्रिया में ऑक्सीकरण और अपचयन एक साथ होते हैं।
  • ऑक्सीकरण में इलेक्ट्रॉन का त्याग होता है और ऑक्सीकरण संख्या बढ़ती है।
  • अपचयन में इलेक्ट्रॉन ग्रहण होते हैं और ऑक्सीकरण संख्या घटती है।
  • ऑक्सीकारक स्वयं अपचयित होता है और अपचायक स्वयं ऑक्सीकृत होता है।
  • ऑक्सीकरण संख्या से रेडॉक्स अभिक्रियाओं को पहचाना और संतुलित किया जा सकता है।
  • बैटरी, दहन, श्वसन और धातु निष्कर्षण में रेडॉक्स प्रक्रियाएँ महत्त्वपूर्ण हैं।

अध्याय 9: हाइड्रोजन (Hydrogen)

9.1 हाइड्रोजन क्या है?

हाइड्रोजन (Hydrogen): हाइड्रोजन एक रासायनिक तत्व है जिसका प्रतीक H और परमाणु क्रमांक 1 है। यह आवर्त सारणी का सबसे हल्का तत्व है। सामान्य परिस्थितियों में हाइड्रोजन गैस के रूप में द्विपरमाणुक अणु H₂ बनाता है।

  • प्रतीक: H
  • परमाणु क्रमांक: 1
  • परमाणु द्रव्यमान: लगभग 1.008 u
  • अणुसूत्र: H₂
  • इलेक्ट्रॉनिक विन्यास: 1s¹
  • आवर्त सारणी: प्रथम आवर्त, समूह 1 के ऊपर स्थित

9.2 हाइड्रोजन की खोज

हाइड्रोजन गैस की पहचान वैज्ञानिक हेनरी कैवेंडिश ने 1766 में की थी। बाद में एंटोनी लैवॉज़ियर ने इसका नाम Hydrogen रखा। यह नाम ग्रीक शब्दों से बना है, जिनका अर्थ पानी बनाने वाला है।

9.3 हाइड्रोजन की स्थिति आवर्त सारणी में

हाइड्रोजन का इलेक्ट्रॉनिक विन्यास 1s¹ है। इसके बाहरी कोश में एक इलेक्ट्रॉन होता है। इस कारण यह कुछ गुणों में क्षार धातुओं से मिलता-जुलता है, लेकिन इसके कई गुण हैलोजन और अधातुओं से भी मिलते हैं। इसलिए हाइड्रोजन की स्थिति विशेष मानी जाती है।

9.4 हाइड्रोजन के समस्थानिक (Isotopes)

हाइड्रोजन के तीन प्रमुख समस्थानिक हैं। इनके परमाणु क्रमांक समान, लेकिन द्रव्यमान संख्या अलग होती है।

1. प्रोटियम (Protium)

  • प्रतीक: ¹H
  • नाभिक में एक प्रोटॉन होता है।
  • इसमें न्यूट्रॉन नहीं होता।
  • यह प्रकृति में पाया जाने वाला हाइड्रोजन का सबसे सामान्य समस्थानिक है।

2. ड्यूटेरियम (Deuterium)

  • प्रतीक: ²H या D
  • नाभिक में एक प्रोटॉन और एक न्यूट्रॉन होता है।
  • इसके ऑक्साइड D₂O को भारी पानी कहते हैं।

3. ट्रिटियम (Tritium)

  • प्रतीक: ³H या T
  • नाभिक में एक प्रोटॉन और दो न्यूट्रॉन होते हैं।
  • यह रेडियोधर्मी होता है।

9.5 हाइड्रोजन के समस्थानिकों में अंतर

गुण प्रोटियम ड्यूटेरियम ट्रिटियम
प्रतीक ¹H ²H या D ³H या T
प्रोटॉन 1 1 1
न्यूट्रॉन 0 1 2
द्रव्यमान संख्या 1 2 3
रेडियोधर्मिता स्थिर स्थिर रेडियोधर्मी

9.6 हाइड्रोजन के भौतिक गुण

  • हाइड्रोजन रंगहीन गैस है।
  • यह गंधहीन और स्वादहीन होती है।
  • सामान्य परिस्थितियों में H₂ अणु के रूप में पाई जाती है।
  • यह बहुत हल्की गैस है।
  • पानी में इसकी विलेयता कम होती है।
  • यह अत्यधिक ज्वलनशील है और हवा के साथ ज्वलनशील मिश्रण बना सकती है।

9.7 हाइड्रोजन के रासायनिक गुण

1. ऑक्सीजन के साथ अभिक्रिया

हाइड्रोजन ऑक्सीजन के साथ जलकर पानी बनाती है।

संतुलित समीकरण:

2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O

2. क्लोरीन के साथ अभिक्रिया

उपयुक्त परिस्थितियों में हाइड्रोजन क्लोरीन के साथ अभिक्रिया करके हाइड्रोजन क्लोराइड बनाती है।

समीकरण:

H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl

3. नाइट्रोजन के साथ अभिक्रिया

उद्योगों में उचित तापमान, दाब और उत्प्रेरक की उपस्थिति में हाइड्रोजन तथा नाइट्रोजन से अमोनिया बनाया जाता है।

समीकरण:

N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃

4. धातु ऑक्साइड का अपचयन

कुछ धातु ऑक्साइडों को गर्म करने पर हाइड्रोजन उनका अपचयन कर सकती है।

उदाहरण:

CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O

9.8 हाइड्रोजन बनाने की विधियाँ

1. प्रयोगशाला में धातु और अम्ल से

कुछ सक्रिय धातुएँ तनु अम्लों के साथ अभिक्रिया करके हाइड्रोजन गैस बनाती हैं।

उदाहरण:

Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂

इस विधि का अध्ययन प्रयोगशाला में उचित सुरक्षा और शिक्षक की देखरेख में किया जाता है।

2. पानी के विद्युत अपघटन से

पानी के विद्युत अपघटन में विद्युत ऊर्जा की सहायता से पानी को हाइड्रोजन और ऑक्सीजन में बदला जा सकता है।

कुल समीकरण:

2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂

3. प्राकृतिक गैस से

औद्योगिक स्तर पर प्राकृतिक गैस में मौजूद मीथेन से भाप की सहायता से हाइड्रोजन बनाई जा सकती है। इस प्रक्रिया को स्टीम रिफॉर्मिंग कहते हैं।

एक प्रमुख समीकरण:

CH₄ + H₂O → CO + 3H₂

इसके बाद कार्बन मोनोऑक्साइड की जल-गैस शिफ्ट अभिक्रिया से अतिरिक्त हाइड्रोजन प्राप्त की जा सकती है।

समीकरण:

CO + H₂O → CO₂ + H₂

9.9 हाइड्रोजन के प्रमुख यौगिक

1. पानी (Water)

पानी का रासायनिक सूत्र H₂O है। प्रत्येक पानी के अणु में दो हाइड्रोजन परमाणु और एक ऑक्सीजन परमाणु होता है।

  • पानी एक ध्रुवीय अणु है।
  • यह अनेक आयनिक और ध्रुवीय पदार्थों के लिए अच्छा विलायक है।
  • पानी के अणुओं के बीच हाइड्रोजन बंध बनते हैं।

2. भारी पानी (Heavy Water)

भारी पानी का सूत्र D₂O है। इसमें सामान्य हाइड्रोजन के स्थान पर ड्यूटेरियम होता है।

  • इसका मोलर द्रव्यमान सामान्य पानी से अधिक होता है।
  • कुछ परमाणु रिएक्टरों में इसका उपयोग न्यूट्रॉन मॉडरेटर के रूप में किया जाता है।

3. हाइड्रोजन पेरॉक्साइड (Hydrogen Peroxide)

हाइड्रोजन पेरॉक्साइड का रासायनिक सूत्र H₂O₂ है। यह एक ऑक्सीकारक पदार्थ है और उचित परिस्थितियों में विघटित होकर पानी तथा ऑक्सीजन बना सकता है।

समीकरण:

2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂

इसके उपयोग और भंडारण में सांद्रता के अनुसार सावधानी आवश्यक होती है।

9.10 हाइड्राइड (Hydrides)

हाइड्रोजन के अन्य तत्वों के साथ बने द्विघटकीय यौगिकों को सामान्यतः हाइड्राइड कहते हैं। इन्हें प्रमुख रूप से तीन वर्गों में बाँटा जाता है।

1. आयनिक या लवणीय हाइड्राइड

कुछ सक्रिय धातुओं के हाइड्राइड में हाइड्रोजन, H⁻ आयन के रूप में माना जाता है।

उदाहरण: NaH, CaH₂

2. सहसंयोजक हाइड्राइड

इनमें हाइड्रोजन और दूसरे तत्व के बीच सहसंयोजक बंध होता है।

उदाहरण: CH₄, NH₃, H₂O

3. धात्विक हाइड्राइड

कई संक्रमण धातुएँ हाइड्रोजन को अपनी धात्विक संरचना में समाहित कर सकती हैं। ऐसे पदार्थों को धात्विक हाइड्राइड कहा जाता है।

उदाहरण: पैलेडियम में हाइड्रोजन का अवशोषण।

9.11 हाइड्रोजन बंध (Hydrogen Bonding)

जब हाइड्रोजन किसी अत्यधिक विद्युतऋणात्मक परमाणु, जैसे N, O या F से जुड़ा हो, तो वह दूसरे उपयुक्त परमाणु के साथ आकर्षण उत्पन्न कर सकता है। इसे हाइड्रोजन बंध कहते हैं।

उदाहरण: पानी (H₂O), अमोनिया (NH₃) और हाइड्रोजन फ्लोराइड (HF)।

हाइड्रोजन बंध पानी के अपेक्षाकृत अधिक क्वथनांक जैसे कई गुणों को समझाने में मदद करता है।

9.12 हाइड्रोजन का उपयोग

  • अमोनिया के औद्योगिक निर्माण में।
  • पेट्रोलियम उद्योग में कुछ हाइड्रोकार्बनों के प्रसंस्करण में।
  • ईंधन सेल में विद्युत ऊर्जा उत्पन्न करने में।
  • कुछ धातु ऑक्साइडों के अपचयन में।
  • रासायनिक उद्योग में विभिन्न पदार्थों के निर्माण में।
  • कुछ अंतरिक्ष प्रणोदन प्रणालियों में तरल हाइड्रोजन का उपयोग होता है।

9.13 हाइड्रोजन ऊर्जा और ईंधन सेल

हाइड्रोजन को ऊर्जा वाहक के रूप में उपयोग किया जा सकता है। ईंधन सेल में हाइड्रोजन और ऑक्सीजन की विद्युत-रासायनिक अभिक्रिया से बिजली और पानी बन सकते हैं।

कुल अभिक्रिया:

2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O

  • ईंधन सेल में ऊर्जा सीधे विद्युत ऊर्जा के रूप में प्राप्त की जा सकती है।
  • उपयोग के स्थान पर पानी बनना इसका एक लाभ है।
  • हाइड्रोजन का कुल पर्यावरणीय प्रभाव इस बात पर निर्भर करता है कि उसे कैसे बनाया गया और कैसे पहुँचाया गया।

9.14 महत्त्वपूर्ण रासायनिक समीकरण

  • पानी का निर्माण: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
  • हाइड्रोजन क्लोराइड का निर्माण: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl
  • अमोनिया का निर्माण: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃
  • जिंक और हाइड्रोक्लोरिक अम्ल: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂
  • कॉपर ऑक्साइड का अपचयन: CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O
  • पानी का विद्युत अपघटन: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂
  • हाइड्रोजन पेरॉक्साइड का विघटन: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂
  • मीथेन की स्टीम रिफॉर्मिंग: CH₄ + H₂O → CO + 3H₂

9.15 परीक्षा के लिए महत्त्वपूर्ण प्रश्न

  1. हाइड्रोजन का परमाणु क्रमांक और इलेक्ट्रॉनिक विन्यास लिखिए।
  2. हाइड्रोजन के तीन समस्थानिकों के नाम और प्रतीक लिखिए।
  3. प्रोटियम, ड्यूटेरियम और ट्रिटियम में अंतर बताइए।
  4. हाइड्रोजन के चार भौतिक गुण लिखिए।
  5. हाइड्रोजन की प्रयोगशाला और औद्योगिक निर्माण विधियों का वर्णन कीजिए।
  6. हाइड्राइड क्या हैं? इनके प्रमुख प्रकार लिखिए।
  7. भारी पानी क्या है? इसके उपयोग लिखिए।
  8. हाइड्रोजन पेरॉक्साइड का सूत्र और एक रासायनिक गुण लिखिए।
  9. हाइड्रोजन बंध क्या है? उदाहरण दीजिए।
  10. हाइड्रोजन के पाँच उपयोग लिखिए।

9.16 बहुविकल्पीय प्रश्न (MCQ)

प्रश्न 1: हाइड्रोजन का परमाणु क्रमांक कितना है?

(A) 0

(B) 1

(C) 2

(D) 8

उत्तर: (B) 1

प्रश्न 2: भारी पानी का सूत्र क्या है?

(A) H₂O

(B) H₂O₂

(C) D₂O

(D) HO₂

उत्तर: (C) D₂O

प्रश्न 3: हाइड्रोजन के किस समस्थानिक में दो न्यूट्रॉन होते हैं?

(A) प्रोटियम

(B) ड्यूटेरियम

(C) ट्रिटियम

(D) इनमें से कोई नहीं

उत्तर: (C) ट्रिटियम

प्रश्न 4: अमोनिया का रासायनिक सूत्र क्या है?

(A) NH₃

(B) NO₂

(C) N₂O

(D) HNO₃

उत्तर: (A) NH₃

प्रश्न 5: हाइड्रोजन पेरॉक्साइड का सूत्र क्या है?

(A) H₂O

(B) H₂O₂

(C) HO₂

(D) H₃O

उत्तर: (B) H₂O₂

प्रश्न 6: सामान्य हाइड्रोजन अणु का सूत्र क्या है?

(A) H

(B) H₂

(C) H₃

(D) H⁺

उत्तर: (B) H₂

9.17 अध्याय का सारांश

  • हाइड्रोजन का प्रतीक H और परमाणु क्रमांक 1 है।
  • हाइड्रोजन के तीन प्रमुख समस्थानिक प्रोटियम, ड्यूटेरियम और ट्रिटियम हैं।
  • सामान्य परिस्थितियों में हाइड्रोजन द्विपरमाणुक गैस H₂ के रूप में पाई जाती है।
  • हाइड्रोजन ऑक्सीजन के साथ अभिक्रिया करके पानी बनाती है।
  • हाइड्राइड आयनिक, सहसंयोजक या धात्विक प्रकार के हो सकते हैं।
  • भारी पानी का सूत्र D₂O है।
  • हाइड्रोजन पेरॉक्साइड का सूत्र H₂O₂ है।
  • हाइड्रोजन का उपयोग अमोनिया निर्माण, ईंधन सेल और कई औद्योगिक प्रक्रियाओं में किया जाता है।

Class 11 Chemistry - English Medium

Chapter 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

1.1 Introduction to Chemistry

Chemistry: Chemistry is the branch of science that deals with the study of the composition, structure, properties and transformations of matter.

Chemistry plays an important role in our daily life. It is involved in medicines, food, agriculture, clothing, fuels, cosmetics and many industrial processes.

Importance of Chemistry:

  • It helps us understand the composition and properties of substances.
  • It is used in the manufacturing of medicines and vaccines.
  • It helps in the production of fertilizers and pesticides.
  • It plays an important role in environmental protection.
  • It is useful in developing new materials and technologies.

1.2 Matter and Its Classification

Matter: Anything that has mass and occupies space is called matter.

Examples: Air, water, wood, iron, oxygen and carbon dioxide.

Classification of Matter:

Matter can be classified into two main categories:

  1. Physical Classification
  2. Chemical Classification

1.3 Physical Classification of Matter

On the basis of physical state, matter is classified into three main states:

1. Solid: A solid has a definite shape and definite volume. Its particles are closely packed.

Examples: Iron, wood, stone and ice.

2. Liquid: A liquid has a definite volume but no definite shape. It takes the shape of its container.

Examples: Water, milk and oil.

3. Gas: A gas has neither a definite shape nor a definite volume. It fills the entire available space.

Examples: Oxygen, hydrogen and nitrogen.

1.4 Chemical Classification of Matter

On the basis of chemical composition, matter is divided into two main categories:

1. Pure Substances: A pure substance consists of only one type of chemical substance and has a fixed composition.

Pure substances are divided into:

  • Elements: Substances that cannot be broken down into simpler substances by ordinary chemical methods.
  • Compounds: Substances formed when two or more elements combine chemically in a fixed proportion.

Examples of Elements: Hydrogen (H), Oxygen (O), Iron (Fe), Copper (Cu).

Examples of Compounds: Water (H₂O), Carbon dioxide (CO₂), Sodium chloride (NaCl).

2. Mixtures: A mixture is formed when two or more substances are mixed physically in any proportion.

Mixtures are of two types:

  • Homogeneous Mixture: A mixture having uniform composition throughout.
  • Heterogeneous Mixture: A mixture having non-uniform composition throughout.

Examples:

  • Homogeneous: Salt solution, sugar solution and air.
  • Heterogeneous: Sand and water, oil and water.

1.5 Properties of Matter

Properties of matter are broadly classified into two categories:

1. Physical Properties: Properties that can be observed or measured without changing the chemical identity of a substance.

Examples: Colour, density, melting point, boiling point and temperature.

2. Chemical Properties: Properties that describe the ability of a substance to undergo chemical changes and form new substances.

Examples: Burning, rusting, oxidation and reaction with acids.

1.6 Measurement in Chemistry

Measurement is the process of determining the magnitude of a physical quantity using a suitable standard unit.

Every measurement consists of two parts:

  • A numerical value.
  • A unit.

Example: 25 kg, where 25 is the numerical value and kg is the unit.

1.7 International System of Units (SI)

The International System of Units (SI) is a globally accepted system of measurement.

Seven Fundamental SI Units:

Physical Quantity SI Unit Symbol
Length Metre m
Mass Kilogram kg
Time Second s
Electric Current Ampere A
Temperature Kelvin K
Amount of Substance Mole mol
Luminous Intensity Candela cd

1.8 Scientific Notation

Scientific notation is a method of expressing very large or very small numbers in a convenient form.

It is generally written as:

N = a × 10ⁿ

Where:

  • a is a number greater than or equal to 1 and less than 10.
  • n is an integer.

Examples:

  • 300000 = 3 × 10⁵
  • 45000 = 4.5 × 10⁴
  • 0.00025 = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴
  • 0.0000006 = 6 × 10⁻⁷

1.9 Significant Figures

Significant Figures: The meaningful digits in a measured quantity, including all certain digits and the first uncertain digit, are called significant figures.

Rules for Significant Figures:

  1. All non-zero digits are significant.
  2. Zeros between two non-zero digits are significant.
  3. Leading zeros are not significant.
  4. Trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant.
  5. Trailing zeros in a whole number without a decimal point may be ambiguous.

Examples:

  • 245 has 3 significant figures.
  • 2.05 has 3 significant figures.
  • 0.0045 has 2 significant figures.
  • 2.500 has 4 significant figures.

1.10 Accuracy and Precision

Accuracy: Accuracy refers to how close a measured value is to the true or accepted value.

Precision: Precision refers to how close repeated measurements are to one another.

A measurement can be precise without being accurate.

1.11 Laws of Chemical Combination

Chemical combination takes place according to certain laws. These laws explain how elements and compounds combine during chemical reactions.

1. Law of Conservation of Mass

Statement: Matter can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. The total mass of reactants is equal to the total mass of products.

Example:

2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O

The total mass remains conserved during the reaction in a closed system.

2. Law of Definite Proportions

Statement: A pure chemical compound always contains the same elements combined in the same fixed proportion by mass, irrespective of its source or method of preparation.

Example: Water always contains hydrogen and oxygen in a mass ratio of 1:8.

3. Law of Multiple Proportions

Statement: When two elements combine to form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other element are in a simple whole-number ratio.

Example: Carbon forms two common oxides: CO and CO₂.

For a fixed mass of carbon, the masses of oxygen combining with it are in the ratio 1:2.

4. Gay-Lussac's Law of Gaseous Volumes

Statement: When gases react, their volumes and the volumes of gaseous products bear a simple whole-number ratio, provided all volumes are measured at the same temperature and pressure.

Example:

2 volumes of hydrogen + 1 volume of oxygen → 2 volumes of water vapour.

5. Avogadro's Law

Statement: Equal volumes of all gases, at the same temperature and pressure, contain equal numbers of molecules.

V ∝ n

At constant temperature and pressure, the volume of a gas is directly proportional to the number of moles.

1.12 Dalton's Atomic Theory

John Dalton proposed his atomic theory in the early nineteenth century to explain the laws of chemical combination.

Main Postulates:

  • All matter is made up of extremely small particles called atoms.
  • Atoms of the same element have the same chemical identity.
  • Atoms of different elements have different chemical identities.
  • Atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios to form compounds.
  • In ordinary chemical reactions, atoms are rearranged but are not created or destroyed.

Note: Modern discoveries have shown that atoms contain subatomic particles and that atoms of the same element can have different masses due to isotopes.

1.13 Atomic Mass

Atomic Mass: Atomic mass is the mass of an atom expressed in unified atomic mass units (u).

One unified atomic mass unit is defined as one-twelfth of the mass of one carbon-12 atom.

1 u = 1/12 × Mass of one carbon-12 atom

Examples:

  • Hydrogen: approximately 1.008 u.
  • Carbon: approximately 12.011 u.
  • Oxygen: approximately 15.999 u.

1.14 Molecular Mass

Molecular Mass: The sum of the atomic masses of all atoms present in one molecule is called its molecular mass.

Example: Water (H₂O)

Molecular mass = 2 × Atomic mass of H + Atomic mass of O

= 2 × 1 + 16 = 18 u

Example: Carbon dioxide (CO₂)

= 12 + 2 × 16 = 44 u

1.15 Formula Mass

Formula Mass: The sum of the atomic masses of all atoms represented in the formula unit of an ionic compound is called formula mass.

Example: Sodium Chloride (NaCl)

Formula mass = 23 + 35.5 = 58.5 u

Since ionic compounds generally form extended crystal lattices rather than separate molecules, the term formula mass is used instead of molecular mass.

1.16 Mole Concept

Mole: A mole is the amount of substance that contains exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ elementary entities.

This number is called the Avogadro constant.

Nₐ = 6.02214076 × 10²³ mol⁻¹

One mole may contain:

  • Atoms.
  • Molecules.
  • Ions.
  • Electrons.
  • Other specified elementary entities.

Example: One mole of water contains 6.02214076 × 10²³ water molecules.

1.17 Molar Mass

Molar Mass: The mass of one mole of a substance is called its molar mass.

Its SI unit is kg mol⁻¹, while g mol⁻¹ is commonly used in chemistry.

Example:

Molar mass of water = 18 g mol⁻¹.

Moles (n) = Given Mass / Molar Mass

n = m / M

1.18 Relationship Between Moles, Mass and Particles

Number of particles:

N = n × Nₐ

Number of moles:

n = N / Nₐ

Mass:

m = n × M

Where:

  • n = Number of moles.
  • N = Number of particles.
  • Nₐ = Avogadro constant.
  • m = Given mass.
  • M = Molar mass.

1.19 Percentage Composition

Percentage Composition: The percentage by mass of each element present in a compound is called percentage composition.

Percentage of an element = (Mass of element in one mole of compound / Molar mass of compound) × 100

Example: Percentage of hydrogen in water

Molar mass of H₂O = 18 g mol⁻¹.

Mass of hydrogen = 2 g.

Percentage of H = (2 / 18) × 100

= 11.11%

Percentage of oxygen = 88.89%.

1.20 Empirical Formula

Empirical Formula: The formula that represents the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of different elements in a compound is called its empirical formula.

Examples:

  • Glucose molecular formula: C₆H₁₂O₆.
  • Glucose empirical formula: CH₂O.
  • Benzene molecular formula: C₆H₆.
  • Benzene empirical formula: CH.

1.21 Molecular Formula

Molecular Formula: The formula that shows the actual number of atoms of each element present in one molecule of a substance is called its molecular formula.

Relationship:

Molecular Formula = (Empirical Formula)ₙ

n = Molecular Mass / Empirical Formula Mass

1.22 Stoichiometry

Stoichiometry: Stoichiometry is the quantitative study of reactants and products involved in a chemical reaction.

It is based on a balanced chemical equation.

Example:

2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O

This equation tells us that:

  • 2 moles of hydrogen react with 1 mole of oxygen.
  • 2 moles of water are formed.
  • The mole ratio is 2:1:2.

1.23 Limiting Reagent

Limiting Reagent: The reactant that is completely consumed first in a chemical reaction and limits the amount of product formed is called the limiting reagent.

Example:

2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O

If 2 moles of H₂ react with 2 moles of O₂, hydrogen is the limiting reagent because only 1 mole of oxygen is required for 2 moles of hydrogen.

1.24 Concentration of Solutions

Solution: A homogeneous mixture of two or more substances is called a solution.

Solute: The substance that is dissolved.

Solvent: The substance in which the solute is dissolved.

1.25 Mass Percentage

Mass percentage expresses the mass of solute present in 100 parts by mass of solution.

Mass % = (Mass of Solute / Mass of Solution) × 100

1.26 Volume Percentage

Volume percentage expresses the volume of solute present in 100 parts by volume of solution.

Volume % = (Volume of Solute / Volume of Solution) × 100

1.27 Parts Per Million (ppm)

Parts per million is used to express very low concentrations of a substance.

ppm = (Mass of solute / Mass of solution) × 10⁶

For dilute aqueous solutions, 1 ppm is approximately equal to 1 mg/L when the solution density is close to 1 kg/L.

1.28 Mole Fraction

Mole Fraction: The ratio of the number of moles of one component to the total number of moles of all components in a solution is called mole fraction.

Xₐ = nₐ / (nₐ + nᵦ)

Important Property:

Xₐ + Xᵦ = 1

1.29 Molarity

Molarity: The number of moles of solute dissolved per litre of solution is called molarity.

Molarity = Moles of Solute / Volume of Solution in Litres

Unit: mol L⁻¹ or M.

1.30 Molality

Molality: The number of moles of solute dissolved per kilogram of solvent is called molality.

Molality = Moles of Solute / Mass of Solvent in kg

Unit: mol kg⁻¹.

1.31 Important Difference Between Molarity and Molality

Molarity Molality
Moles per litre of solution. Moles per kilogram of solvent.
Unit: mol L⁻¹. Unit: mol kg⁻¹.
Depends on solution volume. Depends on solvent mass.
Changes with temperature. Generally independent of temperature.

1.32 Solved Numerical Problems

Example 1: Calculate the number of moles in 36 g of water.

Given:

  • Mass = 36 g
  • Molar mass of water = 18 g mol⁻¹

Formula:

n = m / M

Solution:

n = 36 / 18 = 2 mol

Answer: 2 moles.

Example 2: Calculate the number of molecules in 2 moles of water.

Formula:

N = n × Nₐ

Solution:

N = 2 × 6.022 × 10²³

N = 1.2044 × 10²⁴ molecules

Answer: 1.2044 × 10²⁴ molecules.

Example 3: Calculate the molarity of a solution containing 0.5 mole of NaCl in 2 litres of solution.

Formula:

M = n / V

Solution:

M = 0.5 / 2 = 0.25 mol L⁻¹

Answer: 0.25 M.

1.33 Important Chemical Formulas

  • Number of moles: n = m/M
  • Number of particles: N = n × Nₐ
  • Molar mass: M = m/n
  • Mass percentage: (Mass of solute / Mass of solution) × 100
  • Mole fraction: Xₐ = nₐ / n(total)
  • Molarity: M = n/V(L)
  • Molality: m = n/Mass of solvent(kg)
  • Percentage composition: (Mass of element / Molar mass of compound) × 100
  • Empirical formula multiplier: n = Molecular mass / Empirical formula mass

1.36 Chapter Summary

  • Chemistry is the study of matter, its composition, properties and transformations.
  • Matter has mass and occupies space.
  • Matter can be classified into pure substances and mixtures.
  • The SI system contains seven fundamental units.
  • Significant figures represent meaningful digits in measurements.
  • Chemical combination follows definite laws.
  • Atoms combine in fixed ratios to form compounds.
  • One mole contains exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ specified entities.
  • Molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance.
  • Stoichiometry deals with quantitative relationships in chemical reactions.
  • Molarity and molality are important ways of expressing solution concentration.
  • The limiting reagent determines the maximum amount of product that can form.

Chapter 2: Structure of Atom

2.1 Introduction to Atomic Structure

Atom: An atom is the smallest unit of an element that retains its chemical identity. It consists of a small, dense nucleus surrounded by electrons.

An atom mainly consists of three subatomic particles:

  • Electron: A negatively charged particle.
  • Proton: A positively charged particle.
  • Neutron: A neutral particle with no electrical charge.

2.2 Discovery of Electron

J. J. Thomson discovered the electron in 1897 through experiments involving cathode rays.

Cathode Rays: Cathode rays are streams of negatively charged particles produced in a discharge tube under suitable conditions.

Properties of Cathode Rays:

  • They travel in straight lines.
  • They consist of negatively charged particles.
  • They are deflected by electric and magnetic fields.
  • Their properties are independent of the nature of the gas and electrode material.
  • They can produce fluorescence when they strike certain materials.

Properties of Electron:

  • Symbol: e⁻
  • Charge: −1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C
  • Mass: 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg
  • Relative charge: −1

2.3 Discovery of Proton

Positive rays were observed in discharge tube experiments. These rays consist of positively charged particles and are also called canal rays or anode rays.

The hydrogen nucleus was identified as the proton.

Properties of Proton:

  • Symbol: p⁺
  • Charge: +1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C
  • Mass: 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg
  • Relative charge: +1

2.4 Discovery of Neutron

James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932 by studying radiation produced when beryllium was bombarded with alpha particles.

Properties of Neutron:

  • Symbol: n⁰
  • Charge: Zero
  • Mass: 1.675 × 10⁻²⁷ kg approximately
  • Location: Inside the nucleus.

2.5 Comparison of Fundamental Particles

Particle Charge Mass (kg) Location
Electron −1 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ Outside nucleus
Proton +1 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ Inside nucleus
Neutron 0 1.675 × 10⁻²⁷ Inside nucleus

2.6 Thomson's Atomic Model

J. J. Thomson proposed an atomic model in which the atom was considered to be a positively charged sphere with negatively charged electrons embedded in it.

This model is also known as the Plum Pudding Model or Watermelon Model.

Main Features:

  • The atom was considered to be a sphere of positive charge.
  • Electrons were embedded in the positively charged sphere.
  • The total positive and negative charges were equal.
  • The atom was electrically neutral.

Limitation: Thomson's model could not explain the results of Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment.

2.7 Rutherford's Nuclear Model

Ernest Rutherford performed the famous alpha-particle scattering experiment using a thin gold foil.

Experimental Observations:

  • Most alpha particles passed through the gold foil without deflection.
  • Some alpha particles were deflected through small angles.
  • A very small number of alpha particles were deflected through large angles.
  • Very few alpha particles returned almost in the direction from which they came.

Conclusions:

  • Most of the space inside an atom is empty.
  • Almost all the mass and positive charge of an atom are concentrated in a tiny central nucleus.
  • The nucleus is extremely small compared with the size of the atom.
  • Electrons occupy the region outside the nucleus.

Limitations:

  • It could not explain the stability of atoms according to classical electromagnetic theory.
  • It could not explain the line spectrum of hydrogen.
  • It did not describe the allowed energies of electrons.

2.8 Bohr's Atomic Model

Niels Bohr proposed a model of the atom in 1913, mainly to explain the hydrogen atomic spectrum.

Main Postulates:

  • Electrons revolve around the nucleus only in certain permitted stationary orbits.
  • Each permitted orbit has a definite energy.
  • An electron does not continuously radiate energy while remaining in a stationary orbit.
  • Energy is absorbed when an electron moves to a higher energy level.
  • Energy is emitted when an electron moves to a lower energy level.

Energy Difference:

ΔE = E₂ − E₁ = hν

Where:

  • ΔE = Difference between two energy levels.
  • h = Planck's constant.
  • ν = Frequency of radiation.

2.9 Bohr's Radius

The radius of the nth orbit of a hydrogen-like species is given by:

rₙ = 0.529 × n²/Z Å

Where:

  • rₙ = Radius of the nth orbit.
  • n = Principal quantum number.
  • Z = Atomic number.
  • Å = Angstrom.

Example: Calculate the radius of the second orbit of a hydrogen atom.

Given: n = 2, Z = 1.

r₂ = 0.529 × 2² / 1

r₂ = 0.529 × 4 = 2.116 Å

Answer: 2.116 Å.

2.10 Energy of Electron in Bohr's Orbit

The energy of an electron in the nth orbit of a hydrogen-like species is:

Eₙ = −13.6 × Z²/n² eV

Where:

  • Eₙ = Energy of the electron.
  • Z = Atomic number.
  • n = Principal quantum number.
  • eV = Electron volt.

Example: Calculate the energy of an electron in the second orbit of hydrogen.

Given: Z = 1, n = 2.

E₂ = −13.6 × 1²/2²

E₂ = −13.6/4 = −3.4 eV

Answer: −3.4 eV.

2.11 Limitations of Bohr's Model

  • It successfully explains hydrogen and hydrogen-like one-electron species.
  • It cannot accurately explain the spectra of multi-electron atoms.
  • It cannot explain the fine structure of spectral lines.
  • It does not account for the wave nature of electrons.
  • It is not consistent with the modern uncertainty principle.

2.12 Electromagnetic Radiation

Electromagnetic Radiation: Energy that travels through space in the form of oscillating electric and magnetic fields is called electromagnetic radiation.

Examples: Radio waves, microwaves, infrared radiation, visible light, ultraviolet radiation, X-rays and gamma rays.

Important Terms:

  • Wavelength (λ): Distance between two successive points in the same phase of a wave.
  • Frequency (ν): Number of wave cycles passing a point per second.
  • Amplitude: Maximum displacement of a wave from its mean position.
  • Wave Number: Number of waves per unit length.

c = νλ

ν = c/λ

Wave Number = 1/λ

Where c is the speed of light in vacuum, approximately 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s.

2.13 Electromagnetic Spectrum

The complete range of electromagnetic radiation arranged according to wavelength or frequency is called the electromagnetic spectrum.

Order of Electromagnetic Spectrum:

  1. Radio Waves
  2. Microwaves
  3. Infrared Radiation
  4. Visible Light
  5. Ultraviolet Radiation
  6. X-rays
  7. Gamma Rays

Important Facts:

  • Radio waves have relatively long wavelengths.
  • Gamma rays have extremely short wavelengths.
  • Frequency increases from radio waves to gamma rays.
  • Photon energy also increases with frequency.

2.14 Planck's Quantum Theory

Max Planck proposed that energy is emitted or absorbed by matter in discrete packets called quanta.

The energy of one quantum is directly proportional to the frequency of radiation.

E = hν

Where:

  • E = Energy of one quantum.
  • h = Planck's constant = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
  • ν = Frequency of radiation.

Important Point: Higher-frequency radiation has higher energy per photon.

2.15 Photoelectric Effect

Photoelectric Effect: The emission of electrons from a metal surface when electromagnetic radiation of sufficiently high frequency falls on it is called the photoelectric effect.

The emitted electrons are called photoelectrons.

Einstein's Photoelectric Equation:

hν = Φ + K(max)

Where:

  • hν = Energy of incident photon.
  • Φ = Work function of the metal.
  • K(max) = Maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons.

Threshold Frequency: The minimum frequency of incident radiation required to produce photoelectric emission is called threshold frequency.

Φ = hν₀

Where ν₀ is the threshold frequency.

2.16 Atomic Spectrum

Atomic Spectrum: The spectrum produced when atoms absorb or emit electromagnetic radiation at particular frequencies is called an atomic spectrum.

Atomic spectra are generally classified into two types:

  • Emission Spectrum: Produced when excited atoms release energy as radiation.
  • Absorption Spectrum: Produced when atoms absorb radiation of specific frequencies.

2.17 Hydrogen Line Spectrum

When an electron in a hydrogen atom moves from a higher energy level to a lower energy level, it emits radiation of a definite frequency.

The resulting spectrum contains separate lines rather than a continuous range of wavelengths.

Important Spectral Series:

Series Final Energy Level Spectral Region
Lyman n = 1 Ultraviolet
Balmer n = 2 Visible and near ultraviolet
Paschen n = 3 Infrared
Brackett n = 4 Infrared
Pfund n = 5 Infrared

Rydberg Equation:

1/λ = R(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²)

For emission, n₂ is greater than n₁.

Where R is the Rydberg constant, approximately 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹ for hydrogen.

2.18 Dual Nature of Matter

According to the wave-particle duality principle, microscopic particles such as electrons show both particle-like and wave-like properties.

Louis de Broglie proposed that every moving material particle is associated with a wave.

De Broglie Equation:

λ = h/p

For a non-relativistic particle:

λ = h/mv

Where:

  • λ = De Broglie wavelength.
  • h = Planck's constant.
  • p = Momentum.
  • m = Mass of particle.
  • v = Velocity of particle.

2.19 Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle

Statement: It is impossible to determine simultaneously the exact position and exact momentum of a microscopic particle with unlimited precision.

Δx × Δp ≥ h/4π

Where:

  • Δx = Uncertainty in position.
  • Δp = Uncertainty in momentum.
  • h = Planck's constant.

This principle is fundamental to quantum mechanics and explains why electrons cannot be described as moving along perfectly defined classical paths.

2.20 Quantum Mechanical Model of Atom

The quantum mechanical model describes the behaviour of electrons using wave functions and probability distributions.

Orbital: An orbital is a region in space around the nucleus where the probability of finding an electron is high.

The wave function is represented by the symbol ψ.

The square of the wave function, |ψ|², represents probability density.

Important Features:

  • Electrons do not move in fixed circular paths.
  • Electron behaviour is described using quantum mechanics.
  • Each orbital has a definite energy and shape.
  • An orbital can accommodate a maximum of two electrons with opposite spins.

2.21 Quantum Numbers

Four quantum numbers are used to describe the state of an electron in an atom.

1. Principal Quantum Number (n)

It describes the main energy level and is related to the size and energy of an orbital.

Allowed values: n = 1, 2, 3, 4, ...

2. Azimuthal Quantum Number (l)

It describes the subshell and is related to the shape of the orbital.

Allowed values: l = 0 to n − 1.

  • l = 0 → s subshell.
  • l = 1 → p subshell.
  • l = 2 → d subshell.
  • l = 3 → f subshell.

3. Magnetic Quantum Number (mₗ)

It describes the orientation of an orbital in space.

Allowed values: −l to +l, including zero.

4. Spin Quantum Number (mₛ)

It describes the spin state of an electron.

Allowed values:

mₛ = +1/2 or −1/2

2.22 Number of Orbitals in Subshells

The number of orbitals in a subshell is given by:

Number of Orbitals = 2l + 1

Subshell l Value Number of Orbitals Maximum Electrons
s 0 1 2
p 1 3 6
d 2 5 10
f 3 7 14

2.23 Shapes of Atomic Orbitals

s-Orbitals: Spherical in shape.

p-Orbitals: Generally dumbbell-shaped and have three orientations: pₓ, pᵧ and p𝓏.

d-Orbitals: Five orbitals with different orientations and shapes. Most are commonly represented by four lobes.

f-Orbitals: Seven orbitals with more complicated shapes.

2.24 Maximum Number of Electrons in a Shell

The maximum number of electrons that can be accommodated in a shell is given by:

Maximum Electrons = 2n²

Examples:

  • K shell (n = 1): 2 × 1² = 2 electrons.
  • L shell (n = 2): 2 × 2² = 8 electrons.
  • M shell (n = 3): 2 × 3² = 18 electrons.
  • N shell (n = 4): 2 × 4² = 32 electrons.

2.25 Aufbau Principle

Aufbau Principle: Electrons are filled into orbitals in the order of increasing orbital energy.

The (n + l) rule helps determine the relative energies of orbitals.

  • The orbital with lower (n + l) value has lower energy.
  • If two orbitals have the same (n + l) value, the orbital with lower n has lower energy.

Common Filling Order:

1s → 2s → 2p → 3s → 3p → 4s → 3d → 4p → 5s → 4d → 5p → 6s → 4f → 5d → 6p

2.26 Pauli Exclusion Principle

Statement: No two electrons in an atom can have the same set of all four quantum numbers.

Therefore, one orbital can contain a maximum of two electrons with opposite spins.

2.27 Hund's Rule of Maximum Multiplicity

Statement: Electrons occupy degenerate orbitals singly with parallel spins before pairing begins.

Degenerate orbitals are orbitals having the same energy.

Example: In the 2p³ configuration, the three electrons occupy three different p orbitals singly before pairing.

2.28 Electronic Configuration

Electronic Configuration: The distribution of electrons among different shells, subshells and orbitals of an atom is called electronic configuration.

Examples:

  • Hydrogen (Z = 1): 1s¹
  • Helium (Z = 2): 1s²
  • Lithium (Z = 3): 1s² 2s¹
  • Carbon (Z = 6): 1s² 2s² 2p²
  • Nitrogen (Z = 7): 1s² 2s² 2p³
  • Oxygen (Z = 8): 1s² 2s² 2p⁴
  • Neon (Z = 10): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶
  • Sodium (Z = 11): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹
  • Magnesium (Z = 12): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s²
  • Chlorine (Z = 17): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵
  • Calcium (Z = 20): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s²

2.29 Exceptional Electronic Configurations

Some elements have electronic configurations that differ from the simple predicted filling order. This is associated with the relative stability of certain electronic arrangements.

Chromium (Z = 24):

[Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹

Copper (Z = 29):

[Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹

These are important examples of exceptional configurations in the first transition series.

2.30 Important Formulas of This Chapter

  • Speed of light: c = νλ
  • Photon energy: E = hν
  • Photon energy in terms of wavelength: E = hc/λ
  • De Broglie wavelength: λ = h/mv
  • Uncertainty principle: ΔxΔp ≥ h/4π
  • Bohr radius: rₙ = 0.529n²/Z Å
  • Bohr energy: Eₙ = −13.6Z²/n² eV
  • Maximum electrons in a shell: 2n²
  • Number of orbitals in a subshell: 2l + 1
  • Number of orbitals in a shell: n²
  • Rydberg equation: 1/λ = R(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²)

2.31 Solved Numerical Problems

Example 1: Calculate the frequency of radiation having a wavelength of 600 nm.

Given:

  • λ = 600 nm = 600 × 10⁻⁹ m
  • c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s

Formula:

ν = c/λ

Solution:

ν = (3 × 10⁸)/(600 × 10⁻⁹)

ν = 5 × 10¹⁴ Hz

Answer: 5 × 10¹⁴ Hz.

Example 2: Calculate the energy of a photon having a frequency of 5 × 10¹⁴ Hz.

Given:

  • h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s
  • ν = 5 × 10¹⁴ Hz

Formula:

E = hν

Solution:

E = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ × 5 × 10¹⁴

E = 3.313 × 10⁻¹⁹ J

Answer: 3.313 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

Example 3: Find the number of orbitals in the third shell.

Given: n = 3.

Formula:

Number of orbitals = n²

Solution:

= 3² = 9

Answer: 9 orbitals.

Example 4: Find the maximum number of electrons in the fourth shell.

Given: n = 4.

Maximum electrons = 2n²

= 2 × 4² = 32

Answer: 32 electrons.

2.34 Chapter Summary

  • An atom consists of electrons, protons and neutrons.
  • J. J. Thomson discovered the electron.
  • James Chadwick discovered the neutron.
  • Rutherford proposed the nuclear model of the atom.
  • Bohr explained the hydrogen spectrum using quantised energy levels.
  • Planck introduced the quantum theory of energy.
  • Einstein explained the photoelectric effect using photons.
  • De Broglie proposed the wave nature of moving particles.
  • Heisenberg formulated the uncertainty principle.

Chapter 3: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

3.1 Introduction

Classification of Elements: The process of arranging elements into groups on the basis of their similar properties is called classification of elements.

There are more than 100 known elements. Studying each element separately is difficult. Therefore, scientists classified elements to make their study easier and systematic.

Periodic Properties: The properties of elements that show a regular variation when elements are arranged in increasing order of atomic number are called periodic properties.

3.2 Need for Classification of Elements

Classification of elements is important for the following reasons:

  1. It makes the study of elements easier.
  2. It helps us understand the similarities between elements.
  3. It helps predict the properties of unknown elements.
  4. It provides a systematic arrangement of elements.
  5. It helps us understand the relationship between atomic structure and properties.

3.3 Early Attempts at Classification

Several scientists tried to classify elements on the basis of their properties.

3.3.1 Dobereiner's Triads

Scientist: Johann Wolfgang Dobereiner

In 1829, Dobereiner arranged some elements into groups of three elements. These groups were called Dobereiner's triads.

Dobereiner's Law of Triads: The atomic mass of the middle element of a triad was approximately equal to the average of the atomic masses of the other two elements.

Example: Lithium, Sodium and Potassium.

Element Symbol Atomic Mass (Approx.)
Lithium Li 7
Sodium Na 23
Potassium K 39

Calculation:

Average atomic mass = (7 + 39) / 2 = 23

Therefore, the atomic mass of sodium is approximately equal to the average of lithium and potassium.

Limitations:

  • Only a few elements could be arranged into triads.
  • Most known elements did not follow this rule.

3.3.2 Newlands' Law of Octaves

Scientist: John Newlands

In 1865, Newlands arranged elements in increasing order of their atomic masses.

Law of Octaves: When elements are arranged in increasing order of atomic masses, every eighth element has properties similar to the first element.

Newlands compared this arrangement with the musical notes, in which the eighth note resembles the first note.

Example: Lithium and Sodium showed similar properties in his arrangement.

Limitations:

  • It was applicable only up to calcium.
  • Newlands did not leave gaps for undiscovered elements.
  • Some dissimilar elements were placed together.

3.3.3 Mendeleev's Periodic Table

Scientist: Dmitri Ivanovich Mendeleev

In 1869, Mendeleev proposed a periodic table in which elements were arranged in increasing order of their atomic masses.

Mendeleev's Periodic Law: The properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic masses.

Main Features:

  • Elements were arranged mainly in increasing order of atomic masses.
  • Elements with similar properties were placed in the same groups.
  • Gaps were left for undiscovered elements.
  • Mendeleev predicted the properties of some undiscovered elements.

Achievements:

  1. He provided a systematic classification of elements.
  2. He left gaps for undiscovered elements.
  3. He correctly predicted the properties of several unknown elements.
  4. Some atomic masses were corrected on the basis of their positions in the table.

Limitations:

  • The position of hydrogen was uncertain.
  • Isotopes could not be given separate positions based on atomic mass.
  • Some elements did not follow the increasing order of atomic masses.

3.4 Modern Periodic Law

Scientist: Henry Moseley

In 1913, Henry Moseley showed that atomic number is a more fundamental property than atomic mass for classifying elements.

Modern Periodic Law: The physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.

Atomic Number (Z): The number of protons present in the nucleus of an atom is called its atomic number.

For a neutral atom:

Atomic Number = Number of Protons = Number of Electrons

3.5 Modern Periodic Table

The modern periodic table is based on the increasing order of atomic numbers.

Important Features:

  • It contains 18 vertical columns called groups.
  • It contains 7 horizontal rows called periods.
  • Elements are arranged in increasing order of atomic number.
  • Elements with similar valence-shell electronic configurations generally show similar chemical properties.

3.6 Groups and Periods

Groups: The vertical columns in the periodic table are called groups.

There are 18 groups in the modern periodic table.

Periods: The horizontal rows in the periodic table are called periods.

There are 7 periods in the modern periodic table.

Period Number of Elements
1st Period2
2nd Period8
3rd Period8
4th Period18
5th Period18
6th Period32
7th PeriodIncomplete

3.7 Blocks of the Periodic Table

The modern periodic table is divided into four blocks on the basis of the subshell into which the last electron enters.

Block Last Electron Enters Groups
s-block s-subshell 1 and 2
p-block p-subshell 13 to 18
d-block d-subshell 3 to 12
f-block f-subshell Lanthanides and Actinides

3.8 Names of Important Groups

Group Name
1Alkali Metals (except Hydrogen)
2Alkaline Earth Metals
13Boron Family
14Carbon Family
15Nitrogen Family
16Oxygen Family (Chalcogens)
17Halogens
18Noble Gases

3.9 Electronic Configuration and Position

The position of an element in the periodic table can be determined from its electronic configuration.

Rules:

  1. The period number is generally equal to the highest principal quantum number (n) in the ground-state electronic configuration.
  2. For s- and p-block elements, the group can generally be determined from the number of valence electrons.
  3. For d-block elements, the group number is generally the total number of electrons in the (n-1)d and ns subshells.

Example 1: Sodium (Na)

Atomic Number = 11

Electronic Configuration = 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹

Highest shell number = 3, so it belongs to Period 3.

One valence electron, so it belongs to Group 1.

Example 2: Chlorine (Cl)

Atomic Number = 17

Electronic Configuration = 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵

Highest shell number = 3, so it belongs to Period 3.

Seven valence electrons, so it belongs to Group 17.

3.10 Periodic Trends

When we move across a period or down a group, the properties of elements change in a regular pattern. These changes are called periodic trends.

3.11 Atomic Radius

Atomic Radius: The distance from the centre of the nucleus to the outermost shell of an atom is described as its atomic radius.

Trend Across a Period:

Atomic radius generally decreases from left to right across a period.

Reason: Nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same principal shell. The stronger attraction pulls electrons closer to the nucleus.

Trend Down a Group:

Atomic radius generally increases from top to bottom in a group.

Reason: A new electron shell is added at each step down the group.

3.12 Ionic Radius

Ionic Radius: The effective size of an ion is called its ionic radius.

Cation: A positively charged ion formed by the loss of electrons.

Example: Na⁺, Mg²⁺

Anion: A negatively charged ion formed by the gain of electrons.

Example: Cl⁻, O²⁻

Important Rules:

  • A cation is generally smaller than its parent atom.
  • An anion is generally larger than its parent atom.
  • For an isoelectronic series, radius decreases as nuclear charge increases.

Example: O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺ and Mg²⁺ have 10 electrons each.

Their sizes follow:

O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺

3.13 Ionisation Enthalpy

Ionisation Enthalpy: The enthalpy required to remove the most loosely bound electron from an isolated gaseous atom is called ionisation enthalpy.

First Ionisation Enthalpy:

X(g) → X⁺(g) + e⁻

Trend Across a Period:

Ionisation enthalpy generally increases from left to right.

Trend Down a Group:

Ionisation enthalpy generally decreases from top to bottom.

Reason: Across a period, effective nuclear charge generally increases. Down a group, atomic size and shielding generally increase.

Important Exceptions:

  • Be has higher first ionisation enthalpy than B.
  • N has higher first ionisation enthalpy than O.

3.14 Electron Gain Enthalpy

Electron Gain Enthalpy: The enthalpy change that occurs when an isolated gaseous atom accepts an electron to form a negative ion is called electron gain enthalpy.

General Reaction:

X(g) + e⁻ → X⁻(g)

Trend Across a Period:

Electron gain enthalpy generally becomes more negative across a period, although there are exceptions.

Trend Down a Group:

It generally becomes less negative down a group, but the trend is not perfectly regular.

Important Exceptions:

  • Chlorine has a more negative electron gain enthalpy than fluorine.
  • Group 18 elements generally have positive or nearly zero electron gain enthalpy.
  • Group 2 and Group 15 elements have relatively less negative values than expected.

3.15 Electronegativity

Electronegativity: The tendency of an atom in a chemical bond to attract the shared pair of electrons towards itself is called electronegativity.

Trend Across a Period: Electronegativity generally increases from left to right.

Trend Down a Group: Electronegativity generally decreases from top to bottom.

Important Fact: Fluorine is the most electronegative element.

3.16 Valency

Valency: The combining capacity of an element is called its valency.

For many main-group elements, valency can be related to the number of electrons in the valence shell.

Example:

  • Sodium (Na) = 1
  • Magnesium (Mg) = 2
  • Aluminium (Al) = 3
  • Carbon (C) = 4
  • Oxygen (O) = 2
  • Chlorine (Cl) = 1

3.17 Metallic Character

Metallic Character: The tendency of an element to lose electrons and form positive ions is called metallic character.

Trend Across a Period: Metallic character generally decreases from left to right.

Trend Down a Group: Metallic character generally increases from top to bottom.

3.18 Non-Metallic Character

Non-Metallic Character: The tendency of an element to accept electrons or attract electrons in a bond is associated with its non-metallic character.

Trend Across a Period: Non-metallic character generally increases from left to right.

Trend Down a Group: Non-metallic character generally decreases from top to bottom.

3.19 Chemical Reactivity

The chemical reactivity of elements depends on their electronic configuration and their tendency to lose, gain or share electrons.

Metals: For many metals, reactivity increases down a group because losing an electron becomes easier.

Example: Alkali metals generally become more reactive down Group 1.

Non-Metals: For halogens, reactivity generally decreases down Group 17 because the tendency to gain an electron decreases.

Example: Fluorine is more reactive than chlorine, bromine and iodine.

3.20 Shielding Effect

Shielding Effect: The decrease in the attraction between the nucleus and the outer electrons due to the presence of inner-shell electrons is called the shielding effect.

As the number of inner electron shells increases, shielding generally increases.

3.21 Effective Nuclear Charge

Effective Nuclear Charge (Zeff): The net positive charge experienced by an electron in a multi-electron atom is called effective nuclear charge.

A simplified relation is:

Zeff ≈ Z − S

Where:

  • Z = Actual nuclear charge (atomic number)
  • S = Shielding constant

Across a period, effective nuclear charge generally increases.

3.22 Oxidation State

Oxidation State: The apparent charge assigned to an atom in a compound according to certain rules is called its oxidation state.

Examples:

  • Na in NaCl = +1
  • Mg in MgO = +2
  • O in most compounds = −2
  • Cl in NaCl = −1

3.23 Periodic Trends: Quick Revision Table

Property Across a Period (→) Down a Group (↓)
Atomic Radius Generally decreases Generally increases
Ionisation Enthalpy Generally increases Generally decreases
Electronegativity Generally increases Generally decreases
Metallic Character Generally decreases Generally increases
Non-Metallic Character Generally increases Generally decreases

3.24 Solved Examples

Example 1: Find the period and group of an element with atomic number 12.

Solution:

Atomic number = 12

Electronic configuration = 2, 8, 2

Number of occupied shells = 3

Valence electrons = 2

Answer: Period 3, Group 2.

Example 2: Which is larger: Na or Na⁺?

Solution: Na⁺ is formed when sodium loses one electron. Its outermost shell is removed, so the ionic radius becomes smaller.

Answer: Na is larger than Na⁺.

Example 3: Arrange the following in increasing atomic radius: Li, Na, K.

Solution: All three elements belong to Group 1. Atomic radius increases down the group.

Answer: Li < Na < K.

Example 4: Which element is more electronegative: F or Cl?

Answer: Fluorine (F) is more electronegative than chlorine (Cl).

3.25 Important Definitions for Exams

  1. Periodic Law: The properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.
  2. Atomic Radius: A measure of the size of an atom.
  3. Ionisation Enthalpy: Enthalpy required to remove an electron from an isolated gaseous atom.
  4. Electron Gain Enthalpy: Enthalpy change when an isolated gaseous atom accepts an electron.
  5. Electronegativity: The tendency of an atom in a bond to attract shared electrons.
  6. Valency: The combining capacity of an element.
  7. Shielding Effect: Reduction in nuclear attraction due to inner-shell electrons.
  8. Effective Nuclear Charge: Net positive charge experienced by an electron in an atom.

3.28 Chapter Summary

  • Elements are classified to make their study easier and systematic.
  • Dobereiner proposed the Law of Triads in 1829.
  • Newlands proposed the Law of Octaves in 1865.
  • Mendeleev arranged elements mainly in increasing order of atomic masses.
  • Henry Moseley established the importance of atomic number.
  • The modern periodic table contains 18 groups and 7 periods.
  • The periodic table has s, p, d and f blocks.
  • Atomic radius generally decreases across a period and increases down a group.
  • Ionisation enthalpy generally increases across a period and decreases down a group.
  • Fluorine is the most electronegative element.
  • Periodic properties depend on atomic number and electronic configuration.

3.29 Important Points to Remember

  • Modern Periodic Law is based on atomic number, not atomic mass.
  • There are 18 groups and 7 periods.
  • Group 1 elements are called alkali metals, except hydrogen.
  • Group 17 elements are called halogens.
  • Group 18 elements are called noble gases.
  • Fluorine is the most electronegative element.
  • Chlorine has a more negative electron gain enthalpy than fluorine.
  • Cations are generally smaller than their parent atoms.
  • Anions are generally larger than their parent atoms.

Chapter 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

4.1 Introduction

Chemical Bond: The attractive force that holds atoms or ions together in a molecule or compound is called a chemical bond.

Atoms combine with one another to achieve a more stable electronic configuration. Chemical bonding explains how atoms form molecules and compounds.

Examples: H₂, O₂, H₂O, NaCl and CO₂.

4.2 Why Do Atoms Combine?

Atoms combine to achieve a stable electronic configuration and lower energy.

Many atoms achieve stability by attaining an electronic configuration similar to that of noble gases.

Main Reasons:

  • To attain a stable electronic configuration.
  • To decrease their potential energy.
  • To form stable molecules or compounds.

4.3 Kossel-Lewis Approach

Walther Kossel and Gilbert N. Lewis explained chemical bonding on the basis of the electronic configurations of atoms.

According to the Lewis approach, atoms can achieve stable configurations by losing, gaining or sharing electrons.

4.4 Octet Rule

Octet Rule: Atoms tend to gain, lose or share electrons to achieve eight electrons in their valence shell.

Examples:

  • Na loses one electron to form Na⁺.
  • Cl gains one electron to form Cl⁻.
  • O shares electrons to form H₂O.

Important: Hydrogen and helium follow the duplet rule because their first shell can hold a maximum of two electrons.

4.5 Limitations of the Octet Rule

The octet rule does not explain the bonding in all molecules.

1. Incomplete Octet: Some atoms have fewer than eight electrons around the central atom.

Examples: BeCl₂, BF₃.

2. Odd Electron Molecules: Some molecules contain an odd number of electrons.

Examples: NO, NO₂.

3. Expanded Octet: Some central atoms have more than eight electrons in their valence shell in the Lewis representation.

Examples: PCl₅, SF₆.

4.6 Types of Chemical Bonds

The main types of chemical bonds are:

  1. Ionic Bond
  2. Covalent Bond
  3. Coordinate Bond
  4. Metallic Bond

4.7 Ionic Bond (Electrovalent Bond)

Ionic Bond: The electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions is called an ionic bond.

An ionic bond is generally formed by the transfer of electrons from one atom to another.

Example: Formation of Sodium Chloride (NaCl)

Sodium has one valence electron.

Na → Na⁺ + e⁻

Chlorine needs one electron to complete its octet.

Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻

The oppositely charged ions attract each other.

Na⁺ + Cl⁻ → NaCl

Other Examples: MgO, CaCl₂ and KBr.

4.8 Properties of Ionic Compounds

  • They are generally crystalline solids.
  • They usually have high melting and boiling points.
  • They are generally soluble in polar solvents such as water.
  • They conduct electricity in molten state or aqueous solution.
  • They generally do not conduct electricity in solid state because their ions are fixed in position.

4.9 Covalent Bond

Covalent Bond: A chemical bond formed by the sharing of one or more pairs of electrons between atoms is called a covalent bond.

Example: Formation of Hydrogen Molecule (H₂)

Each hydrogen atom has one electron. Two hydrogen atoms share one pair of electrons.

H + H → H₂

Other Examples: Cl₂, O₂, N₂, CH₄ and H₂O.

4.10 Types of Covalent Bonds

1. Single Bond: A bond formed by sharing one pair of electrons.

Example: H–H, Cl–Cl.

2. Double Bond: A bond formed by sharing two pairs of electrons.

Example: O=O, C=O.

3. Triple Bond: A bond formed by sharing three pairs of electrons.

Example: N≡N.

4.11 Coordinate Bond

Coordinate Bond: A covalent bond in which both shared electrons are donated by the same atom is called a coordinate bond.

Example: Formation of ammonium ion (NH₄⁺).

NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺

Nitrogen in NH₃ donates its lone pair of electrons to H⁺.

4.12 Lewis Structures

Lewis Structure: A representation of a molecule showing its valence electrons as dots and shared electron pairs as lines is called a Lewis structure.

Steps to Draw Lewis Structures:

  1. Calculate the total number of valence electrons.
  2. Choose the central atom, usually the least electronegative atom (hydrogen is never the central atom).
  3. Connect the atoms using single bonds.
  4. Complete the octets of the outer atoms first.
  5. Place the remaining electrons on the central atom.
  6. If needed, form multiple bonds to complete the central atom's octet.

Example: Lewis Structure of Water (H₂O)

Oxygen has 6 valence electrons and each hydrogen has 1.

Total valence electrons = 6 + 1 + 1 = 8.

Oxygen forms two single bonds with two hydrogen atoms and has two lone pairs.

Example: Lewis Structure of Carbon Dioxide (CO₂)

Carbon has 4 valence electrons and each oxygen has 6.

Total valence electrons = 4 + 6 + 6 = 16.

Its structure is O=C=O.

4.13 Formal Charge

Formal Charge: The charge assigned to an atom in a Lewis structure by assuming that bonding electrons are shared equally between bonded atoms is called formal charge.

Formula:

Formal Charge = V − L − (B / 2)

Where:

  • V = Number of valence electrons in the free atom.
  • L = Number of non-bonding electrons.
  • B = Number of bonding electrons.

Example: Calculate the formal charge on nitrogen in NH₄⁺.

V = 5, L = 0, B = 8.

Formal Charge = 5 − 0 − (8 / 2) = +1.

4.14 Resonance

Resonance: When a molecule or ion cannot be represented adequately by a single Lewis structure and is represented by two or more contributing structures, the phenomenon is called resonance.

Examples: O₃, CO₃²⁻ and NO₃⁻.

The actual molecule is called a resonance hybrid of its contributing structures.

4.15 Bond Parameters

The important parameters used to describe a chemical bond are:

  1. Bond Length
  2. Bond Angle
  3. Bond Enthalpy
  4. Bond Order
  5. Polarity

4.16 Bond Length

Bond Length: The equilibrium distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms is called bond length.

Bond length is generally measured in picometres (pm) or angstroms (Å).

Relation: For bonds between the same two atoms, a higher bond order generally means a shorter bond length.

4.17 Bond Angle

Bond Angle: The angle between two bonds around the central atom is called the bond angle.

Examples:

  • CH₄ = 109.5° approximately.
  • NH₃ = 107° approximately.
  • H₂O = 104.5° approximately.

4.18 Bond Enthalpy

Bond Enthalpy: The energy required to break one mole of a particular type of bond in gaseous molecules is called bond enthalpy.

Bond enthalpy is generally expressed in kJ mol⁻¹.

For the same pair of atoms, triple bonds are generally stronger than double bonds, and double bonds are generally stronger than single bonds.

4.19 Bond Order

Bond Order: The number of chemical bonds between two atoms is called bond order in simple Lewis structures.

Examples:

  • H–H = Bond order 1.
  • O=O = Bond order 2.
  • N≡N = Bond order 3.

Bond Order Formula (Molecular Orbital Theory):

Bond Order = (Nᵦ − Nₐ) / 2

Where:

  • Nᵦ = Number of electrons in bonding molecular orbitals.
  • Nₐ = Number of electrons in antibonding molecular orbitals.

4.20 Polarity of Bonds

Non-Polar Covalent Bond: A covalent bond in which the shared electron pair is equally or nearly equally shared between the bonded atoms.

Examples: H₂, Cl₂.

Polar Covalent Bond: A covalent bond in which the shared electron pair is attracted more strongly by one atom.

Examples: HCl, HF.

4.21 Dipole Moment

Dipole Moment: The measure of separation of positive and negative charges in a molecule is called dipole moment.

Formula:

μ = q × r

Where:

  • μ = Dipole moment.
  • q = Magnitude of separated charge.
  • r = Distance between the centres of positive and negative charges.

Its SI unit is coulomb metre (C m). It is also commonly expressed in Debye (D).

4.22 VSEPR Theory

VSEPR: Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion Theory.

According to VSEPR theory, electron pairs around a central atom repel one another and arrange themselves as far apart as possible to minimise repulsion.

Order of Repulsion:

Lone Pair–Lone Pair > Lone Pair–Bond Pair > Bond Pair–Bond Pair.

4.23 Shapes of Molecules

Molecule Shape Bond Angle
BeCl₂ Linear 180°
BF₃ Trigonal Planar 120°
CH₄ Tetrahedral 109.5°
NH₃ Trigonal Pyramidal 107° approximately
H₂O Bent / V-shaped 104.5° approximately
PCl₅ Trigonal Bipyramidal 90°, 120° and 180°
SF₆ Octahedral 90° and 180°

4.24 Hybridisation

Hybridisation: The mixing of atomic orbitals of comparable energies of the same atom to form an equal number of equivalent hybrid orbitals is called hybridisation.

Important Types:

Hybridisation Geometry Ideal Bond Angle Example
sp Linear 180° BeCl₂
sp² Trigonal Planar 120° BF₃
sp³ Tetrahedral 109.5° CH₄
sp³d Trigonal Bipyramidal 90° and 120° PCl₅
sp³d² Octahedral 90° SF₆

4.25 Sigma (σ) and Pi (π) Bonds

Sigma Bond (σ): A covalent bond formed by head-on or axial overlap of orbitals is called a sigma bond.

Pi Bond (π): A covalent bond formed by sideways or lateral overlap of parallel orbitals is called a pi bond.

Important Facts:

  • A single bond contains one sigma bond.
  • A double bond contains one sigma bond and one pi bond.
  • A triple bond contains one sigma bond and two pi bonds.
  • Sigma bonds are generally stronger than pi bonds.

4.26 Molecular Orbital Theory (MOT)

Molecular Orbital Theory: A theory that explains chemical bonding by considering molecular orbitals formed by the combination of atomic orbitals.

Atomic orbitals combine to form molecular orbitals.

Two Main Types:

  1. Bonding Molecular Orbitals
  2. Antibonding Molecular Orbitals

Bonding Molecular Orbital: It has lower energy than the combining atomic orbitals and stabilises the molecule.

Antibonding Molecular Orbital: It has higher energy than the combining atomic orbitals and destabilises the molecule.

Antibonding orbitals are represented by an asterisk, such as σ* and π*.

4.27 Conditions for Combination of Atomic Orbitals

  1. The combining atomic orbitals should have comparable energies.
  2. They should have proper symmetry with respect to the molecular axis.
  3. They should overlap significantly.

4.28 Magnetic Nature of Molecules

Diamagnetic: A substance in which all electrons are paired is called diamagnetic.

Paramagnetic: A substance that contains one or more unpaired electrons is called paramagnetic.

Examples:

  • N₂ is diamagnetic.
  • O₂ is paramagnetic.

4.29 Hydrogen Bonding

Hydrogen Bond: A weak attractive force between a hydrogen atom bonded to a highly electronegative atom and another electronegative atom is called hydrogen bonding.

Hydrogen bonding is commonly observed when hydrogen is bonded to nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine.

Types of Hydrogen Bonding:

1. Intermolecular Hydrogen Bonding: Hydrogen bonding between different molecules.

Example: Water molecules.

2. Intramolecular Hydrogen Bonding: Hydrogen bonding within the same molecule.

Example: o-nitrophenol.

Importance of Hydrogen Bonding:

  • It affects the boiling points of substances.
  • It contributes to the unusual properties of water.
  • It helps stabilise biological structures such as DNA and proteins.

4.30 Fajan's Rule

Fajan's Rule: The rules proposed by Fajans help predict the covalent character in ionic compounds.

Covalent character generally increases when:

  • The cation is small and highly charged.
  • The anion is large and highly charged.
  • The cation has greater polarising power.
  • The anion has greater polarisability.

4.31 Solved Examples

Example 1: Calculate the total number of valence electrons in H₂O.

Solution:

Oxygen = 6 valence electrons.

Hydrogen = 1 valence electron each.

Total = 6 + 1 + 1 = 8.

Answer: 8 valence electrons.

Example 2: Find the bond order of a molecule having 10 bonding electrons and 4 antibonding electrons.

Solution:

Bond Order = (Nᵦ − Nₐ) / 2

= (10 − 4) / 2

= 6 / 2 = 3.

Answer: Bond order = 3.

Example 3: What is the shape of NH₃?

Solution: Nitrogen has three bond pairs and one lone pair in NH₃.

Answer: Trigonal pyramidal.

Example 4: How many sigma and pi bonds are present in N₂?

Solution: Nitrogen contains a triple bond between the two nitrogen atoms.

Answer: One sigma bond and two pi bonds.

Example 5: What is the formal charge on oxygen in a typical water molecule?

Solution:

V = 6, L = 4, B = 4.

Formal Charge = 6 − 4 − (4 / 2)

= 6 − 4 − 2 = 0.

Answer: Zero.

4.32 Important Definitions for Exams

  1. Chemical Bond: The attractive force that holds atoms or ions together.
  2. Ionic Bond: Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
  3. Covalent Bond: A bond formed by sharing electron pairs.
  4. Coordinate Bond: A covalent bond in which both shared electrons are donated by one atom.
  5. Octet Rule: The tendency of atoms to achieve eight electrons in their valence shell.
  6. Resonance: Representation of a molecule by two or more contributing Lewis structures.
  7. Hybridisation: Mixing of atomic orbitals to form hybrid orbitals.
  8. Dipole Moment: A measure of charge separation in a molecule.
  9. Hydrogen Bond: An attractive interaction involving hydrogen bonded to a highly electronegative atom.

  3. Describe different types of hybridisation with examples.
  4. Explain Molecular Orbital Theory and calculate bond order.
  5. Explain bond parameters and their importance.

Q1. Which scientist proposed the octet rule?

(A) Dalton

(B) Lewis

(C) Rutherford

Answer: (B) Lewis

Q6. How many pi bonds are present in a triple bond?

(B) 1

(D) 3
