CHAPTER 2: ELECTROCHEMISTRY

Class 12th Chemistry | NCERT | Complete Study Notes

1. Introduction to Electrochemistry

Electrochemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with the relationship between chemical energy and electrical energy.

It studies the production of electrical energy from chemical reactions and the use of electrical energy to bring about chemical changes.

Examples:

  • Working of batteries.
  • Electrolysis of water.
  • Electroplating of metals.
  • Corrosion of iron.
  • Charging and discharging of batteries.

Important Terms:

  • Electrochemical Reaction: A chemical reaction involving the transfer of electrons.
  • Oxidation: Loss of electrons by a substance.
  • Reduction: Gain of electrons by a substance.
  • Electrode: A conductor through which electric current enters or leaves an electrolyte.
  • Electrolyte: A substance that conducts electricity in molten state or aqueous solution through the movement of ions.

2. Redox Reactions

Redox reactions are chemical reactions in which oxidation and reduction take place simultaneously.

2.1 Oxidation

Oxidation is defined as the loss of electrons or an increase in oxidation number.

Example:

Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻

2.2 Reduction

Reduction is defined as the gain of electrons or a decrease in oxidation number.

Example:

Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu

2.3 Oxidising Agent

An oxidising agent is a substance that accepts electrons and gets reduced during a redox reaction.

2.4 Reducing Agent

A reducing agent is a substance that donates electrons and gets oxidised during a redox reaction.

2.5 Example of a Redox Reaction

Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu

  • Zinc loses electrons and undergoes oxidation.
  • Copper ions gain electrons and undergo reduction.
  • Zinc acts as the reducing agent.
  • Copper ions act as the oxidising agent.

3. Electrochemical Cells

An electrochemical cell is a device that converts chemical energy into electrical energy or electrical energy into chemical energy.

Electrochemical cells are mainly classified into two types:

  1. Galvanic or Voltaic Cells.
  2. Electrolytic Cells.
3.1 Galvanic Cell

A galvanic cell is an electrochemical cell in which electrical energy is produced from a spontaneous redox reaction.

Example: Daniell Cell.

3.2 Electrolytic Cell

An electrolytic cell is a device in which electrical energy is used to carry out a non-spontaneous chemical reaction.

Example: Electrolysis of molten sodium chloride.

4. Daniell Cell

The Daniell cell is a type of galvanic cell that converts chemical energy into electrical energy through a spontaneous redox reaction involving zinc and copper.

It consists of:

  • A zinc rod dipped in zinc sulphate solution.
  • A copper rod dipped in copper sulphate solution.
  • A salt bridge connecting the two half-cells.
  • An external wire connecting the two electrodes.
4.1 Working of Daniell Cell

At the zinc electrode, oxidation takes place:

Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻

At the copper electrode, reduction takes place:

Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s)

Overall cell reaction:

Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s)

Important Points:

  • Zinc acts as the anode.
  • Copper acts as the cathode.
  • Electrons flow from zinc to copper through the external wire.
  • Oxidation occurs at the anode.
  • Reduction occurs at the cathode.
4.2 Cell Representation

Zn(s) | Zn²⁺(aq) || Cu²⁺(aq) | Cu(s)

Symbols:

  • | represents a phase boundary.
  • || represents the salt bridge.
  • Anode is written on the left side.
  • Cathode is written on the right side.

5. Salt Bridge

A salt bridge is a U-shaped tube containing a concentrated solution of an inert electrolyte such as KCl or KNO₃, often gelled with agar-agar.

5.1 Functions of Salt Bridge
  1. It completes the electrical circuit.
  2. It maintains electrical neutrality in both half-cells.
  3. It prevents direct mixing of the two electrolyte solutions.
  4. It minimises liquid junction potential.
  5. It allows the movement of ions between the two half-cells.
5.2 Movement of Ions
  • Anions from the salt bridge move towards the anode compartment.
  • Cations from the salt bridge move towards the cathode compartment.

Note: A salt bridge does not carry electrons. Electrons flow through the external wire.

6. Electrode Potential

Electrode potential is the potential difference developed between an electrode and the electrolyte in which it is immersed when equilibrium is established.

It indicates the tendency of an electrode to lose or gain electrons.

6.1 Oxidation Potential

It is the tendency of an electrode to lose electrons and undergo oxidation.

6.2 Reduction Potential

It is the tendency of an electrode to gain electrons and undergo reduction.

Important: For the same electrode reaction, oxidation potential and reduction potential have equal magnitudes but opposite signs.

7. Standard Electrode Potential

Standard electrode potential is the electrode potential measured under standard conditions.

Standard conditions generally include:

  • Concentration of dissolved species = 1 M.
  • Gas pressure = 1 bar.
  • Temperature = 298 K, unless otherwise specified.
  • Pure solids and liquids in their standard states.

It is represented by E°.

7.1 Standard Hydrogen Electrode (SHE)

The standard hydrogen electrode is used as a reference electrode for measuring standard electrode potentials of other electrodes.

Its standard electrode potential is assigned a value of zero volts.

E°(H⁺/H₂) = 0.00 V

Construction:

  • A platinum electrode coated with platinum black.
  • Hydrogen gas passed over the electrode at 1 bar pressure.
  • An aqueous solution having hydrogen ion activity equal to unity (approximately 1 M in dilute solution).
  • Temperature generally maintained at 298 K.

Electrode Reaction:

2H⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ H₂(g)

8. Electrochemical Series

The electrochemical series is the arrangement of different electrodes or redox couples in order of their standard reduction potentials.

8.1 Important Features
  • Elements with more negative reduction potentials generally have a greater tendency to undergo oxidation.
  • Elements with more positive reduction potentials generally have a greater tendency to undergo reduction.
  • A strong oxidising agent has a high positive standard reduction potential.
  • A strong reducing agent has a highly negative standard reduction potential.
8.2 Important Standard Reduction Potentials at 298 K
Electrode ReactionE° (V)
Li⁺ + e⁻ → Li-3.04
K⁺ + e⁻ → K-2.93
Ca²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Ca-2.87
Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na-2.71
Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Mg-2.37
Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al-1.66
Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Zn-0.76
Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Fe-0.44
Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb-0.13
2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂0.00
Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu+0.34
I₂ + 2e⁻ → 2I⁻+0.54
Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag+0.80
Br₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Br⁻+1.07
Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻+1.36
F₂ + 2e⁻ → 2F⁻+2.87

Important: These are approximate standard reduction potential values.

9. Electromotive Force (EMF) of a Cell

The electromotive force of a cell is the maximum potential difference between its two electrodes when no current is drawn from the cell.

It is represented by Ecell.

9.1 Formula for Standard EMF

E°cell = E°cathode - E°anode

Here, both electrode potentials are written as reduction potentials.

9.2 Important Points
  • If E°cell is positive, the cell reaction is spontaneous under standard conditions.
  • If E°cell is negative, the forward cell reaction is non-spontaneous under standard conditions.
  • If E°cell is zero, the system is at equilibrium under standard conditions.

10. Electrolytic Conductance

Electrolytic conductance is the ability of an electrolyte solution or molten electrolyte to conduct electricity through the movement of ions.

Electrical current in metallic conductors is carried by electrons, whereas in electrolytic solutions it is carried by ions.

10.1 Metallic Conductors
  • Current is carried by electrons.
  • No chemical change occurs due to ordinary metallic conduction.
  • Conductivity generally decreases with an increase in temperature.
10.2 Electrolytic Conductors
  • Current is carried by positive and negative ions.
  • Electrode reactions may occur.
  • Conductivity generally increases with an increase in temperature.

11. Resistance and Conductance

Resistance is the opposition offered by a conductor to the flow of electric current.

R = V / I

According to Ohm's law:

V = IR

Where:

  • R = Resistance.
  • V = Potential difference.
  • I = Electric current.

SI Unit: Ohm (Ω).

11.1 Conductance

Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance.

G = 1 / R

G = I / V

SI Unit: Siemens (S) or Ω⁻¹.

12. Resistivity and Conductivity

12.1 Resistivity

Resistivity is the resistance of a conductor having unit length and unit cross-sectional area.

R = ρ × l / A

ρ = R × A / l

Where:

  • ρ = Resistivity.
  • l = Length of conductor.
  • A = Cross-sectional area.

SI Unit: Ω m.

12.2 Conductivity

Conductivity is the reciprocal of resistivity. It measures the ability of a material to conduct electricity.

κ = 1 / ρ

κ = G × l / A

SI Unit: S m⁻¹.

13. Conductivity Cell and Cell Constant

A conductivity cell is an apparatus used to measure the conductance of an electrolyte solution.

It generally consists of two platinum electrodes coated with platinum black and placed at a fixed distance from each other.

13.1 Cell Constant

The ratio of the distance between two electrodes to the area of their cross-section is called the cell constant.

Cell Constant = l / A

Unit: m⁻¹ or cm⁻¹.

13.2 Conductivity Formula

κ = Cell Constant / R

κ = Cell Constant × G

13.3 Determination of Cell Constant

A conductivity cell is calibrated using a standard KCl solution whose conductivity is known at a specified temperature.

Cell Constant = Conductivity / Conductance

14. Molar Conductivity

Molar conductivity is the conductance of the volume of solution containing one mole of an electrolyte when placed between two electrodes one unit distance apart.

Λm = κ × 1000 / C

This formula is used when conductivity κ is in S cm⁻¹ and concentration C is in mol L⁻¹.

SI Unit: S m² mol⁻¹.

Common Unit: S cm² mol⁻¹.

14.1 Effect of Dilution on Molar Conductivity
  • Molar conductivity increases with dilution.
  • For strong electrolytes, the increase is generally gradual.
  • For weak electrolytes, the increase is much more significant because their ionisation increases considerably on dilution.

15. Strong and Weak Electrolytes

15.1 Strong Electrolytes

Strong electrolytes are substances that dissociate almost completely into ions in aqueous solution.

Examples:

  • NaCl.
  • KCl.
  • HCl.
  • NaOH.
  • KNO₃.
15.2 Weak Electrolytes

Weak electrolytes are substances that ionise only partially in aqueous solution.

Examples:

  • CH₃COOH.
  • NH₄OH (aqueous ammonia).
  • HF.
  • H₂CO₃.

16. Variation of Molar Conductivity with Concentration

The molar conductivity of an electrolyte generally increases as its concentration decreases.

16.1 Strong Electrolytes

Strong electrolytes are almost completely ionised even at relatively high concentrations. Their molar conductivity increases gradually on dilution mainly because interionic attractions decrease.

Λm = Λm° - A√C

Here:

  • Λm = Molar conductivity at concentration C.
  • Λm° = Limiting molar conductivity.
  • A = Constant depending on the electrolyte, solvent and temperature.
  • C = Concentration.
16.2 Weak Electrolytes

Weak electrolytes are partially ionised. On dilution, their degree of ionisation increases significantly, causing a sharp increase in molar conductivity.

17. Limiting Molar Conductivity

Limiting molar conductivity is the molar conductivity of an electrolyte at infinite dilution, when the concentration approaches zero.

It is represented by Λm°.

Λm° = lim(C→0) Λm

At infinite dilution, interionic interactions become negligible.

18. Kohlrausch's Law of Independent Migration of Ions

Kohlrausch's law states that at infinite dilution, each ion contributes independently to the total limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte, irrespective of the nature of the other ion present.

Λm° = ν+ λ+° + ν− λ−°

Where:

  • Λm° = Limiting molar conductivity of electrolyte.
  • ν+ = Number of cations produced per formula unit.
  • ν− = Number of anions produced per formula unit.
  • λ+° = Limiting ionic conductivity of cation.
  • λ−° = Limiting ionic conductivity of anion.
18.1 Example: NaCl

Λm°(NaCl) = λ°(Na⁺) + λ°(Cl⁻)

18.2 Example: CaCl₂

Λm°(CaCl₂) = λ°(Ca²⁺) + 2λ°(Cl⁻)

18.3 Applications of Kohlrausch's Law
  1. Determination of limiting molar conductivity of weak electrolytes.
  2. Determination of degree of dissociation.
  3. Determination of dissociation constant of weak electrolytes.
  4. Determination of solubility of sparingly soluble salts.
  5. Calculation of ionic conductivities at infinite dilution.
18.4 Calculation of Weak Electrolyte Conductivity

For acetic acid:

Λ°(CH₃COOH) = Λ°(HCl) + Λ°(CH₃COONa) - Λ°(NaCl)

19. Degree of Dissociation

Degree of dissociation is the fraction of the total number of molecules of an electrolyte that dissociate into ions.

α = Λm / Λm°

Where:

  • α = Degree of dissociation.
  • Λm = Molar conductivity at a given concentration.
  • Λm° = Limiting molar conductivity.

Percentage dissociation:

Percentage Dissociation = α × 100

20. Dissociation Constant of a Weak Electrolyte

For a weak electrolyte AB:

AB ⇌ A⁺ + B⁻

Its dissociation constant is:

Ka = Cα² / (1 - α)

For a weak electrolyte with a small degree of dissociation:

Ka ≈ Cα²

Since α = Λm / Λm°:

Ka = C(Λm / Λm°)² / (1 - Λm / Λm°)

21. Electrolysis

Electrolysis is the process of producing a chemical change by passing direct electric current through an electrolyte in molten state or aqueous solution.

21.1 Important Terms
  • Anode: The electrode at which oxidation occurs.
  • Cathode: The electrode at which reduction occurs.
  • Cations: Positively charged ions that move towards the cathode.
  • Anions: Negatively charged ions that move towards the anode.
  • Electrolyte: The conducting ionic medium.
21.2 Electrodes in Different Cells
PropertyGalvanic CellElectrolytic Cell
AnodeNegativePositive
CathodePositiveNegative
OxidationAnodeAnode
ReductionCathodeCathode
Energy ConversionChemical to electricalElectrical to chemical
ReactionSpontaneousNon-spontaneous

Remember: Oxidation always occurs at the anode and reduction always occurs at the cathode, regardless of the type of cell.

22. Faraday's Laws of Electrolysis

22.1 First Law of Electrolysis

Faraday's first law states that the amount of chemical substance deposited or liberated at an electrode is directly proportional to the quantity of electric charge passed through the electrolyte.

m ∝ Q

m = ZQ

m = ZIt

Where:

  • m = Mass deposited or liberated.
  • Z = Electrochemical equivalent.
  • Q = Charge passed.
  • I = Current in amperes.
  • t = Time in seconds.
22.2 Second Law of Electrolysis

When the same quantity of electricity passes through different electrolytes, the masses of substances deposited or liberated are proportional to their equivalent masses.

m₁ / m₂ = E₁ / E₂

Where E represents the equivalent mass.

22.3 Faraday Constant

One Faraday is the charge carried by one mole of electrons.

F = NA × e

F ≈ 96485 C mol⁻¹

Where:

  • NA = Avogadro constant.
  • e = Elementary charge.
22.4 General Formula for Electrolysis

m = (M × I × t) / (n × F)

Where:

  • M = Molar mass of substance.
  • I = Current.
  • t = Time.
  • n = Number of electrons transferred per formula unit.
  • F = Faraday constant.

23. Electrolysis of Important Substances

23.1 Electrolysis of Molten NaCl

At cathode:

Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na

At anode:

2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻

Overall reaction:

2NaCl(l) → 2Na(l) + Cl₂(g)

23.2 Electrolysis of Water

Overall reaction:

2H₂O(l) → 2H₂(g) + O₂(g)

The volume of hydrogen produced is twice the volume of oxygen under the same temperature and pressure conditions.

23.3 Electrolysis of Aqueous CuSO₄ Using Copper Electrodes

At cathode:

Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu(s)

At anode:

Cu(s) → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻

Copper dissolves at the anode and gets deposited at the cathode.

24. Batteries

A battery is a device consisting of one or more electrochemical cells that converts chemical energy into electrical energy.

Batteries are mainly classified into:

  1. Primary Batteries.
  2. Secondary Batteries.
24.1 Primary Batteries

Primary batteries are batteries in which the chemical reactions are generally irreversible. They cannot be recharged by ordinary means.

Examples:

  • Dry cell.
  • Mercury cell.
  • Alkaline primary batteries.
24.2 Secondary Batteries

Secondary batteries are batteries in which the chemical reactions are reversible and which can be recharged by passing electric current in the reverse direction.

Examples:

  • Lead storage battery.
  • Nickel-cadmium battery.
  • Lithium-ion battery.

25. Dry Cell

A dry cell is a primary electrochemical cell commonly used in portable electrical devices.

It is also known as a Leclanché cell.

25.1 Construction
  • Zinc container acts as the anode.
  • Carbon rod acts as the positive current collector.
  • Manganese dioxide and carbon form the cathode mixture.
  • Electrolyte is a moist paste containing NH₄Cl and ZnCl₂.
25.2 Electrode Reactions

Anode reaction:

Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻

A simplified cathode reaction is:

2MnO₂ + 2NH₄⁺ + 2e⁻ → Mn₂O₃ + 2NH₃ + H₂O

Overall simplified reaction:

Zn + 2MnO₂ + 2NH₄Cl → ZnCl₂ + Mn₂O₃ + 2NH₃ + H₂O

Important: A dry cell generally produces about 1.5 V.

26. Mercury Cell

A mercury cell is a primary battery that provides nearly constant voltage during its useful life.

26.1 Construction
  • Anode: Zinc amalgam.
  • Cathode: Mercury(II) oxide mixed with carbon.
  • Electrolyte: KOH or NaOH paste.
26.2 Electrode Reactions

At anode:

Zn(Hg) + 2OH⁻ → ZnO + H₂O + 2e⁻

At cathode:

HgO + H₂O + 2e⁻ → Hg + 2OH⁻

Overall reaction:

Zn(Hg) + HgO → ZnO + Hg

Important: Mercury cells produce approximately 1.35 V and are historically used in small electronic devices.

27. Lead Storage Battery

The lead storage battery is a secondary battery widely used in automobiles and backup power systems.

27.1 Construction
  • Negative electrode: Lead (Pb).
  • Positive electrode: Lead dioxide (PbO₂).
  • Electrolyte: Sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄).
  • Each cell produces approximately 2 V.
  • Six cells connected in series produce approximately 12 V.
27.2 Discharging Reactions

At anode:

Pb + SO₄²⁻ → PbSO₄ + 2e⁻

At cathode:

PbO₂ + 4H⁺ + SO₄²⁻ + 2e⁻ → PbSO₄ + 2H₂O

Overall reaction:

Pb + PbO₂ + 2H₂SO₄ → 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O

27.3 Charging

During charging, the above reaction is reversed by supplying electrical energy from an external source.

Important: During discharge, the concentration of sulphuric acid decreases.

28. Lithium-Ion Batteries

Lithium-ion batteries are rechargeable batteries that work through the movement of lithium ions between two electrodes during charging and discharging.

28.1 Main Components
  • Negative electrode: Commonly graphite.
  • Positive electrode: Lithium metal oxide or phosphate material.
  • Electrolyte: Lithium salt in an organic solvent or another suitable electrolyte system.
  • Separator: Prevents direct electrical contact between electrodes while allowing ion movement.
28.2 Working Principle
  • During discharge, lithium ions move from the negative electrode towards the positive electrode through the electrolyte.
  • Electrons move through the external circuit and provide electrical energy.
  • During charging, an external power source drives the process in the reverse direction.
28.3 Applications
  • Mobile phones.
  • Laptops.
  • Electric vehicles.
  • Portable electronic devices.
  • Energy storage systems.

29. Fuel Cells

A fuel cell is an electrochemical device that converts the chemical energy of a continuously supplied fuel and oxidising agent directly into electrical energy.

29.1 Hydrogen-Oxygen Fuel Cell

In an alkaline hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell, hydrogen and oxygen are supplied continuously to the anode and cathode respectively.

At anode:

2H₂ + 4OH⁻ → 4H₂O + 4e⁻

At cathode:

O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻

Overall reaction:

2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O

29.2 Advantages of Fuel Cells
  • High energy conversion efficiency.
  • Low pollution during operation when hydrogen is the fuel and water is the main product.
  • Continuous electricity production as long as fuel and oxidant are supplied.
  • Useful in space missions and clean-energy systems.
29.3 Applications
  • Spacecraft.
  • Electric vehicles.
  • Backup power systems.
  • Stationary electricity generation.

30. Corrosion

Corrosion is the slow destruction of a metal due to chemical or electrochemical reactions with its environment.

Examples:

  • Rusting of iron.
  • Tarnishing of silver.
  • Formation of a green coating on copper.
30.1 Rusting of Iron

Rusting is the corrosion of iron in the presence of oxygen and moisture.

At the anodic region:

Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻

At the cathodic region:

O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻

Ferrous ions react with hydroxide ions to form iron(II) hydroxide:

Fe²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Fe(OH)₂

Further oxidation produces iron(III) hydroxide and hydrated iron(III) oxide, commonly called rust.

Fe₂O₃ · xH₂O = Rust

30.2 Factors Affecting Corrosion
  • Presence of moisture.
  • Presence of oxygen.
  • Presence of salts and electrolytes.
  • Acidic conditions.
  • Nature and purity of metal.
  • Temperature and environmental conditions.
30.3 Prevention of Corrosion
  1. Painting: Prevents direct contact of metal with air and moisture.
  2. Oiling and Greasing: Provides a protective layer.
  3. Galvanisation: Coating iron or steel with zinc.
  4. Electroplating: Depositing a protective metal layer on another metal.
  5. Alloying: Producing corrosion-resistant alloys such as stainless steel.
  6. Cathodic Protection: Making the metal to be protected the cathode of an electrochemical system.

31. Important Differences

31.1 Galvanic Cell vs Electrolytic Cell
Galvanic CellElectrolytic Cell
Converts chemical energy into electrical energy.Converts electrical energy into chemical energy.
Reaction is spontaneous.Reaction is non-spontaneous.
Anode is negative.Anode is positive.
Cathode is positive.Cathode is negative.
Produces electrical energy.Consumes electrical energy.
31.2 Strong vs Weak Electrolytes
Strong ElectrolytesWeak Electrolytes
Almost completely ionised.Partially ionised.
High degree of ionisation.Low degree of ionisation.
Gradual increase in molar conductivity on dilution.Sharp increase in molar conductivity on dilution.
Examples: NaCl, HCl.Examples: CH₃COOH, HF.
31.3 Resistance vs Conductance
ResistanceConductance
Opposition to current flow.Ability to conduct current.
R = V/I.G = 1/R.
Unit: Ohm.Unit: Siemens.

32. Important Formula Sheet

Electrical Quantities

  • V = IR
  • R = V/I
  • G = 1/R
  • R = ρl/A
  • ρ = RA/l
  • κ = 1/ρ
  • κ = G × Cell Constant
  • Cell Constant = l/A

Conductivity

  • Λm = κ × 1000/C (κ in S cm⁻¹ and C in mol L⁻¹).
  • Λm° = ν+λ+° + ν−λ−°.
  • Λm = Λm° - A√C (strong electrolytes).
  • α = Λm/Λm°.
  • Ka = Cα²/(1-α).

Electrochemical Cells

  • E°cell = E°cathode - E°anode.
  • ΔG° = -nFE°cell.
  • ΔG = -nFEcell.
  • ΔG° = -RT ln K.

Nernst Equation

  • Ecell = E°cell - (RT/nF) ln Q.
  • At 298 K: Ecell = E°cell - (0.0591/n) log Q.

Electrolysis

  • Q = It.
  • m = ZIt.
  • F = 96485 C mol⁻¹.
  • m = MIt/(nF).

Colligative Properties are not part of the main topic of this chapter; focus on electrochemical thermodynamics and conductance formulas here.

33. Important Solved Numerical Problems

Example 1: Calculate EMF of a Cell

Question: Calculate the standard EMF of a cell having E°cathode = +0.34 V and E°anode = -0.76 V.

Solution:

E°cell = E°cathode - E°anode

= 0.34 - (-0.76)

Answer = 1.10 V

Example 2: Calculate Conductance

Question: Calculate the conductance if the resistance of a solution is 50 Ω.

Solution:

G = 1/R

G = 1/50

Answer = 0.02 S

Example 3: Calculate Conductivity

Question: A conductivity cell has a cell constant of 1.25 cm⁻¹ and resistance of 50 Ω. Calculate conductivity.

Solution:

κ = Cell Constant / R

κ = 1.25/50

Answer = 0.025 S cm⁻¹

Example 4: Calculate Molar Conductivity

Question: Conductivity of a solution is 0.01 S cm⁻¹ and concentration is 0.1 mol L⁻¹. Calculate molar conductivity.

Solution:

Λm = κ × 1000/C

= 0.01 × 1000/0.1

Answer = 100 S cm² mol⁻¹

Example 5: Calculate Charge

Question: Calculate the charge passed when a current of 2 A flows for 10 minutes.

Solution:

Time = 10 × 60 = 600 seconds.

Q = It

Q = 2 × 600

Answer = 1200 C

Example 6: Calculate Mass of Copper Deposited

Question: Calculate the mass of copper deposited when 2 A current is passed through CuSO₄ solution for 30 minutes. Molar mass of Cu = 63.5 g mol⁻¹.

Solution:

Time = 30 × 60 = 1800 s.

For copper, n = 2.

m = MIt/(nF)

m = (63.5 × 2 × 1800)/(2 × 96485)

Answer ≈ 1.18 g

Example 7: Calculate Gibbs Energy

Question: Calculate standard Gibbs energy change for a cell reaction with n = 2 and E°cell = 1.10 V. F = 96485 C mol⁻¹.

Solution:

ΔG° = -nFE°cell

= -2 × 96485 × 1.10

Answer ≈ -212.3 kJ mol⁻¹

    (C) 2 V

    (D) -1 V

    (A) Positive

    (B) Negative

    (C) Neutral

    (D) Insulating

    (A) Ohm

    (B) Volt

    (C) Siemens

    (D) Ampere

    (A) S m⁻¹

    (B) S m² mol⁻¹

    (C) Ohm m

    (D) 6.022 C mol⁻¹

  8. Which law is used to calculate the limiting molar conductivity of weak electrolytes?

    (A) Raoult's law

    (B) Henry's law

    (C) Kohlrausch's law

    (D) Boyle's law

    Answer: (C)
  9. Which of the following is a secondary battery?

    (A) Dry cell

    (B) Mercury cell

    (C) Lead storage battery

    (D) Primary alkaline cell

    Answer: (C)
  10. The main product of hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell is:

    (A) Hydrogen peroxide

  11. In an electrolytic cell, the cathode is:

    (A) Positive

    (A) S m² mol⁻¹

    (B) H₂O

    (B) Fe₂O₃·xH₂O

    Answer: (B)
  15. A positive standard EMF indicates:

    (A) A spontaneous cell reaction under standard conditions

    (B) A non-spontaneous cell reaction under standard conditions

    (C) No reaction under standard conditions

    (D) No electron transfer

    Answer: (A)

37. Important Assertion and Reason Questions

Options:

  • (A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason correctly explains Assertion.
  • (B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not correctly explain Assertion.
  • (C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false.
  • (D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true.
  1. Assertion: Molar conductivity increases on dilution.
    Reason: Interionic interactions decrease on dilution and ionisation of weak electrolytes increases.
    Answer: (A)
  2. Assertion: A salt bridge maintains electrical neutrality.
    Reason: Ions from the salt bridge migrate into the half-cells.
    Answer: (A)
  3. Assertion: The anode is negative in a galvanic cell.
    Reason: Oxidation occurs at the anode.
    Answer: (A)
  4. Assertion: The conductivity of an electrolyte generally increases on dilution.
    Reason: The number of ions per unit volume generally decreases on dilution.
    Answer: (D)
  5. Assertion: Lead storage batteries can be recharged.
    Reason: Their cell reactions are reversible under suitable conditions.
    Answer: (A)

  1. What is the symbol of standard electrode potential? Answer: E°

  5. What is the reference electrode? Answer: Standard Hydrogen Electrode
  6. Which electrode is used as the anode in a Daniell cell? Answer: Zinc
  7. Which electrode is used as the cathode in a Daniell cell? Answer: Copper

39. Important Exam Tips

  • Always remember that oxidation takes place at the anode.
  • Reduction always takes place at the cathode.
  • Use reduction potentials in the EMF formula.
  • Do not forget the negative sign in ΔG = -nFE.
  • Convert time into seconds before using Faraday's law.
  • Use the correct number of electrons in electrolysis numericals.
  • Do not confuse conductivity with molar conductivity.
  • Remember that conductivity generally decreases on dilution.
  • Remember that molar conductivity increases on dilution.
  • Use the correct units in all numerical problems.
  • Remember that a primary battery is generally non-rechargeable.
  • Remember that a secondary battery is rechargeable.

40. Chapter Summary

Electrochemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with the conversion of chemical energy into electrical energy and electrical energy into chemical energy.

This chapter explains electrochemical cells, galvanic cells, electrolytic cells, electrode potentials, standard hydrogen electrode, electrochemical series and EMF of cells.

It also explains electrical resistance, conductance, conductivity, molar conductivity, Kohlrausch's law and Faraday's laws of electrolysis.

Finally, the chapter covers primary and secondary batteries, lead storage batteries, fuel cells and corrosion of metals.

END OF CHAPTER 2 – ELECTROCHEMISTRY

Study all definitions, understand the derivations and practise the numerical problems regularly.

CHAPTER 3: CHEMICAL KINETICS

Class 12th Chemistry | Complete Detailed Notes

1. Introduction to Chemical Kinetics

Chemical Kinetics is the branch of chemistry that deals with the study of the rates of chemical reactions, the factors affecting reaction rates and the mechanisms by which chemical reactions occur.

It helps us understand how fast or slow a chemical reaction takes place and how reaction conditions influence its speed.

Examples:

  • Rusting of iron is a slow chemical reaction.
  • Burning of paper is a fast chemical reaction.
  • Decomposition of hydrogen peroxide.
  • Formation of water from hydrogen and oxygen.
  • Digestion of food.

2. Rate of a Chemical Reaction

The rate of a chemical reaction is defined as the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time.

For a reaction:

R → P

Rate of disappearance of reactant:

Rate = -Δ[R] / Δt

Rate of appearance of product:

Rate = Δ[P] / Δt

Where:

  • Δ[R] = Change in concentration of reactant.
  • Δ[P] = Change in concentration of product.
  • Δt = Time interval.

Note: A negative sign is used for reactants because their concentration decreases with time.

3. Average Rate of Reaction

The average rate of a reaction is the change in concentration of a reactant or product divided by the time interval during which the change occurs.

For the reaction:

R → P

Average Rate = -([R]₂ - [R]₁)/(t₂ - t₁)

Or:

Average Rate = ([P]₂ - [P]₁)/(t₂ - t₁)

Important Points:

  • Average rate depends on the time interval selected.
  • It is calculated over a finite period of time.
  • Concentration is generally expressed in mol L⁻¹.
  • Time is generally expressed in seconds.

4. Instantaneous Rate of Reaction

The instantaneous rate of reaction is the rate of a chemical reaction at a particular instant of time.

Mathematically:

Instantaneous Rate = -d[R]/dt

For product formation:

Instantaneous Rate = d[P]/dt

Graphical Representation:

  • It is determined by drawing a tangent to the concentration-time curve at the required time.
  • The slope of the tangent gives the instantaneous rate.

5. Rate of Reaction for a General Chemical Equation

Consider the general reaction:

aA + bB → cC + dD

The rate of reaction is expressed as:

Rate = -(1/a)d[A]/dt

= -(1/b)d[B]/dt

= (1/c)d[C]/dt

= (1/d)d[D]/dt

Where a, b, c and d are the stoichiometric coefficients of the balanced chemical equation.

6. Units of Rate of Reaction

Rate of reaction is expressed as change in concentration per unit time.

SI Unit: mol m⁻³ s⁻¹

Common Unit: mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹ or mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

7. Factors Affecting the Rate of Reaction

The rate of a chemical reaction depends on several factors.

  1. Nature of Reactants: Different substances react at different rates depending on their chemical properties.
  2. Concentration of Reactants: Increasing concentration generally increases the rate of reaction.
  3. Temperature: Increasing temperature generally increases the reaction rate.
  4. Catalyst: A catalyst increases or decreases the reaction rate by providing an alternative reaction pathway with a different activation energy.
  5. Surface Area: Increasing the surface area of a solid reactant generally increases the reaction rate.
  6. Pressure: Increasing pressure generally increases the reaction rate of gaseous reactants by increasing their concentrations.
  7. Light: Some photochemical reactions become faster in the presence of light.

8. Rate Law or Rate Equation

The rate law is an expression that relates the rate of a chemical reaction to the concentrations of reactants, each raised to a suitable power determined experimentally.

For the reaction:

A + B → Products

The rate law may be written as:

Rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ

Where:

  • k = Rate constant.
  • [A] = Concentration of reactant A.
  • [B] = Concentration of reactant B.
  • m = Order with respect to A.
  • n = Order with respect to B.

Note: The powers m and n are generally determined experimentally and cannot usually be obtained from the balanced chemical equation.

9. Rate Constant

The rate constant is defined as the rate of reaction when the concentration of each reactant in the rate law is unity.

For:

Rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ

k = Rate / ([A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ)

Important Properties:

  • The rate constant is independent of reactant concentrations at a fixed temperature for a given reaction.
  • Its value generally changes with temperature.
  • It depends on the nature of the reaction.
  • A catalyst can change the observed rate constant by changing the reaction pathway.

10. Order of a Reaction

The order of a reaction is the sum of the powers of the concentration terms of the reactants in the experimentally determined rate law.

For:

Rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ

Order = m + n

Examples:

  • Rate = k[A] → First order.
  • Rate = k[A]² → Second order.
  • Rate = k[A][B] → Second order.
  • Rate = k[A]⁰ → Zero order.
  • Rate = k[A]²[B] → Third order.

Important Features:

  • Order is determined experimentally.
  • Order may be zero, a positive integer or a fraction.
  • It may sometimes be negative.
  • It is not necessarily equal to the stoichiometric coefficients of the balanced equation.

11. Molecularity of a Reaction

Molecularity is the number of reacting species (atoms, ions or molecules) that collide simultaneously in a single elementary reaction step.

Types:

  • Unimolecular Reaction: Involves one reacting species.
  • Bimolecular Reaction: Involves two reacting species.
  • Termolecular Reaction: Involves three reacting species in a single elementary step.

Examples:

Unimolecular:

NH₄NO₂ → N₂ + 2H₂O

Bimolecular:

NO + O₃ → NO₂ + O₂

Important Features:

  • Molecularity is always a positive integer for an elementary reaction step.
  • It cannot be zero or fractional.
  • It is defined only for an elementary reaction step.
  • It is based on the reaction mechanism.

12. Difference Between Order and Molecularity

Order of Reaction Molecularity
Determined experimentally. Obtained from an elementary reaction step.
Can be zero. Cannot be zero.
May be fractional. Always a positive integer.
Can be negative in some cases. Cannot be negative.
Applies to the experimentally determined rate law. Applies only to an elementary step.

13. Integrated Rate Equation

An integrated rate equation expresses the concentration of a reactant as a function of time.

It is useful for determining the concentration of a reactant at any particular time and calculating the rate constant.

The integrated rate equations for zero-order, first-order and second-order reactions are important in chemical kinetics.

14. Zero Order Reaction

A zero-order reaction is a reaction whose rate is independent of the concentration of the reactant.

Rate law:

Rate = k[A]⁰

Since [A]⁰ = 1:

Rate = k

14.1 Integrated Rate Equation

-[d[A]/dt] = k

On integration:

[A]t = [A]₀ - kt

Where:

  • [A]t = Concentration at time t.
  • [A]₀ = Initial concentration.
  • k = Zero-order rate constant.
  • t = Time.
14.2 Rate Constant Formula

k = ([A]₀ - [A]t)/t

14.3 Half-Life of Zero Order Reaction

Half-life is the time required for the concentration of a reactant to become half of its initial value.

At half-life:

[A]t = [A]₀/2

Therefore:

t₁/₂ = [A]₀ / 2k

14.4 Graph of Zero Order Reaction

For a zero-order reaction, a graph of concentration [A] against time gives a straight line.

  • Slope = -k.
  • Intercept = [A]₀.

Examples:

  • Some photochemical reactions under suitable conditions.
  • Some surface-catalysed reactions when the catalyst surface is saturated.

15. First Order Reaction

A first-order reaction is a reaction whose rate is directly proportional to the first power of the concentration of one reactant.

Rate law:

Rate = k[A]

15.1 Integrated Rate Equation

-d[A]/dt = k[A]

On integration:

ln([A]₀/[A]t) = kt

Using common logarithm:

k = (2.303/t) log([A]₀/[A]t)

15.2 Alternative Form

[A]t = [A]₀e⁻ᵏᵗ

15.3 Half-Life of First Order Reaction

For a first-order reaction:

t₁/₂ = 0.693/k

Important Points:

  • Half-life is independent of the initial concentration.
  • The rate constant is independent of initial concentration.
  • The concentration decreases exponentially with time.
15.4 Graph of First Order Reaction

A plot of ln[A] against time gives a straight line.

  • Slope = -k.
  • Intercept = ln[A]₀.

A plot of log([A]₀/[A]t) against time is also a straight line.

  • Slope = k/2.303.
15.5 Examples of First Order Reactions
  • Decomposition of N₂O₅ under suitable conditions.
  • Radioactive decay.
  • Some decomposition reactions.

16. Second Order Reaction

A second-order reaction is a reaction whose overall order is two.

For a reaction involving one reactant:

Rate = k[A]²

16.1 Integrated Rate Equation

1/[A]t - 1/[A]₀ = kt

Therefore:

k = (1/[A]t - 1/[A]₀)/t

16.2 Half-Life of Second Order Reaction

t₁/₂ = 1/(k[A]₀)

Important Points:

  • Half-life is inversely proportional to the initial concentration.
  • As initial concentration increases, half-life decreases.
  • For a second-order reaction, a plot of 1/[A] against time gives a straight line.

Graph:

  • Slope = k.
  • Intercept = 1/[A]₀.

17. Comparison of Zero, First and Second Order Reactions

Property Zero Order First Order Second Order
Rate law k k[A] k[A]²
Integrated equation [A]t = [A]₀ - kt ln([A]₀/[A]t) = kt 1/[A]t - 1/[A]₀ = kt
Half-life [A]₀/2k 0.693/k 1/k[A]₀
Unit of k mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹ s⁻¹ L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹
Linear graph [A] vs t ln[A] vs t 1/[A] vs t

18. Half-Life of a Reaction

Half-life is the time required for the concentration of a reactant to decrease to half of its initial value.

It is represented by t₁/₂.

Important Half-Life Formulae:

  • Zero order: t₁/₂ = [A]₀/2k
  • First order: t₁/₂ = 0.693/k
  • Second order: t₁/₂ = 1/k[A]₀

19. Pseudo First Order Reaction

A pseudo first-order reaction is a reaction that is actually of a higher order but behaves like a first-order reaction because the concentration of one or more reactants remains practically constant during the reaction.

Example: Hydrolysis of ethyl acetate in excess water.

CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O → CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH

Since water is present in large excess, its concentration remains almost constant.

Therefore, the rate law can be written as:

Rate = k'[CH₃COOC₂H₅]

Where k' is the pseudo first-order rate constant.

20. Temperature Dependence of Reaction Rate

The rate of most chemical reactions increases with an increase in temperature.

For many reactions, the rate constant approximately doubles for every 10°C rise in temperature, although this is only a general rule of thumb and not universal.

Reason:

  • Increasing temperature increases the average kinetic energy of molecules.
  • A greater fraction of molecules acquire sufficient energy to cross the activation energy barrier.
  • The number of effective collisions increases.

21. Activation Energy

Activation energy is the minimum additional energy required by reacting molecules to reach the activated complex or transition state and undergo a chemical reaction.

It is represented by Ea.

Important Points:

  • It is generally expressed in kJ mol⁻¹.
  • Higher activation energy generally results in a slower reaction at a given temperature, assuming comparable reaction conditions.
  • A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy.

22. Arrhenius Equation

Arrhenius equation describes the relationship between the rate constant of a reaction and its absolute temperature.

k = Ae⁻ᴱᵃ/ᴿᵀ

Where:

  • k = Rate constant.
  • A = Arrhenius frequency factor or pre-exponential factor.
  • Ea = Activation energy.
  • R = Gas constant.
  • T = Absolute temperature in Kelvin.
22.1 Logarithmic Form

ln k = ln A - Ea/RT

Using common logarithm:

log k = log A - Ea/(2.303RT)

22.2 Two Temperature Arrhenius Equation

When rate constants are known at two different temperatures:

ln(k₂/k₁) = (Ea/R)(1/T₁ - 1/T₂)

Using common logarithm:

log(k₂/k₁) = Ea/(2.303R) × (T₂-T₁)/(T₁T₂)

Important: Always use temperature in Kelvin.

23. Arrhenius Plot

According to the Arrhenius equation:

ln k = ln A - (Ea/R)(1/T)

A plot of ln k against 1/T gives a straight line.

  • Slope = -Ea/R.
  • Intercept = ln A.

Using common logarithm:

  • Slope = -Ea/2.303R.
  • Intercept = log A.

24. Collision Theory of Chemical Reactions

Collision theory explains that a chemical reaction occurs when reactant molecules collide with sufficient energy and proper orientation.

Conditions for Effective Collision:

  1. Molecules must collide with each other.
  2. They must possess energy equal to or greater than the activation energy.
  3. They must have suitable orientation.

Effective Collision: A collision that leads to the formation of products.

Important: Not every collision between molecules results in a chemical reaction.

25. Activated Complex and Transition State

An activated complex is a temporary, unstable arrangement of atoms formed during the conversion of reactants into products.

The transition state is the highest-energy configuration along the reaction pathway.

  • It has very high potential energy.
  • It is extremely unstable.
  • It may proceed towards product formation or return to reactants.

26. Catalyst

A catalyst is a substance that changes the rate of a chemical reaction without undergoing permanent chemical change itself.

Functions of a Catalyst:

  • Provides an alternative reaction pathway.
  • Changes the activation energy of the reaction pathway.
  • Increases the rate of some reactions.
  • Does not change the equilibrium constant.
  • Does not change the overall Gibbs energy change of the reaction.
  • Helps the system reach equilibrium faster.

27. Positive and Negative Catalysts

27.1 Positive Catalyst

A positive catalyst increases the rate of a chemical reaction.

Example: MnO₂ accelerates the decomposition of potassium chlorate.

2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂

27.2 Negative Catalyst or Inhibitor

A negative catalyst or inhibitor decreases the rate of a chemical reaction.

Example: Certain inhibitors slow down oxidation and other chemical reactions.

28. Photochemical Reactions

Photochemical reactions are chemical reactions initiated by the absorption of light energy.

Examples:

  • Photosynthesis.
  • Photochemical decomposition of silver bromide.
  • Formation of vitamin D in the skin through sunlight-driven chemistry.

Photochemical reaction of silver bromide:

2AgBr → 2Ag + Br₂

This reaction occurs in the presence of light.

29. Important Graphs in Chemical Kinetics

Zero Order Reaction:

  • Plot of [A] against time is a straight line.
  • Slope = -k.

First Order Reaction:

  • Plot of ln[A] against time is a straight line.
  • Slope = -k.

Second Order Reaction:

  • Plot of 1/[A] against time is a straight line.
  • Slope = +k.

Arrhenius Plot:

  • Plot of ln k against 1/T.
  • Slope = -Ea/R.

30. Important Formula Sheet

Rate of Reaction:

  • Rate = -Δ[R]/Δt
  • Rate = Δ[P]/Δt
  • Rate = -d[R]/dt

Rate Law:

  • Rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ
  • Overall order = m+n

Zero Order:

  • [A]t = [A]₀ - kt
  • k = ([A]₀ - [A]t)/t
  • t₁/₂ = [A]₀/2k

First Order:

  • k = (2.303/t) log([A]₀/[A]t)
  • [A]t = [A]₀e⁻ᵏᵗ
  • t₁/₂ = 0.693/k

Second Order:

  • 1/[A]t - 1/[A]₀ = kt
  • t₁/₂ = 1/k[A]₀

Arrhenius Equation:

  • k = Ae⁻ᴱᵃ/ᴿᵀ
  • ln k = ln A - Ea/RT
  • ln(k₂/k₁) = (Ea/R)(1/T₁ - 1/T₂)

Useful Constants:

  • R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹
  • 2.303 = Conversion factor between natural and common logarithms.

31. Important Solved Numerical Problems

Example 1: Average Rate of Reaction

Question: The concentration of a reactant decreases from 0.8 mol L⁻¹ to 0.4 mol L⁻¹ in 20 seconds. Calculate the average rate.

Solution:

Rate = (0.8 - 0.4)/20

= 0.4/20

Answer = 0.02 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹

Example 2: First Order Rate Constant

Question: For a first-order reaction, 50% of the reactant decomposes in 20 minutes. Calculate the rate constant.

Solution:

t₁/₂ = 0.693/k

k = 0.693/20

Answer = 0.03465 min⁻¹

Example 3: Half-Life of a Zero Order Reaction

Question: The initial concentration is 0.8 mol L⁻¹ and the rate constant is 0.02 mol L⁻¹ min⁻¹. Calculate the half-life.

Solution:

t₁/₂ = [A]₀/2k

= 0.8/(2 × 0.02)

Answer = 20 minutes

Example 4: First Order Concentration

Question: A first-order reaction has an initial concentration of 0.5 mol L⁻¹ and a rate constant of 0.1 min⁻¹. Find the concentration after 10 minutes.

Solution:

[A]t = [A]₀e⁻ᵏᵗ

= 0.5 × e⁻¹

Answer ≈ 0.184 mol L⁻¹

Example 5: Order of Reaction

Question: The rate law is Rate = k[A]²[B]. Find the overall order.

Solution:

Order = 2 + 1

Answer = Third Order

Example 6: Calculate Activation Energy

Question: Calculate activation energy if the slope of an Arrhenius plot of ln k against 1/T is -5000 K.

Solution:

Slope = -Ea/R

Ea = 5000 × 8.314

Ea = 41570 J mol⁻¹

Answer = 41.57 kJ mol⁻¹

35. Assertion and Reason Questions

Options:

  • (A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason correctly explains Assertion.
  • (B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not correctly explain Assertion.
  • (C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false.
  • (D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true.
  1. Assertion: The half-life of a first-order reaction is independent of initial concentration.
    Reason: Its half-life is given by 0.693/k.
    Answer: (A)
  2. Assertion: A catalyst increases the rate of a reaction.
    Reason: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy when it acts as a positive catalyst.
    Answer: (A)
  3. Assertion: Molecularity can be fractional.
    Reason: Molecularity is the number of reacting species in an elementary step.
    Answer: (D)
  4. Assertion: Reaction rate generally increases with temperature.
    Reason: A greater fraction of molecules has sufficient energy to overcome activation energy.
    Answer: (A)
  5. Assertion: The order of a reaction is always equal to molecularity.
    Reason: Both are always determined experimentally.
    Answer: (D)

36. Important One-Line Questions

  1. What is the branch of chemistry dealing with reaction rates? Answer: Chemical Kinetics.
  2. What is the symbol of rate constant? Answer: k.
  3. What is the symbol of activation energy? Answer: Ea.
  4. What is the symbol of half-life? Answer: t₁/₂.
  5. What is the order of a zero-order reaction? Answer: Zero.
  6. What is the order of a first-order reaction? Answer: One.
  7. What is the order of a second-order reaction? Answer: Two.
  8. What is the value of R? Answer: 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
  9. Which equation relates temperature and rate constant? Answer: Arrhenius equation.
  10. What does a catalyst change? Answer: Reaction pathway and activation energy.
  11. Which reaction has half-life independent of initial concentration? Answer: First-order reaction.
  12. What is the SI unit of time? Answer: Second.

37. Important Exam Tips

  • Learn all three integrated rate equations.
  • Memorise half-life formulas for zero, first and second-order reactions.
  • Understand the difference between order and molecularity.
  • Practise Arrhenius equation numericals.
  • Always convert temperature into Kelvin.
  • Remember that the order is determined experimentally.
  • Remember that molecularity applies only to an elementary step.
  • Learn the units of rate constants for different reaction orders.
  • Practise logarithmic calculations.
  • Understand the graphical representations of different reaction orders.

38. Chapter Summary

Chemical Kinetics is the study of the rates of chemical reactions and the factors affecting them.

This chapter explains average and instantaneous rates, rate laws, rate constants, reaction orders, molecularity and integrated rate equations.

It also covers zero-order, first-order and second-order reactions, half-life, pseudo first-order reactions, temperature dependence, activation energy, the Arrhenius equation, collision theory and catalysts.

END OF CHAPTER 3 – CHEMICAL KINETICS

Study all definitions, practise derivations and solve numerical problems regularly.

Chapter 4: The d- and f-Block Elements

1. Introduction

The d-block elements are those elements in which the differentiating electron enters the d-orbital of the penultimate shell. These elements are placed in groups 3 to 12 of the periodic table.

The f-block elements are those elements in which the differentiating electron enters the f-orbital of the antepenultimate shell. They are placed separately at the bottom of the periodic table.

2. Position of d-Block Elements

  • They are present in groups 3 to 12.
  • They are also called transition elements.
  • They are located between s-block and p-block elements.
  • They include four transition series: 3d, 4d, 5d and 6d.

3. General Electronic Configuration

The general electronic configuration of d-block elements is:

(n-1)d1-10 ns0-2

Example:

  • Scandium (Sc): [Ar] 3d1 4s2
  • Titanium (Ti): [Ar] 3d2 4s2
  • Iron (Fe): [Ar] 3d6 4s2
  • Copper (Cu): [Ar] 3d10 4s1
  • Zinc (Zn): [Ar] 3d10 4s2

4. Why are Zn, Cd and Hg not Transition Elements?

A transition element must have a partially filled d-orbital in its atom or in at least one of its common oxidation states.

Zn, Cd and Hg have completely filled d-orbitals in their atoms and common ions. Therefore, they are not considered transition elements.

5. Important Characteristics of Transition Elements

A. Metallic Character

All transition elements are metals. They generally have high melting points, boiling points and densities.

B. Variable Oxidation States

Transition elements show variable oxidation states because the energies of ns and (n-1)d orbitals are very close. Electrons from both orbitals can participate in bond formation.

Examples:

  • Iron: +2 and +3
  • Manganese: +2, +4 and +7
  • Copper: +1 and +2
  • Chromium: +2, +3 and +6

C. Formation of Coloured Ions

Many transition metal ions are coloured due to d-d electronic transitions. Electrons absorb certain wavelengths of visible light and move between split d-orbitals.

Examples:

  • Cu2+ – Blue
  • Fe2+ – Pale green
  • Fe3+ – Yellowish brown
  • Ni2+ – Green
  • MnO4- – Purple

Ions having d0 or d10 configuration are generally colourless due to the absence of d-d transitions.

D. Magnetic Properties

Most transition metal ions are paramagnetic because they contain one or more unpaired electrons.

The magnetic moment is calculated by the spin-only formula:

μ = √[n(n + 2)] BM

Where:

  • μ = Magnetic moment
  • n = Number of unpaired electrons
  • BM = Bohr Magneton

E. Catalytic Properties

Transition metals and their compounds often act as catalysts because they can show variable oxidation states and provide suitable surfaces for reactions.

Examples:

  • Iron is used in the Haber process.
  • V2O5 is used in the Contact process.
  • Nickel is used in hydrogenation of oils.

F. Formation of Complex Compounds

Transition metal ions form complex compounds because of their small size, high charge density and availability of vacant orbitals for accepting electron pairs from ligands.

Examples:

  • [Fe(CN)6]4-
  • [Cu(NH3)4]2+
  • [Co(NH3)6]3+

G. Formation of Alloys

Transition metals form alloys because their atomic sizes are generally similar.

Examples:

  • Stainless steel: Iron, chromium and nickel.
  • Brass: Copper and zinc.
  • Bronze: Copper and tin.

6. Important Trends in Transition Elements

A. Atomic and Ionic Radii

Across a transition series, atomic radii generally decrease slightly from left to right because nuclear charge increases. The change is relatively small due to shielding by d-electrons.

B. Ionisation Enthalpy

Ionisation enthalpy generally increases across a transition series, although the trend is not regular.

C. Melting and Boiling Points

Transition elements generally have high melting and boiling points due to strong metallic bonding.

7. Important Compounds of Transition Elements

A. Potassium Dichromate (K2Cr2O7)

Potassium dichromate is an orange crystalline solid. It acts as a strong oxidising agent in acidic medium.

Preparation:

It is prepared from chromite ore (FeCr2O4) through sodium chromate and sodium dichromate.

Important reaction:

Cr2O72- + 14H+ + 6e- → 2Cr3+ + 7H2O

In acidic medium, orange dichromate ions are reduced to green Cr3+ ions.

B. Potassium Permanganate (KMnO4)

Potassium permanganate is a dark purple crystalline solid. It is a powerful oxidising agent.

Reduction in acidic medium:

MnO4- + 8H+ + 5e- → Mn2+ + 4H2O

Reduction in neutral or weakly alkaline medium:

MnO4- + 2H2O + 3e- → MnO2 + 4OH-

Reduction in strongly alkaline medium:

MnO4- + e- → MnO42-

8. f-Block Elements

The f-block elements are also called inner transition elements. Their differentiating electron enters the f-orbital.

Two Series of f-Block Elements

  • Lanthanoids: 4f series, atomic numbers 58–71.
  • Actinoids: 5f series, atomic numbers 90–103.

9. Lanthanoids

Lanthanoids are the elements in which the 4f orbitals are progressively filled. They are also known as rare earth elements.

General Electronic Configuration

[Xe] 4f1-14 5d0-1 6s2

Properties of Lanthanoids

  • They are generally silvery-white metals.
  • They are electropositive in nature.
  • The most common oxidation state is +3.
  • Many lanthanoid ions are coloured.
  • Many lanthanoid ions show paramagnetism.

Lanthanoid Contraction

The gradual decrease in atomic and ionic radii of lanthanoids from left to right with increasing atomic number is called lanthanoid contraction.

Cause:

The 4f electrons have poor shielding effect. Therefore, effective nuclear charge increases across the series, causing a decrease in size.

Consequences of Lanthanoid Contraction

  1. The elements of the 4d and 5d series often have similar atomic radii, such as Zr and Hf.
  2. Separation of lanthanoids becomes difficult because their ionic sizes and chemical properties are similar.
  3. The basic strength of lanthanoid hydroxides decreases from La(OH)3 to Lu(OH)3.

10. Actinoids

Actinoids are the elements in which the 5f orbitals are progressively filled.

General Electronic Configuration

[Rn] 5f1-14 6d0-1 7s2

Properties of Actinoids

  • All actinoids are radioactive.
  • They show variable oxidation states.
  • Most actinoids are synthetic or occur in very small amounts.
  • They are generally more reactive than lanthanoids.
  • They show actinoid contraction.

Actinoid Contraction

The gradual decrease in atomic and ionic radii of actinoids with increasing atomic number is called actinoid contraction.

It occurs mainly due to the poor shielding effect of 5f electrons.

11. Difference Between Lanthanoids and Actinoids

Lanthanoids Actinoids
4f orbitals are filled. 5f orbitals are filled.
Most common oxidation state is +3. Show a wider range of oxidation states.
Most are non-radioactive, except promethium. All are radioactive.
Less tendency to form complexes. Greater tendency to form complexes.
Generally less reactive. Generally more reactive.

12. Important Uses of d- and f-Block Elements

  • Iron is used in construction and manufacturing steel.
  • Copper is used in electrical wiring.
  • Nickel is used in alloys and hydrogenation catalysts.
  • Chromium is used in stainless steel and plating.
  • Manganese dioxide is used in dry-cell batteries.
  • Uranium is used as nuclear fuel.
  • Cerium compounds are used in glass polishing.

13. Important Definitions

1. Transition Elements: Elements having partially filled d-orbitals in their atoms or in at least one common oxidation state.

2. Inner Transition Elements: Elements in which the differentiating electron enters an f-orbital.

3. Variable Oxidation State: The ability of an element to exhibit more than one oxidation state.

4. Lanthanoid Contraction: Gradual decrease in the size of lanthanoid atoms and ions with increasing atomic number.

5. Actinoid Contraction: Gradual decrease in the size of actinoid atoms and ions with increasing atomic number.

6. Paramagnetism: Attraction of a substance towards a magnetic field due to the presence of unpaired electrons.

14. Important Formulas

  • Magnetic moment: μ = √[n(n + 2)] BM
  • d-block configuration: (n-1)d1-10 ns0-2
  • f-block configuration: (n-2)f1-14 (n-1)d0-1 ns2

15. Important Questions and Answers

Q1. Why do transition elements show variable oxidation states?

Because the energies of ns and (n-1)d orbitals are very close, electrons from both orbitals can take part in bonding.

Q2. Why are transition metal ions coloured?

Due to d-d electronic transitions, in which electrons absorb visible light and move between split d-orbitals.

Q3. Why do transition elements act as catalysts?

Due to their variable oxidation states and ability to provide suitable surfaces for chemical reactions.

Q4. What is lanthanoid contraction?

It is the gradual decrease in the atomic and ionic radii of lanthanoids with increasing atomic number.

Q5. Why are actinoids radioactive?

Their nuclei are unstable, so they undergo radioactive decay.

Q6. Why is Cu2+ coloured but Zn2+ colourless?

Cu2+ has a partially filled 3d orbital and can show d-d transitions. Zn2+ has a completely filled 3d orbital, so d-d transitions are not possible.

16. Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs)

Q1. The general electronic configuration of d-block elements is:

(A) ns2 np1
(B) (n-1)d1-10 ns0-2
(C) ns1
(D) np6

Answer: (B)

Q2. Which element is not a transition element?

(A) Fe
(B) Cu
(C) Zn
(D) Cr

Answer: (C) Zn

Q3. The most common oxidation state of lanthanoids is:

(A) +1
(B) +2
(C) +3
(D) +4

Answer: (C) +3

Q4. Which compound is purple in colour?

(A) KMnO4
(B) K2Cr2O7
(C) NaCl
(D) ZnSO4

Answer: (A) KMnO4

Q5. All actinoids are:

(A) Colourless
(B) Radioactive
(C) Gases
(D) Non-metals

Answer: (B) Radioactive

Q6. The magnetic moment depends on:

(A) Atomic mass
(B) Number of unpaired electrons
(C) Atomic number only
(D) Density

Answer: (B) Number of unpaired electrons

17. Chapter Summary

  • d-block elements are present in groups 3 to 12.
  • Transition elements show variable oxidation states.
  • Many transition metal ions are coloured and paramagnetic.
  • Transition metals often act as catalysts.
  • f-block elements are called inner transition elements.
  • Lanthanoids involve filling of 4f orbitals.
  • Actinoids involve filling of 5f orbitals.
  • Lanthanoid contraction is caused by poor shielding of 4f electrons.
  • All actinoids are radioactive.

Chapter 5: Coordination Compounds

1. Introduction

Coordination compounds are compounds in which a central metal atom or ion is surrounded by a fixed number of ions or molecules called ligands. These ligands are attached to the central metal through coordinate bonds.

Examples:

  • [Co(NH3)6]Cl3
  • K4[Fe(CN)6]
  • [Cu(NH3)4]SO4
  • [Ag(NH3)2]Cl

2. Important Terms Used in Coordination Compounds

A. Central Metal Atom or Ion

The metal atom or ion to which ligands are directly attached is called the central metal atom or ion.

Example: In [Co(NH3)6]3+, Co3+ is the central metal ion.

B. Ligands

Ligands are ions or molecules that donate at least one lone pair of electrons to the central metal atom or ion to form a coordinate bond.

Examples:

  • NH3 – Ammine
  • H2O – Aqua
  • Cl- – Chlorido
  • CN- – Cyanido
  • OH- – Hydroxido
  • CO – Carbonyl

C. Coordination Number

The number of donor atoms directly attached to the central metal atom or ion is called its coordination number.

Examples:

  • [Ag(NH3)2]+ – Coordination number 2
  • [Cu(NH3)4]2+ – Coordination number 4
  • [Co(NH3)6]3+ – Coordination number 6

D. Coordination Sphere

The central metal ion and the ligands directly attached to it are collectively called the coordination sphere. It is written inside square brackets.

Example: In [Co(NH3)6]Cl3, [Co(NH3)6]3+ is the coordination sphere.

E. Counter Ions

The ions present outside the coordination sphere are called counter ions. They balance the charge of the coordination ion.

Example: In [Co(NH3)6]Cl3, three Cl- ions are counter ions.

F. Coordination Polyhedron

The spatial arrangement of ligands around the central metal ion is called the coordination polyhedron.

Examples:

  • Coordination number 2 – Linear
  • Coordination number 4 – Tetrahedral or Square planar
  • Coordination number 6 – Octahedral

3. Types of Ligands

A. Monodentate Ligands

Ligands that donate one pair of electrons through only one donor atom are called monodentate ligands.

Examples: NH3, H2O, Cl-, CN-.

B. Bidentate Ligands

Ligands that can donate two pairs of electrons through two donor atoms are called bidentate ligands.

Examples:

  • Ethane-1,2-diamine (en)
  • Oxalate ion (C2O4)2-

C. Polydentate Ligands

Ligands that have more than two donor atoms and can attach to the central metal through several sites are called polydentate ligands.

Example: EDTA4- is a hexadentate ligand.

D. Ambidentate Ligands

Ligands that can coordinate through either of two different donor atoms are called ambidentate ligands.

Examples:

  • NO2- – Can coordinate through N or O.
  • SCN- – Can coordinate through S or N.

4. Classification of Coordination Compounds

A. Cationic Complexes

Complexes in which the coordination sphere carries a positive charge are called cationic complexes.

Example: [Co(NH3)6]Cl3.

B. Anionic Complexes

Complexes in which the coordination sphere carries a negative charge are called anionic complexes.

Example: K4[Fe(CN)6].

C. Neutral Complexes

Complexes in which the coordination entity has no overall charge are called neutral complexes.

Example: [Ni(CO)4].

5. Oxidation Number of Central Metal Ion

The oxidation number is the charge assigned to the central metal ion after considering the charges of the ligands.

Example 1: Find the oxidation state of Co in [Co(NH3)6]Cl3.

Let oxidation state of Co = x.
NH3 is neutral and three Cl- ions are outside the bracket.
Therefore, x = +3.

Answer: +3

Example 2: Find the oxidation state of Fe in K4[Fe(CN)6].

Let oxidation state of Fe = x.
Each CN- has charge -1.
x + 6(-1) = -4
x - 6 = -4
x = +2.

Answer: +2

6. Nomenclature of Coordination Compounds

Coordination compounds are named according to IUPAC rules. The following rules are important:

  1. Name the cation first and the anion second.
  2. Within a complex, name ligands before the central metal.
  3. Ligands are named in alphabetical order, ignoring multiplicative prefixes.
  4. Use di, tri, tetra, penta and hexa to indicate the number of simple ligands.
  5. Use bis, tris and tetrakis for complicated ligand names or names containing prefixes.
  6. Write the oxidation state of the central metal in Roman numerals in parentheses.
  7. For an anionic complex, the metal name generally ends in -ate.

Common Ligand Names

Ligand IUPAC Name
NH3Ammine
H2OAqua
COCarbonyl
Cl-Chlorido
Br-Bromido
CN-Cyanido
OH-Hydroxido
NO2-Nitro / Nitrito (depending on bonding)

Examples of IUPAC Names

  • [Co(NH3)6]Cl3 – Hexaamminecobalt(III) chloride.
  • K4[Fe(CN)6] – Potassium hexacyanidoferrate(II).
  • [Ag(NH3)2]Cl – Diamminesilver(I) chloride.
  • [Ni(CO)4] – Tetracarbonylnickel(0).

7. Isomerism in Coordination Compounds

The existence of two or more coordination compounds having the same molecular formula but different arrangements of atoms or ligands is called isomerism.

A. Structural Isomerism

1. Ionisation Isomerism

It occurs when a ligand inside the coordination sphere and a counter ion outside the sphere exchange positions.

Example:

  • [Co(NH3)5Br]SO4
  • [Co(NH3)5SO4]Br

2. Hydrate Isomerism

It occurs when water molecules are present inside or outside the coordination sphere in different ways.

Example:

  • [Cr(H2O)6]Cl3
  • [Cr(H2O)5Cl]Cl2.H2O

3. Linkage Isomerism

It occurs when an ambidentate ligand attaches to the central metal through different donor atoms.

Example: Nitro and nitrito complexes of NO2-.

4. Coordination Isomerism

It occurs when ligands are exchanged between the cationic and anionic complex ions in a compound containing both.

Example:

  • [Co(NH3)6][Cr(CN)6]
  • [Cr(NH3)6][Co(CN)6]

B. Stereoisomerism

1. Geometrical Isomerism

It occurs when ligands have different spatial arrangements around the central metal ion.

Example: cis and trans forms of [Pt(NH3)2Cl2].

  • Cis: Similar ligands are adjacent to each other.
  • Trans: Similar ligands are opposite to each other.

2. Optical Isomerism

Optical isomers are non-superimposable mirror images of each other. They rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions.

Example: [Co(en)3]3+.

8. Bonding in Coordination Compounds

A. Werner's Theory

Alfred Werner proposed a theory to explain the structure and bonding of coordination compounds.

Main postulates:

  1. Metals show primary and secondary valencies.
  2. Primary valency corresponds to oxidation state.
  3. Secondary valency corresponds to coordination number.
  4. Primary valencies are ionisable.
  5. Secondary valencies are non-ionisable.
  6. Secondary valencies have fixed spatial arrangements.

B. Valence Bond Theory (VBT)

According to VBT, ligands donate lone pairs of electrons into vacant hybrid orbitals of the central metal ion. These overlapping orbitals form coordinate bonds.

Hybridisation and Geometry

Hybridisation Geometry Example
sp Linear [Ag(NH3)2]+
sp3 Tetrahedral [NiCl4]2-
dsp2 Square planar [Ni(CN)4]2-
d2sp3 Octahedral [Fe(CN)6]4-
sp3d2 Octahedral [CoF6]3-

9. Strong Field and Weak Field Ligands

Ligands are classified according to their ability to split the d-orbitals of the central metal ion.

Weak Field Ligands

These produce relatively small crystal field splitting and often form high-spin complexes.

Examples: I-, Br-, Cl-, F- and H2O.

Strong Field Ligands

These produce relatively large crystal field splitting and can form low-spin complexes.

Examples: CN-, CO and NO2-.

10. Crystal Field Theory (CFT)

Crystal Field Theory explains the bonding, colour and magnetic properties of coordination compounds by considering the electrostatic interaction between the central metal ion and surrounding ligands.

A. Octahedral Complexes

In an octahedral complex, six ligands approach the central metal ion along the x, y and z axes.

The five d-orbitals split into two energy groups:

  • Lower energy: t2g (dxy, dyz, dzx)
  • Higher energy: eg (dx2-y2, dz2)

The energy difference between these groups is called octahedral crystal field splitting energy (Δo).

B. Tetrahedral Complexes

In tetrahedral complexes, the d-orbitals split into:

  • Lower energy: e orbitals.
  • Higher energy: t2 orbitals.

Tetrahedral splitting energy is smaller than octahedral splitting energy. Approximately, Δt = 4/9 Δo.

11. Colour of Coordination Compounds

Many coordination compounds are coloured because electrons absorb visible light and move from lower-energy d-orbitals to higher-energy d-orbitals.

The colour observed is generally complementary to the colour of light absorbed.

Complexes with d0 or d10 configurations generally do not show d-d transitions and are often colourless, although other electronic transitions can produce colour.

12. Magnetic Properties

Magnetic behaviour depends mainly on the number of unpaired electrons present in the complex.

  • Paramagnetic: Contains one or more unpaired electrons.
  • Diamagnetic: All electrons are paired.

Spin-only magnetic moment formula:

μ = √[n(n + 2)] BM

Where n is the number of unpaired electrons.

13. Stability of Coordination Compounds

The stability of a coordination compound refers to the tendency of the complex to remain formed in solution.

Stability is often expressed using the formation constant (Kf). A larger formation constant generally indicates greater thermodynamic stability.

14. Chelate Effect

When a polydentate ligand attaches to a central metal ion through two or more donor atoms and forms ring structures, the resulting complex is called a chelate complex.

The increased stability of many such complexes compared with similar complexes containing monodentate ligands is called the chelate effect.

Example: Complexes formed by EDTA4-.

15. Applications of Coordination Compounds

  • Biological systems: Haemoglobin contains iron, while chlorophyll contains magnesium.
  • Medicine: Cisplatin is used in the treatment of certain types of cancer.
  • Analytical chemistry: EDTA is used in complexometric titrations to estimate metal ions.
  • Metallurgy: Complex formation is used in the extraction and purification of some metals.
  • Photography: Thiosulfate forms a soluble complex with silver ions during photographic fixing.

16. Important Formulae and Facts

  • Magnetic moment: μ = √[n(n + 2)] BM
  • Octahedral splitting: Δo
  • Tetrahedral splitting: Δt = 4/9 Δo
  • Coordination number = Number of donor atoms attached to the metal.
  • Oxidation state = Charge balance of the coordination entity.

17. Important Questions and Answers

Q1. What is a coordination compound?

A compound in which a central metal atom or ion is surrounded by ligands attached through coordinate bonds is called a coordination compound.

Q2. What is a ligand?

A ligand is an ion or molecule that donates an electron pair to a central metal atom or ion.

Q3. What is coordination number?

It is the number of donor atoms directly bonded to the central metal atom or ion.

Q4. What is chelation?

Chelation is the formation of ring structures when a polydentate ligand coordinates to a central metal ion through multiple donor atoms.

Q5. What is linkage isomerism?

It is a type of structural isomerism in which an ambidentate ligand attaches to the central metal through different donor atoms.

Q6. What is the difference between strong and weak field ligands?

Strong field ligands produce larger d-orbital splitting, whereas weak field ligands produce smaller d-orbital splitting.

18. Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs)

Q1. The central metal ion in [Co(NH3)6]Cl3 is:

(A) Co+
(B) Co2+
(C) Co3+
(D) Co4+

Answer: (C) Co3+

Q2. Which of the following is a bidentate ligand?

(A) NH3
(B) H2O
(C) en
(D) Cl-

Answer: (C) en

Q3. The coordination number of Co in [Co(NH3)6]3+ is:

(A) 2
(B) 4
(C) 6
(D) 8

Answer: (C) 6

Q4. Which of the following is a strong field ligand?

(A) I-
(B) Cl-
(C) CN-
(D) F-

Answer: (C) CN-

Q5. The geometry of [Ag(NH3)2]+ is:

(A) Linear
(B) Tetrahedral
(C) Square planar
(D) Octahedral

Answer: (A) Linear

Q6. Which theory explains d-orbital splitting?

(A) Atomic theory
(B) Crystal Field Theory
(C) Kinetic theory
(D) Collision theory

Answer: (B) Crystal Field Theory

19. Chapter Summary

  • Coordination compounds contain a central metal and ligands.
  • Ligands donate electron pairs to the central metal ion.
  • Coordination number counts directly attached donor atoms.
  • Ligands may be mono-, bi- or polydentate.
  • Coordination compounds show structural and stereoisomerism.
  • Werner's theory explains primary and secondary valencies.
  • VBT explains bonding through hybridisation.
  • CFT explains d-orbital splitting and many colour and magnetic properties.
  • Coordination compounds have biological, medical and industrial applications.

Chapter 6: Haloalkanes and Haloarenes

1. Introduction

Haloalkanes and haloarenes are organic compounds in which one or more hydrogen atoms of hydrocarbons are replaced by halogen atoms such as fluorine, chlorine, bromine or iodine.

Halogens: Fluorine (F), Chlorine (Cl), Bromine (Br), Iodine (I).

2. Classification of Halo Compounds

A. Haloalkanes (Alkyl Halides)

Compounds in which a halogen atom is attached to an sp3-hybridised carbon atom of an alkyl group are called haloalkanes.

General formula: R-X

Examples: CH3Cl, C2H5Br, CH3CH2CH2Cl.

B. Haloarenes (Aryl Halides)

Compounds in which a halogen atom is directly attached to an sp2-hybridised carbon atom of an aromatic ring are called haloarenes.

General formula: Ar-X

Example: C6H5Cl (Chlorobenzene).

3. Classification on the Basis of Number of Halogen Atoms

A. Monohalo Compounds

Compounds containing one halogen atom.

Example: CH3Cl.

B. Dihalo Compounds

Compounds containing two halogen atoms.

Example: CH2Cl2.

C. Trihalo Compounds

Compounds containing three halogen atoms.

Example: CHCl3.

D. Polyhalo Compounds

Compounds containing more than three halogen atoms.

Example: CCl4.

4. Classification of Haloalkanes on the Basis of Carbon Attached to Halogen

A. Primary (1°) Haloalkane

A haloalkane in which the carbon atom attached to the halogen is bonded to only one other carbon atom is called a primary haloalkane.

Example: CH3CH2Cl.

B. Secondary (2°) Haloalkane

A haloalkane in which the carbon atom attached to the halogen is bonded to two other carbon atoms is called a secondary haloalkane.

Example: CH3CHClCH3.

C. Tertiary (3°) Haloalkane

A haloalkane in which the carbon atom attached to the halogen is bonded to three other carbon atoms is called a tertiary haloalkane.

Example: (CH3)3CCl.

5. Nomenclature of Haloalkanes and Haloarenes

IUPAC Naming Rules

  1. Select the longest carbon chain containing the halogen-bearing carbon.
  2. Number the chain to give the substituents the lowest possible locants.
  3. Use fluoro, chloro, bromo and iodo as prefixes.
  4. Write substituents in alphabetical order.
  5. For aromatic compounds, use benzene as the parent structure where appropriate.

Examples

  • CH3Cl – Chloromethane.
  • CH3CH2Br – Bromoethane.
  • CH3CHClCH3 – 2-Chloropropane.
  • CH2Cl2 – Dichloromethane.
  • C6H5Cl – Chlorobenzene.
  • C6H5Br – Bromobenzene.

6. Nature of C-X Bond

The carbon-halogen bond is polar because halogens are more electronegative than carbon.

Carbon acquires a partial positive charge (δ+) and halogen acquires a partial negative charge (δ-).

Bond representation: Cδ+ - Xδ-

Bond Length

Bond length increases with the size of the halogen atom.

Order: C-F < C-Cl < C-Br < C-I

Bond Strength

Bond strength generally decreases as the size of the halogen atom increases.

Order: C-F > C-Cl > C-Br > C-I

7. Methods of Preparation of Haloalkanes

A. From Alcohols

Haloalkanes can be prepared by replacing the hydroxyl group of alcohols with halogen atoms.

Using hydrogen halides:

ROH + HX → RX + H2O

Using thionyl chloride:

ROH + SOCl2 → RCl + SO2 + HCl

Thionyl chloride is often preferred because its gaseous by-products escape, helping to obtain a relatively pure alkyl chloride.

B. From Hydrocarbons by Free Radical Halogenation

Alkanes react with chlorine or bromine in the presence of sunlight or ultraviolet light.

CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl

Condition: UV light or sunlight.

C. Addition of Hydrogen Halides to Alkenes

Hydrogen halides add across the double bond of alkenes to form haloalkanes.

CH2=CH2 + HBr → CH3CH2Br

D. Halogen Exchange Reactions

Finkelstein Reaction:

Alkyl chlorides or bromides react with sodium iodide in dry acetone to form alkyl iodides.

R-Cl + NaI → R-I + NaCl

Swarts Reaction:

Alkyl chlorides or bromides react with metallic fluorides to form alkyl fluorides.

R-Cl + AgF → R-F + AgCl

8. Methods of Preparation of Haloarenes

A. Direct Halogenation of Benzene

Benzene reacts with chlorine in the presence of anhydrous ferric chloride to form chlorobenzene.

C6H6 + Cl2 → C6H5Cl + HCl

Condition: Anhydrous FeCl3.

B. From Diazonium Salts

Sandmeyer Reaction:

Aromatic diazonium salts react with cuprous chloride or cuprous bromide to form aryl halides.

C6H5N2+Cl- + CuCl → C6H5Cl + N2

Gattermann Reaction:

Diazonium salts react with HCl or HBr in the presence of copper powder to form aryl chlorides or bromides.

Balz-Schiemann Reaction:

Aryl diazonium tetrafluoroborate on heating gives aryl fluoride.

C6H5N2+BF4- → C6H5F + BF3 + N2

9. Physical Properties of Haloalkanes

  • Most haloalkanes are colourless in pure form.
  • Many have characteristic sweet smells.
  • They are generally insoluble or only slightly soluble in water.
  • They are generally soluble in organic solvents.
  • Many have higher boiling points than corresponding alkanes.

Boiling Point

For a given alkyl group, boiling point generally increases with increasing molecular mass of the halogen.

General order: R-F < R-Cl < R-Br < R-I

For isomeric haloalkanes, increased branching generally decreases boiling point because the surface area decreases.

10. Chemical Reactions of Haloalkanes

A. Nucleophilic Substitution Reactions

In these reactions, a nucleophile replaces the halogen atom in a haloalkane.

General reaction: R-X + Nu- → R-Nu + X-

Examples

1. Formation of Alcohol:

R-X + KOH(aq) → R-OH + KX

2. Formation of Nitrile:

R-X + KCN → R-CN + KX

3. Formation of Isocyanide:

R-X + AgCN → R-NC + AgX

4. Formation of Ether:

R-X + NaOR' → R-O-R' + NaX

5. Formation of Amine:

R-X + 2NH3 → R-NH2 + NH4X

11. SN1 and SN2 Mechanisms

A. SN2 Mechanism

SN2 stands for Substitution Nucleophilic Bimolecular. It is a one-step reaction in which bond formation and bond breaking occur simultaneously.

Rate law:

Rate = k[RX][Nu-]

Characteristics:

  • It occurs in a single step.
  • The nucleophile attacks from the side opposite to the leaving group.
  • It generally gives inversion of configuration (Walden inversion).
  • Primary haloalkanes generally react faster than secondary and tertiary ones.
  • Steric hindrance slows down the reaction.

Reactivity order:

CH3X > 1° > 2° > 3°

B. SN1 Mechanism

SN1 stands for Substitution Nucleophilic Unimolecular. It generally occurs in two steps.

Step 1: Formation of Carbocation

R-X → R+ + X-

Step 2: Attack of Nucleophile

R+ + Nu- → R-Nu

Rate law:

Rate = k[RX]

Characteristics:

  • It generally occurs in two or more steps.
  • A carbocation intermediate is formed.
  • Carbocation rearrangement may occur.
  • It generally favours tertiary haloalkanes.
  • It may produce racemisation at a chiral centre.

Reactivity order:

3° > 2° > 1° > CH3X

12. Elimination Reactions

When a haloalkane is heated with alcoholic KOH, a hydrogen atom and a halogen atom are removed from adjacent carbon atoms to form an alkene.

CH3CH2Br + KOH(alc) → CH2=CH2 + KBr + H2O

Saytzeff's Rule

In the elimination of HX from an unsymmetrical haloalkane, the major product is generally the more substituted alkene.

13. Reaction with Metals

A. Wurtz Reaction

Two molecules of an alkyl halide react with sodium metal in dry ether to form a higher alkane.

2R-X + 2Na → R-R + 2NaX

B. Fittig Reaction

Two molecules of an aryl halide react with sodium metal in dry ether to form a biaryl compound.

2Ar-X + 2Na → Ar-Ar + 2NaX

C. Wurtz-Fittig Reaction

An aryl halide and an alkyl halide react with sodium in dry ether to form an alkyl arene.

Ar-X + R-X + 2Na → Ar-R + 2NaX

14. Chemical Reactions of Haloarenes

A. Nucleophilic Substitution

Haloarenes are generally less reactive towards nucleophilic substitution than haloalkanes because of the partial double-bond character of the carbon-halogen bond.

B. Electrophilic Substitution

Halogens are deactivating but ortho-para directing in electrophilic aromatic substitution reactions.

1. Nitration:
