Chlorobenzene reacts with concentrated HNO3 in the presence of concentrated H2SO4 to form mainly ortho- and para-nitrochlorobenzene.

2. Sulphonation:

Chlorobenzene reacts with fuming sulphuric acid to form ortho- and para-chlorobenzenesulphonic acid.

3. Halogenation:

Chlorobenzene reacts with chlorine in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst to form ortho- and para-dichlorobenzene.

15. Why are Haloarenes Less Reactive than Haloalkanes?

  1. Resonance gives the carbon-halogen bond in haloarenes partial double-bond character.
  2. The carbon atom attached to halogen is sp2-hybridised and has greater s-character than the sp3 carbon of haloalkanes.
  3. The carbon-halogen bond in haloarenes is shorter and stronger.
  4. Formation of a phenyl carbocation is highly unfavourable.

16. Polyhalogen Compounds

A. Dichloromethane (CH2Cl2)

Dichloromethane is a colourless volatile liquid used as a solvent and in industrial processes.

B. Chloroform (CHCl3)

Chloroform is a colourless liquid with a characteristic smell. It was historically used as an anaesthetic but is no longer used for routine anaesthesia because of toxicity.

Oxidation reaction:

2CHCl3 + O2 → 2COCl2 + 2HCl

Phosgene (COCl2) is highly poisonous. Chloroform must be stored carefully in tightly closed, amber-coloured bottles.

C. Carbon Tetrachloride (CCl4)

Carbon tetrachloride is a colourless liquid. It was formerly used in fire extinguishers and as a solvent, but its use is restricted because of toxicity and environmental concerns.

D. Freons

Freons are chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), which were widely used as refrigerants and aerosol propellants. Many CFCs damage the ozone layer.

E. DDT

DDT (dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane) is a synthetic insecticide. It is persistent in the environment and can accumulate in food chains. Its use is restricted or banned in many countries.

17. Important Differences

Haloalkanes Haloarenes
Halogen is attached to sp3 carbon. Halogen is directly attached to sp2 carbon.
Generally more reactive towards nucleophilic substitution. Generally less reactive towards nucleophilic substitution.
Example: CH3Cl. Example: C6H5Cl.

18. Important Reagents and Their Uses

Reagent Purpose
Aqueous KOH Formation of alcohols
Alcoholic KOH Elimination to form alkenes
KCN Formation of nitriles
AgCN Formation of isocyanides
NaI in dry acetone Finkelstein reaction
Na in dry ether Wurtz and related reactions
SOCl2 Conversion of alcohols into alkyl chlorides

19. Important Definitions

1. Haloalkane: An organic compound in which a halogen atom is attached to an sp3-hybridised carbon atom.

2. Haloarene: An aromatic compound in which a halogen atom is directly attached to an aromatic ring.

3. Nucleophile: An electron-rich species that donates an electron pair to form a bond.

4. SN1 Reaction: A nucleophilic substitution reaction whose rate depends only on the concentration of the substrate.

5. SN2 Reaction: A bimolecular nucleophilic substitution reaction involving a single concerted step.

6. Elimination Reaction: A reaction in which atoms or groups are removed from adjacent atoms to form a multiple bond.

7. Ambidentate Nucleophile: A nucleophile that can attack through two different atoms.

20. Important Questions and Answers

Q1. Why is chloroform stored in dark-coloured bottles?

Chloroform can oxidise in the presence of air and light to form poisonous phosgene gas. Dark bottles reduce exposure to light.

Q2. Why is chlorobenzene less reactive than chloroethane?

In chlorobenzene, resonance gives the C-Cl bond partial double-bond character. The bond is therefore stronger and harder to break.

Q3. What is the difference between SN1 and SN2 reactions?

SN1 is a stepwise reaction with a carbocation intermediate and a first-order rate law. SN2 is a one-step reaction with a second-order rate law.

Q4. What is the Finkelstein reaction?

It is the conversion of alkyl chlorides or bromides into alkyl iodides using sodium iodide in dry acetone.

Q5. What is the Wurtz reaction?

It is the reaction of alkyl halides with sodium metal in dry ether to produce higher alkanes.

Q6. Why are halogens ortho-para directing?

Halogens donate electron density to the aromatic ring by resonance, increasing electron density at the ortho and para positions, although their inductive effect deactivates the ring.

21. Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs)

Q1. The general formula of haloalkanes is:

(A) R-OH
(B) R-X
(C) R-COOH
(D) R-NH2

Answer: (B) R-X

Q2. Which reagent is used in the Finkelstein reaction?

(A) NaOH
(B) NaI in dry acetone
(C) H2SO4
(D) KMnO4

Answer: (B) NaI in dry acetone

Q3. Which reaction generally follows a one-step mechanism?

(A) SN1
(B) SN2
(C) Both always
(D) Neither

Answer: (B) SN2

Q4. The major product of Wurtz reaction is:

(A) Alcohol
(B) Ether
(C) Higher alkane
(D) Aldehyde

Answer: (C) Higher alkane

Q5. Which compound can produce phosgene on oxidation?

(A) Methane
(B) Chloroform
(C) Ethanol
(D) Benzene

Answer: (B) Chloroform

Q6. Halogens in haloarenes are:

(A) Activating and meta directing
(B) Deactivating and ortho-para directing
(C) Activating and para only directing
(D) Deactivating and meta directing

Answer: (B) Deactivating and ortho-para directing

Q7. Which reagent converts an alcohol into an alkyl chloride?

(A) SOCl2
(B) NaCl
(C) H2O
(D) NaOH

Answer: (A) SOCl2

22. Chapter Summary

  • Haloalkanes contain halogen attached to sp3 carbon.
  • Haloarenes contain halogen directly attached to an aromatic ring.
  • The C-X bond is polar.
  • Haloalkanes undergo nucleophilic substitution and elimination reactions.
  • SN1 reactions involve carbocation formation.
  • SN2 reactions occur in a single concerted step.
  • Finkelstein reaction prepares alkyl iodides.
  • Wurtz reaction produces higher alkanes.
  • Haloarenes are generally less reactive towards nucleophilic substitution.
  • Halogens are deactivating but ortho-para directing in benzene rings.
  • Some polyhalogen compounds have important environmental and health effects.

Chapter 7: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers

1. Introduction

Alcohols, phenols and ethers are important classes of organic compounds containing oxygen atoms. They are widely used in industries, medicines, solvents and chemical manufacturing.

  • Alcohols contain the hydroxyl group (-OH) attached to an sp3 carbon.
  • Phenols contain the hydroxyl group directly attached to an aromatic ring.
  • Ethers contain an oxygen atom bonded to two alkyl or aryl groups.

2. Alcohols

Alcohols are organic compounds in which one or more hydroxyl groups (-OH) are attached to saturated carbon atoms.

General formula of monohydric alcohols: R-OH

Examples:

  • CH3OH – Methanol
  • C2H5OH – Ethanol
  • CH3CH2CH2OH – Propan-1-ol

3. Classification of Alcohols

A. On the Basis of Number of -OH Groups

1. Monohydric Alcohols:

Alcohols containing one hydroxyl group are called monohydric alcohols.

Example: CH3OH, C2H5OH.

2. Dihydric Alcohols:

Alcohols containing two hydroxyl groups are called dihydric alcohols.

Example: HO-CH2-CH2-OH (Ethane-1,2-diol).

3. Trihydric Alcohols:

Alcohols containing three hydroxyl groups are called trihydric alcohols.

Example: HOCH2-CHOH-CH2OH (Propane-1,2,3-triol).

B. On the Basis of the Carbon Attached to -OH

1. Primary (1°) Alcohol:

An alcohol in which the carbon atom attached to the hydroxyl group is bonded to only one other carbon atom (or no carbon atom in methanol) is called a primary alcohol.

Example: CH3CH2OH.

2. Secondary (2°) Alcohol:

An alcohol in which the carbon atom attached to -OH is bonded to two other carbon atoms is called a secondary alcohol.

Example: CH3CHOHCH3.

3. Tertiary (3°) Alcohol:

An alcohol in which the carbon atom attached to -OH is bonded to three other carbon atoms is called a tertiary alcohol.

Example: (CH3)3COH.

4. Phenols

Phenols are organic compounds in which one or more hydroxyl groups are directly attached to an aromatic ring carbon atom.

General formula: Ar-OH

Example: C6H5OH (Phenol).

Classification of Phenols

  • Monohydric phenols – Contain one -OH group.
  • Dihydric phenols – Contain two -OH groups.
  • Trihydric phenols – Contain three -OH groups.

Examples:

  • Phenol – C6H5OH
  • Catechol – Benzene-1,2-diol
  • Resorcinol – Benzene-1,3-diol
  • Hydroquinone – Benzene-1,4-diol
  • Pyrogallol – Benzene-1,2,3-triol

5. Ethers

Ethers are organic compounds in which an oxygen atom is bonded to two alkyl groups, two aryl groups or one alkyl and one aryl group.

General formula: R-O-R'

Examples:

  • CH3-O-CH3 – Methoxymethane
  • C2H5-O-C2H5 – Ethoxyethane
  • CH3-O-C2H5 – Methoxyethane
  • C6H5-O-CH3 – Methoxybenzene (Anisole)

6. Nomenclature of Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers

A. IUPAC Nomenclature of Alcohols

  1. Select the longest carbon chain containing the -OH group.
  2. Number the chain from the end nearest to the -OH group.
  3. Replace the final 'e' of the alkane name with 'ol'.
  4. Show the position of the hydroxyl group using a number.

Examples:

  • CH3OH – Methanol
  • CH3CH2OH – Ethanol
  • CH3CH2CH2OH – Propan-1-ol
  • CH3CHOHCH3 – Propan-2-ol
  • HOCH2CH2OH – Ethane-1,2-diol

B. IUPAC Nomenclature of Phenols

Phenol is used as the parent name when the -OH group is directly attached to a benzene ring.

  • 2-Methylphenol – o-Cresol
  • 3-Methylphenol – m-Cresol
  • 4-Methylphenol – p-Cresol
  • Benzene-1,2-diol – Catechol

C. IUPAC Nomenclature of Ethers

Ethers are generally named as alkoxyalkanes. The smaller alkyl group with oxygen is named as an alkoxy substituent.

  • CH3OCH3 – Methoxymethane
  • CH3OC2H5 – Methoxyethane
  • C2H5OC2H5 – Ethoxyethane

7. Preparation of Alcohols

A. From Alkenes by Hydration

Alkenes react with water in the presence of an acid catalyst to form alcohols.

CH2=CH2 + H2O → CH3CH2OH

Condition: Acid catalyst.

B. By Hydroboration-Oxidation

Alkenes react with diborane or BH3 followed by oxidation with alkaline hydrogen peroxide to form alcohols.

Reagents: 1. BH3/THF
2. H2O2/OH-

This reaction generally gives anti-Markovnikov addition of the hydroxyl group.

C. From Haloalkanes

Haloalkanes react with aqueous KOH to form alcohols.

R-X + KOH(aq) → R-OH + KX

D. By Reduction of Aldehydes and Ketones

Aldehydes:

RCHO + 2[H] → RCH2OH

Ketones:

RCOR' + 2[H] → RCHOHR'

Common reducing agents include NaBH4 and LiAlH4.

E. By Reduction of Carboxylic Acids

Carboxylic acids can be reduced to primary alcohols using LiAlH4.

RCOOH + 4[H] → RCH2OH + H2O

F. By Reduction of Esters

Esters on reduction with LiAlH4 produce alcohols.

RCOOR' + 4[H] → RCH2OH + R'OH

8. Preparation of Phenols

A. From Haloarenes

Chlorobenzene is heated with aqueous sodium hydroxide at high temperature and pressure to form sodium phenoxide. Acidification gives phenol.

C6H5Cl + 2NaOH → C6H5ONa + NaCl + H2O

C6H5ONa + HCl → C6H5OH + NaCl

B. From Benzene Sulphonic Acid

Benzene sulphonic acid or its sodium salt on fusion with NaOH gives sodium phenoxide. Acidification gives phenol.

C. From Diazonium Salts

Benzene diazonium chloride on warming with water produces phenol.

C6H5N2+Cl- + H2O → C6H5OH + N2 + HCl

D. From Cumene

Cumene is oxidised by air to cumene hydroperoxide. Acidic hydrolysis produces phenol and acetone.

Cumene + O2 → Cumene hydroperoxide

Cumene hydroperoxide → Phenol + Acetone

9. Preparation of Ethers

A. Dehydration of Alcohols

Two molecules of alcohol react with concentrated sulphuric acid at about 413 K to form an ether.

2C2H5OH → C2H5OC2H5 + H2O

Condition: Concentrated H2SO4, about 413 K.

B. Williamson Ether Synthesis

Sodium alkoxide reacts with an alkyl halide to form an ether. This reaction is known as Williamson ether synthesis.

RONa + R'X → ROR' + NaX

It generally proceeds through an SN2 mechanism. Primary alkyl halides are preferred because bulky alkyl halides often undergo elimination.

10. Physical Properties of Alcohols

A. Nature

Lower alcohols are generally colourless liquids. Higher alcohols may be liquids or solids.

B. Hydrogen Bonding

Alcohol molecules form intermolecular hydrogen bonds because of the presence of the -OH group.

Hydrogen bonding is responsible for their relatively high boiling points.

C. Boiling Points

Alcohols generally have higher boiling points than corresponding alkanes and ethers because of intermolecular hydrogen bonding.

D. Solubility in Water

Lower alcohols are highly soluble in water because they form hydrogen bonds with water molecules.

Solubility generally decreases as the length of the hydrocarbon chain increases.

11. Physical Properties of Phenols

  • Pure phenol is generally a colourless crystalline solid.
  • It may turn pink or reddish on exposure to air.
  • Phenol has a relatively high boiling point due to hydrogen bonding.
  • It is moderately soluble in water.
  • It is soluble in many organic solvents.

12. Physical Properties of Ethers

  • Lower ethers are generally colourless and volatile liquids.
  • Ethers have a characteristic smell.
  • They are slightly soluble in water.
  • They are generally soluble in organic solvents.
  • Their boiling points are lower than those of corresponding alcohols.

13. Chemical Reactions of Alcohols

A. Reaction with Sodium Metal

Alcohols react with sodium metal to form sodium alkoxides and hydrogen gas.

2ROH + 2Na → 2RONa + H2

B. Reaction with Hydrogen Halides

Alcohols react with hydrogen halides to form haloalkanes.

ROH + HX → RX + H2O

C. Reaction with Phosphorus Halides

Alcohols react with phosphorus trichloride to form alkyl chlorides.

3ROH + PCl3 → 3RCl + H3PO3

D. Reaction with Thionyl Chloride

ROH + SOCl2 → RCl + SO2 + HCl

E. Dehydration of Alcohols

Alcohols lose water when heated with concentrated sulphuric acid to form alkenes.

CH3CH2OH → CH2=CH2 + H2O

Condition: Concentrated H2SO4, about 443 K.

F. Oxidation of Alcohols

Primary Alcohol:

Primary alcohols are oxidised to aldehydes and then to carboxylic acids under suitable conditions.

RCH2OH → RCHO → RCOOH

Secondary Alcohol:

Secondary alcohols are oxidised to ketones.

R2CHOH → R2C=O

Tertiary Alcohol:

Tertiary alcohols resist oxidation under mild conditions. Strong oxidising conditions can cause carbon-carbon bond cleavage.

G. Dehydrogenation of Alcohols

Primary and secondary alcohols pass over heated copper at 573 K to form aldehydes and ketones respectively.

RCH2OH → RCHO + H2

R2CHOH → R2C=O + H2

14. Chemical Reactions of Phenols

A. Acidic Nature of Phenol

Phenol is weakly acidic because it can lose a proton to form the resonance-stabilised phenoxide ion.

C6H5OH ⇌ C6H5O- + H+

B. Reaction with Sodium

2C6H5OH + 2Na → 2C6H5ONa + H2

C. Reaction with Sodium Hydroxide

Phenol reacts with sodium hydroxide to form sodium phenoxide.

C6H5OH + NaOH → C6H5ONa + H2O

Phenol does not react with sodium bicarbonate to release carbon dioxide under ordinary conditions because it is weaker than carbonic acid.

D. Bromination

Phenol reacts with bromine water to produce 2,4,6-tribromophenol as a white precipitate.

C6H5OH + 3Br2 → C6H2Br3OH + 3HBr

E. Nitration

Phenol reacts with dilute nitric acid to form a mixture of ortho-nitrophenol and para-nitrophenol.

With concentrated nitric acid, phenol forms 2,4,6-trinitrophenol, also called picric acid.

F. Kolbe's Reaction (Kolbe-Schmitt Reaction)

Sodium phenoxide reacts with carbon dioxide under pressure and is then acidified to produce salicylic acid (2-hydroxybenzoic acid) as the major product.

Sodium phenoxide + CO2 → Sodium salicylate

Sodium salicylate + H+ → Salicylic acid

G. Reimer-Tiemann Reaction

Phenol reacts with chloroform and aqueous sodium hydroxide to give mainly salicylaldehyde after acidification.

Reagents: CHCl3, NaOH, followed by acidification.

H. Reaction with Zinc Dust

Phenol on heating with zinc dust forms benzene.

C6H5OH + Zn → C6H6 + ZnO

15. Chemical Reactions of Ethers

A. Cleavage by Hydrogen Halides

Ethers react with concentrated HI or HBr to break the carbon-oxygen bond and form alcohols or alkyl halides.

ROR' + HI → RI + R'OH

With excess HI and suitable conditions, the alcohol formed can further react to give another alkyl iodide.

B. Reaction of Anisole with HI

Anisole reacts with HI to form phenol and methyl iodide.

C6H5OCH3 + HI → C6H5OH + CH3I

The alkyl-oxygen bond is cleaved because the aryl-oxygen bond has partial double-bond character.

C. Electrophilic Substitution in Anisole

The -OCH3 group activates the benzene ring and directs incoming electrophiles mainly to the ortho and para positions.

1. Bromination:

Anisole reacts with bromine to give ortho- and para-bromoanisole, with para generally favoured.

2. Nitration:

Anisole reacts with nitrating mixture to form ortho- and para-nitroanisole.

3. Friedel-Crafts Reaction:

Anisole undergoes Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation to give mainly ortho and para products.

16. Acidity of Alcohols and Phenols

Why is Phenol More Acidic than Alcohol?

Phenol is more acidic than alcohol because the phenoxide ion formed after losing H+ is stabilised by resonance. Alkoxide ions formed from alcohols do not have this type of resonance stabilisation.

Effect of Substituents on Phenol Acidity

  • Electron-withdrawing groups generally increase acidity.
  • Electron-donating groups generally decrease acidity.
  • Nitro groups increase the stability of the phenoxide ion.
  • Methyl groups generally decrease acidity.

17. Important Named Reactions

1. Williamson Ether Synthesis

RONa + R'X → ROR' + NaX

Used for the preparation of ethers.

2. Kolbe-Schmitt Reaction

Sodium phenoxide reacts with CO2 followed by acidification to form salicylic acid.

3. Reimer-Tiemann Reaction

Phenol reacts with CHCl3 and NaOH followed by acidification to form salicylaldehyde.

4. Cumene Process

Oxidation of cumene followed by acidic decomposition produces phenol and acetone.

18. Important Differences

Alcohols Phenols
-OH is attached to sp3 carbon. -OH is directly attached to an aromatic ring.
Generally less acidic. More acidic than ordinary alcohols.
Do not normally react with NaOH. React with NaOH to form phenoxide salts.
Alcohols Ethers
Contain an -OH group. Contain an R-O-R' linkage.
Show intermolecular hydrogen bonding. Cannot hydrogen-bond with themselves.
Generally have higher boiling points. Generally have lower boiling points.

19. Important Chemical Tests

A. Lucas Test

Lucas reagent is a mixture of concentrated HCl and anhydrous ZnCl2. It is used to distinguish primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols.

  • Tertiary alcohol: Immediate turbidity.
  • Secondary alcohol: Turbidity after a few minutes.
  • Primary alcohol: No turbidity at room temperature; reaction is very slow.

B. Neutral Ferric Chloride Test

Phenol gives a violet, blue or green coloured complex with neutral ferric chloride, depending on the compound.

C. Bromine Water Test

Phenol decolourises bromine water and produces a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

20. Important Formulae and Reagents

  • Alcohol: R-OH
  • Phenol: Ar-OH
  • Ether: R-O-R'
  • Lucas reagent: Concentrated HCl + anhydrous ZnCl2
  • Williamson synthesis: RONa + R'X
  • Kolbe-Schmitt reaction: Sodium phenoxide + CO2
  • Reimer-Tiemann reaction: Phenol + CHCl3 + NaOH
  • Cumene process: Cumene oxidation followed by acid cleavage

21. Important Questions and Answers

Q1. Why do alcohols have higher boiling points than ethers?

Alcohols form intermolecular hydrogen bonds due to their hydroxyl groups. Ethers cannot form similar hydrogen bonds with themselves, so their boiling points are generally lower.

Q2. Why is phenol more acidic than ethanol?

Phenol forms a resonance-stabilised phenoxide ion, whereas ethanol forms an alkoxide ion without comparable resonance stabilisation.

Q3. What is Williamson ether synthesis?

It is the reaction of sodium alkoxide with an alkyl halide to form an ether.

Q4. What is Reimer-Tiemann reaction?

It is the reaction of phenol with chloroform and sodium hydroxide followed by acidification to produce mainly salicylaldehyde.

Q5. What is Kolbe-Schmitt reaction?

It is the reaction of sodium phenoxide with carbon dioxide under pressure followed by acidification to produce salicylic acid.

Q6. What is the Lucas test?

It is a test used to distinguish primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols using concentrated HCl and anhydrous ZnCl2.

Q7. Why does phenol react with NaOH but not with NaHCO3?

Phenol is sufficiently acidic to react with NaOH, but it is weaker than carbonic acid and therefore does not normally liberate CO2 from sodium bicarbonate.

22. Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs)

Q1. The functional group of alcohols is:

(A) -CHO
(B) -COOH
(C) -OH
(D) -NH2

Answer: (C) -OH

Q2. Which of the following is a secondary alcohol?

(A) CH3OH
(B) CH3CH2OH
(C) CH3CHOHCH3
(D) (CH3)3COH

Answer: (C) CH3CHOHCH3

Q3. Phenol reacts with NaOH to form:

(A) Benzene
(B) Sodium phenoxide
(C) Ethanol
(D) Acetone

Answer: (B) Sodium phenoxide

Q4. Which reaction is used for ether preparation?

(A) Williamson synthesis
(B) Wurtz reaction
(C) Sandmeyer reaction
(D) Cannizzaro reaction

Answer: (A) Williamson synthesis

Q5. Phenol reacts with bromine water to form:

(A) Benzene
(B) 2,4,6-Tribromophenol
(C) Ethanol
(D) Toluene

Answer: (B) 2,4,6-Tribromophenol

Q6. The Lucas reagent contains:

(A) HCl and ZnCl2
(B) H2SO4 and NaOH
(C) HNO3 and HCl
(D) NaCl and H2O

Answer: (A) HCl and ZnCl2

Q7. Oxidation of a secondary alcohol generally gives:

(A) Aldehyde
(B) Ketone
(C) Ether
(D) Alkane

Answer: (B) Ketone

Q8. The major product of Reimer-Tiemann reaction is:

(A) Salicylaldehyde
(B) Benzaldehyde
(C) Ethanal
(D) Acetone

Answer: (A) Salicylaldehyde

23. Chapter Summary

  • Alcohols contain the -OH group attached to saturated carbon.
  • Phenols contain -OH directly attached to an aromatic ring.
  • Ethers contain an oxygen atom between two carbon groups.
  • Alcohols are classified as primary, secondary and tertiary.
  • Phenol is more acidic than ordinary alcohols.
  • Alcohols form hydrogen bonds and have relatively high boiling points.
  • Williamson synthesis is used to prepare ethers.
  • Kolbe-Schmitt reaction produces salicylic acid.
  • Reimer-Tiemann reaction produces salicylaldehyde.
  • Lucas test helps distinguish different classes of alcohols.
  • Phenol gives a characteristic reaction with bromine water.

Chapter 8: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids

1. Introduction

Aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids are important classes of organic compounds containing the carbonyl group or carboxyl group.

  • Aldehydes contain the -CHO functional group.
  • Ketones contain the >C=O functional group.
  • Carboxylic acids contain the -COOH functional group.

2. Aldehydes

Aldehydes are organic compounds in which a carbonyl group is bonded to at least one hydrogen atom.

Functional group: -CHO

General formula: R-CHO

Examples:

  • HCHO – Methanal (Formaldehyde)
  • CH3CHO – Ethanal (Acetaldehyde)
  • CH3CH2CHO – Propanal
  • C6H5CHO – Benzaldehyde

3. Ketones

Ketones are organic compounds in which the carbonyl carbon is bonded to two carbon-containing groups.

Functional group: >C=O

General formula: R-CO-R'

Examples:

  • CH3COCH3 – Propanone (Acetone)
  • CH3COCH2CH3 – Butan-2-one
  • C6H5COCH3 – Acetophenone

4. Carboxylic Acids

Carboxylic acids are organic compounds containing the carboxyl functional group (-COOH).

General formula: R-COOH

Examples:

  • HCOOH – Methanoic acid (Formic acid)
  • CH3COOH – Ethanoic acid (Acetic acid)
  • CH3CH2COOH – Propanoic acid
  • C6H5COOH – Benzoic acid

5. Classification

A. On the Basis of Carbon Skeleton

  • Aliphatic aldehydes – CH3CHO.
  • Aromatic aldehydes – C6H5CHO.
  • Aliphatic ketones – CH3COCH3.
  • Aromatic ketones – C6H5COCH3.
  • Aliphatic carboxylic acids – CH3COOH.
  • Aromatic carboxylic acids – C6H5COOH.

B. On the Basis of Number of Functional Groups

  • Monocarboxylic acids – Contain one -COOH group.
  • Dicarboxylic acids – Contain two -COOH groups.
  • Tricarboxylic acids – Contain three -COOH groups.

6. Nomenclature of Aldehydes

  1. Select the longest carbon chain containing the -CHO group.
  2. Replace the final 'e' of the alkane name with 'al'.
  3. The aldehyde carbon is always numbered as carbon 1.
  4. For rings, use the suffix carbaldehyde where appropriate.

Examples:

  • HCHO – Methanal.
  • CH3CHO – Ethanal.
  • CH3CH2CHO – Propanal.
  • CH3CH2CH2CHO – Butanal.
  • C6H5CHO – Benzaldehyde.

7. Nomenclature of Ketones

  1. Select the longest chain containing the carbonyl group.
  2. Replace the final 'e' of the alkane name with 'one'.
  3. Number the chain to give the carbonyl group the lowest possible number.

Examples:

  • CH3COCH3 – Propanone.
  • CH3COCH2CH3 – Butan-2-one.
  • CH3COCH2CH2CH3 – Pentan-2-one.
  • C6H5COCH3 – 1-Phenylethan-1-one (Acetophenone).

8. Nomenclature of Carboxylic Acids

  1. Select the longest chain containing the -COOH group.
  2. Replace the final 'e' of the alkane name with 'oic acid'.
  3. The carboxyl carbon is numbered as carbon 1.

Examples:

  • HCOOH – Methanoic acid.
  • CH3COOH – Ethanoic acid.
  • CH3CH2COOH – Propanoic acid.
  • CH3CH2CH2COOH – Butanoic acid.
  • C6H5COOH – Benzoic acid.

9. Nature of the Carbonyl Group

The carbonyl group consists of a carbon atom double-bonded to an oxygen atom.

Structure: C=O

Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon. Therefore, the carbonyl bond is polar.

Representation: Cδ+ = Oδ-

  • Carbonyl carbon is electrophilic.
  • Oxygen is electron-rich.
  • Nucleophiles generally attack the carbonyl carbon.

10. Preparation of Aldehydes

A. Oxidation of Primary Alcohols

Primary alcohols on controlled oxidation form aldehydes.

RCH2OH + [O] → RCHO + H2O

B. Dehydrogenation of Alcohols

Primary alcohols pass over heated copper at 573 K to form aldehydes.

RCH2OH → RCHO + H2

C. Rosenmund Reduction

Acid chlorides are reduced to aldehydes using hydrogen in the presence of poisoned palladium catalyst.

RCOCl + H2 → RCHO + HCl

Catalyst: Pd/BaSO4 (poisoned catalyst).

D. Stephen Reaction

Nitriles are reduced with SnCl2 and HCl, followed by hydrolysis, to form aldehydes.

RCN → RCH=NH → RCHO

Reagents: SnCl2/HCl followed by hydrolysis.

E. Etard Reaction

The methyl group of an aromatic compound such as toluene is oxidised to an aldehyde using chromyl chloride.

C6H5CH3 → C6H5CHO

Reagent: CrO2Cl2.

F. Gattermann-Koch Reaction

Benzene or substituted benzene reacts with carbon monoxide and hydrogen chloride in the presence of AlCl3 and CuCl to form an aromatic aldehyde.

C6H6 + CO + HCl → C6H5CHO

11. Preparation of Ketones

A. Oxidation of Secondary Alcohols

Secondary alcohols on oxidation form ketones.

R2CHOH + [O] → R2C=O + H2O

B. Dehydrogenation of Secondary Alcohols

Secondary alcohols pass over heated copper at 573 K to form ketones.

R2CHOH → R2C=O + H2

C. From Acid Chlorides

Acid chlorides react with dialkylcadmium to form ketones.

2RCOCl + R'2Cd → 2RCOR' + CdCl2

D. From Nitriles

Nitriles react with Grignard reagents followed by hydrolysis to produce ketones.

RCN + R'MgX → Intermediate → RCOR'

E. Friedel-Crafts Acylation

Benzene reacts with an acid chloride in the presence of anhydrous AlCl3 to form an aromatic ketone.

C6H6 + CH3COCl → C6H5COCH3

12. Preparation of Carboxylic Acids

A. Oxidation of Primary Alcohols and Aldehydes

Primary alcohols and aldehydes can be oxidised to carboxylic acids.

RCH2OH + 2[O] → RCOOH + H2O

RCHO + [O] → RCOOH

B. Hydrolysis of Nitriles

Nitriles on acidic or alkaline hydrolysis produce carboxylic acids or their salts.

RCN + 2H2O + HCl → RCOOH + NH4Cl

C. Hydrolysis of Amides

Amides on hydrolysis form carboxylic acids.

RCONH2 + H2O → RCOOH + NH3

D. From Grignard Reagents

Grignard reagents react with carbon dioxide followed by acidic hydrolysis to form carboxylic acids.

RMgX + CO2 → RCOOMgX

RCOOMgX + H3O+ → RCOOH

E. Hydrolysis of Esters

Esters on acidic or alkaline hydrolysis produce carboxylic acids or carboxylate salts.

RCOOR' + H2O → RCOOH + R'OH

13. Physical Properties of Aldehydes and Ketones

  • Lower aldehydes and ketones are generally colourless liquids or gases.
  • Many have characteristic odours.
  • The carbonyl group makes them polar compounds.
  • They have higher boiling points than corresponding hydrocarbons.
  • They have lower boiling points than corresponding alcohols.
  • Lower members are soluble in water because they form hydrogen bonds with water.
  • Water solubility decreases as the hydrocarbon chain increases.

14. Physical Properties of Carboxylic Acids

  • Lower carboxylic acids are generally colourless liquids.
  • Higher carboxylic acids may be solids.
  • They have relatively high boiling points.
  • They form intermolecular hydrogen-bonded dimers.
  • Lower carboxylic acids are soluble in water.
  • Water solubility decreases as the alkyl chain becomes longer.

15. Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones

A. Nucleophilic Addition Reactions

Aldehydes and ketones undergo nucleophilic addition because the carbonyl carbon is electron-deficient.

R2C=O + Nu- → R2C(O-)Nu

B. Addition of Hydrogen Cyanide

Aldehydes and ketones react with HCN to form cyanohydrins.

R2C=O + HCN → R2C(OH)CN

C. Addition of Sodium Bisulphite

Aldehydes and many ketones react with sodium bisulphite to form crystalline addition compounds.

R2C=O + NaHSO3 → Addition product

D. Addition of Grignard Reagent

Grignard reagents add to aldehydes and ketones. Hydrolysis of the intermediate produces alcohols.

  • Formaldehyde gives primary alcohols.
  • Other aldehydes give secondary alcohols.
  • Ketones give tertiary alcohols.

E. Reaction with Alcohols

Aldehydes react with alcohols in the presence of acid to form hemiacetals and then acetals.

Aldehyde + Alcohol → Hemiacetal

Hemiacetal + Alcohol → Acetal + H2O

F. Reaction with Ammonia Derivatives

Aldehydes and ketones react with ammonia derivatives to form compounds containing C=N bonds.

Reagent Product
NH2OH Oxime
NH2NH2 Hydrazone
C6H5NHNH2 Phenylhydrazone
Semicarbazide Semicarbazone
2,4-DNP 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazone

16. Reduction Reactions

A. Reduction to Alcohols

Aldehydes and ketones are reduced to alcohols using NaBH4 or LiAlH4.

RCHO + 2[H] → RCH2OH

RCOR' + 2[H] → RCHOHR'

B. Clemmensen Reduction

Aldehydes and ketones are reduced to hydrocarbons using zinc amalgam and concentrated hydrochloric acid.

R-CO-R' → R-CH2-R'

Reagent: Zn(Hg)/conc. HCl.

C. Wolff-Kishner Reduction

Aldehydes and ketones are reduced to hydrocarbons using hydrazine and strong base on heating.

R2C=O → R2CH2

Reagents: NH2NH2, KOH, heat.

17. Oxidation Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones

A. Oxidation of Aldehydes

Aldehydes are easily oxidised to carboxylic acids.

RCHO + [O] → RCOOH

B. Oxidation of Ketones

Ketones resist mild oxidation. Under strong conditions, carbon-carbon bond cleavage may occur.

18. Important Tests for Aldehydes and Ketones

A. Tollens' Test

Aldehydes reduce Tollens' reagent to metallic silver, producing a silver mirror on the inner wall of the test tube.

Observation: Silver mirror.

B. Fehling's Test

Many aliphatic aldehydes reduce Fehling's solution to form a brick-red precipitate of cuprous oxide (Cu2O).

Observation: Brick-red precipitate.

Aromatic aldehydes generally do not give Fehling's test.

C. Schiff's Test

Aldehydes generally restore the pink or magenta colour of Schiff's reagent.

D. Iodoform Test

Compounds containing the CH3CO- group, and ethanol or suitable compounds oxidisable to it, give a yellow precipitate of iodoform (CHI3).

Observation: Yellow precipitate.

19. Reactions Due to Alpha Hydrogen

A. Aldol Condensation

Aldehydes and ketones containing at least one alpha hydrogen undergo aldol condensation in the presence of dilute base.

2CH3CHO → CH3CH(OH)CH2CHO

The product is 3-hydroxybutanal, commonly called aldol. On heating, it loses water to form an alpha,beta-unsaturated aldehyde.

CH3CH(OH)CH2CHO → CH3CH=CHCHO + H2O

B. Cross Aldol Condensation

Aldol condensation between two different carbonyl compounds is called cross aldol condensation.

If both compounds have alpha hydrogen atoms, a mixture of products may form.

C. Cannizzaro Reaction

Aldehydes without alpha hydrogen undergo disproportionation in concentrated alkali. One molecule is oxidised to a carboxylate salt and another is reduced to an alcohol.

2HCHO + NaOH → HCOONa + CH3OH

20. Chemical Reactions of Carboxylic Acids

A. Acidic Nature

Carboxylic acids release hydrogen ions in aqueous solution. Their conjugate base, the carboxylate ion, is stabilised by resonance.

RCOOH ⇌ RCOO- + H+

B. Reaction with Metals

Carboxylic acids react with active metals to produce salts and hydrogen gas.

2RCOOH + 2Na → 2RCOONa + H2

C. Reaction with Sodium Hydroxide

RCOOH + NaOH → RCOONa + H2O

D. Reaction with Sodium Bicarbonate

Carboxylic acids react with sodium bicarbonate to release carbon dioxide gas.

RCOOH + NaHCO3 → RCOONa + H2O + CO2

Observation: Brisk effervescence.

E. Esterification

Carboxylic acids react with alcohols in the presence of concentrated sulphuric acid to form esters.

RCOOH + R'OH ⇌ RCOOR' + H2O

F. Formation of Acid Chlorides

Carboxylic acids react with thionyl chloride to form acid chlorides.

RCOOH + SOCl2 → RCOCl + SO2 + HCl

G. Formation of Amides

Carboxylic acids react with ammonia to form ammonium carboxylate, which on heating gives an amide.

RCOOH + NH3 → RCOONH4

RCOONH4 → RCONH2 + H2O

H. Reduction

Carboxylic acids are reduced to primary alcohols using LiAlH4.

RCOOH + 4[H] → RCH2OH + H2O

I. Decarboxylation

Sodium salts of carboxylic acids on heating with soda lime produce alkanes containing one carbon atom less than the original acid.

RCOONa + NaOH → RH + Na2CO3

Condition: Soda lime and heat.

J. Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction

Carboxylic acids containing an alpha hydrogen undergo alpha-halogenation in the presence of chlorine or bromine and red phosphorus.

RCH2COOH + Br2 → RCHBrCOOH + HBr

21. Acidity of Carboxylic Acids

Carboxylic acids are acidic because they release H+ and form resonance-stabilised carboxylate ions.

Effect of Electron-Withdrawing Groups

Electron-withdrawing groups increase acidity by stabilising the carboxylate ion.

Example: ClCH2COOH is stronger than CH3COOH.

Effect of Electron-Donating Groups

Electron-donating groups generally decrease acidity by destabilising the carboxylate ion.

Effect of Distance

The electron-withdrawing effect decreases as the substituent moves farther away from the -COOH group.

22. Important Named Reactions

  • Rosenmund Reduction: Acid chloride to aldehyde.
  • Stephen Reaction: Nitrile to aldehyde.
  • Etard Reaction: Oxidation of an aromatic methyl group to an aldehyde.
  • Gattermann-Koch Reaction: Introduction of -CHO into an aromatic ring.
  • Friedel-Crafts Acylation: Formation of aromatic ketones.
  • Clemmensen Reduction: Carbonyl group to methylene group in acidic medium.
  • Wolff-Kishner Reduction: Carbonyl group to methylene group in basic medium.
  • Aldol Condensation: Carbonyl compounds with alpha hydrogen form aldol products.
  • Cannizzaro Reaction: Aldehydes without alpha hydrogen undergo disproportionation.
  • HVZ Reaction: Alpha-halogenation of carboxylic acids.

23. Important Differences

Aldehydes Ketones
Contain -CHO group. Contain >C=O group between two carbon groups.
Carbonyl carbon is bonded to at least one hydrogen. Carbonyl carbon is bonded to two carbon groups.
Generally oxidised easily. Resist mild oxidation.
Generally give Tollens' test. Generally do not give Tollens' test.
Carboxylic Acids Alcohols
Contain -COOH group. Contain -OH group.
Generally stronger acids. Very weakly acidic.
React with NaHCO3 to release CO2. Do not normally release CO2 with NaHCO3.

24. Important Reagents and Their Uses

Reagent Use
NaBH4 Reduction of aldehydes and ketones to alcohols.
LiAlH4 Reduction of several carbonyl compounds and acids.
Zn(Hg)/HCl Clemmensen reduction.
NH2NH2/KOH Wolff-Kishner reduction.
Tollens' reagent Test for aldehydes.
Fehling's solution Test for many aliphatic aldehydes.
2,4-DNP Test for carbonyl compounds.
HCN Formation of cyanohydrins.
NaHSO3 Bisulphite addition compound formation.
Br2/red phosphorus HVZ reaction.
Soda lime Decarboxylation.

25. Important Questions and Answers

Q1. Why are aldehydes more reactive than ketones towards nucleophilic addition?

Aldehydes have less steric hindrance and generally a smaller electron-donating effect than ketones. Therefore, their carbonyl carbon is more accessible and more electrophilic.

Q2. Why do carboxylic acids have high boiling points?

Carboxylic acids form hydrogen-bonded dimers. This association increases their boiling points.

Q3. What is Cannizzaro reaction?

Aldehydes without alpha hydrogen undergo disproportionation in concentrated alkali to produce an alcohol and a carboxylate salt.

Q4. What is Aldol condensation?

Aldehydes or ketones containing alpha hydrogen react in dilute base to form beta-hydroxy carbonyl compounds.

Q5. What is Rosenmund reduction?

It is the reduction of an acid chloride to an aldehyde using hydrogen and poisoned palladium catalyst.

Q6. What is Clemmensen reduction?

It is the reduction of aldehydes and ketones to hydrocarbons using Zn(Hg) and concentrated HCl.

Q7. What is the iodoform test?

It is a chemical test in which methyl ketones and certain related compounds produce a yellow precipitate of CHI3.

Q8. Why does ethanoic acid react with sodium bicarbonate?

Ethanoic acid is stronger than carbonic acid and displaces it from sodium bicarbonate, releasing CO2 gas.

26. Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs)

Q1. The functional group of aldehydes is:

(A) -OH
(B) -CHO
(C) -COOH
(D) -NH2

Answer: (B) -CHO

Q2. Acetone is the common name of:

(A) Methanal
(B) Ethanal
(C) Propanone
(D) Propanal

Answer: (C) Propanone

Q3. Tollens' reagent is generally used to identify:

(A) Aldehydes
(B) Alkanes
(C) Ethers
(D) Alcohols

Answer: (A) Aldehydes

Q4. Which reaction converts acid chlorides into aldehydes?

(A) Cannizzaro reaction
(B) Rosenmund reduction
(C) Aldol condensation
(D) HVZ reaction

Answer: (B) Rosenmund reduction

Q5. Which reagent is used in Clemmensen reduction?

(A) NaBH4
(B) Zn(Hg)/HCl
(C) HCN
(D) NaOH only

Answer: (B) Zn(Hg)/HCl

Q6. Which compound gives a positive iodoform test?

(A) Methanal
(B) Propanone
(C) Benzaldehyde
(D) Methanoic acid

Answer: (B) Propanone

Q7. The functional group of carboxylic acids is:

(A) -CHO
(B) -COOH
(C) -O-
(D) -CO-

Answer: (B) -COOH

Q8. Which reaction is shown by aldehydes without alpha hydrogen?

(A) Aldol condensation
(B) Cannizzaro reaction
(C) Esterification
(D) Wurtz reaction

Answer: (B) Cannizzaro reaction

Q9. The brick-red precipitate in Fehling's test is:

(A) CuO
(B) Cu2O
(C) Ag
(D) CuSO4

Answer: (B) Cu2O

Q10. Soda lime is used in:

(A) Esterification
(B) Decarboxylation
(C) Nitration
(D) Bromination

Answer: (B) Decarboxylation

27. Chapter Summary

  • Aldehydes contain the -CHO group.
  • Ketones contain the >C=O group between two carbon groups.
  • Carboxylic acids contain the -COOH group.
  • The carbonyl carbon is electrophilic.
  • Aldehydes and ketones undergo nucleophilic addition reactions.
  • Aldehydes are generally more reactive than ketones towards nucleophilic addition.
  • Tollens' test gives a silver mirror with aldehydes.
  • Fehling's test gives a brick-red precipitate with many aliphatic aldehydes.
  • Aldol condensation requires alpha hydrogen.
  • Cannizzaro reaction is shown by aldehydes without alpha hydrogen.
  • Carboxylic acids react with sodium bicarbonate to release CO2.
  • Clemmensen and Wolff-Kishner reactions convert carbonyl groups into methylene groups.
  • HVZ reaction introduces halogen at the alpha carbon of a carboxylic acid.

Chapter 9: Amines

Class 12 Chemistry Notes

1. Introduction

Amines are organic compounds derived from ammonia (NH3) by replacing one or more hydrogen atoms with alkyl or aryl groups.

General formula:

  • Primary amine: R-NH2
  • Secondary amine: R2NH
  • Tertiary amine: R3N

Examples:

  • CH3NH2 – Methylamine
  • (CH3)2NH – Dimethylamine
  • (CH3)3N – Trimethylamine
  • C6H5NH2 – Aniline

2. Classification of Amines

A. On the basis of the number of hydrogen atoms replaced

1. Primary Amines (1°)

Amines in which one hydrogen atom of ammonia is replaced by an alkyl or aryl group are called primary amines.

General formula: R-NH2

Example: CH3NH2 (Methylamine)

2. Secondary Amines (2°)

Amines in which two hydrogen atoms of ammonia are replaced by alkyl or aryl groups are called secondary amines.

General formula: R-NH-R'

Example: (CH3)2NH (Dimethylamine)

3. Tertiary Amines (3°)

Amines in which all three hydrogen atoms of ammonia are replaced by alkyl or aryl groups are called tertiary amines.

General formula: R3N

Example: (CH3)3N (Trimethylamine)

B. On the basis of the nature of groups

  • Aliphatic amines: Nitrogen is attached to an alkyl group. Example: CH3NH2.
  • Aromatic amines: Nitrogen is directly attached to an aromatic ring. Example: C6H5NH2.

3. Nomenclature of Amines

A. Common system

The names of alkyl groups are written followed by the word amine.

  • CH3NH2 – Methylamine
  • C2H5NH2 – Ethylamine
  • (CH3)2NH – Dimethylamine
  • (C2H5)2NH – Diethylamine

B. IUPAC system

In IUPAC nomenclature, the suffix 'e' of the parent alkane is generally replaced by 'amine'.

  • CH3NH2 – Methanamine
  • C2H5NH2 – Ethanamine
  • CH3CH2CH2NH2 – Propan-1-amine
  • CH3CH(NH2)CH3 – Propan-2-amine

When another group is attached to nitrogen, its position is indicated by N-.

Example: CH3NHCH2CH3 – N-methylethanamine.

4. Structure of Amines

  • Nitrogen is generally sp3 hybridised in simple amines.
  • It has one lone pair of electrons.
  • The shape around nitrogen is trigonal pyramidal.
  • The bond angle in ammonia is about 107°.
  • The lone pair is responsible for the basic nature of amines.

5. Preparation of Amines

1. Reduction of Nitro Compounds

Nitro compounds are reduced to primary amines using hydrogen in the presence of a catalyst or metals such as Sn/HCl and Fe/HCl.

Reaction:

R-NO2 + 3H2 → R-NH2 + 2H2O

Example:

C6H5NO2 + 3H2 → C6H5NH2 + 2H2O

Nitrobenzene gives aniline.

2. Ammonolysis of Alkyl Halides

Alkyl halides react with alcoholic ammonia to form amines.

Reaction:

R-X + 2NH3 → R-NH2 + NH4X

A mixture of primary, secondary, tertiary amines and quaternary ammonium salts may be formed.

3. Reduction of Nitriles

Nitriles on reduction give primary amines containing one additional carbon atom compared with the alkyl group originally attached to the nitrile carbon.

Reaction:

R-CN + 2H2 → R-CH2NH2

Reagents: LiAlH4 or H2/Ni.

4. Reduction of Amides

Amides are reduced to amines using lithium aluminium hydride.

Reaction:

R-CONH2 + 4[H] → R-CH2NH2 + H2O

Reagent: LiAlH4.

5. Gabriel Phthalimide Synthesis

This method is used for the preparation of primary aliphatic amines.

  • Phthalimide reacts with alcoholic KOH to form potassium phthalimide.
  • Potassium phthalimide reacts with an alkyl halide.
  • Hydrolysis or hydrazinolysis gives a primary amine.

Important point: This method is not suitable for preparing aromatic primary amines.

6. Hoffmann Bromamide Degradation Reaction

When an amide is treated with bromine and aqueous potassium hydroxide, a primary amine containing one carbon atom less than the parent amide is formed.

General reaction:

R-CONH2 + Br2 + 4KOH → R-NH2 + 2KBr + K2CO3 + 2H2O

Example:

CH3CONH2 + Br2 + 4KOH → CH3NH2 + 2KBr + K2CO3 + 2H2O

Important: The product has one carbon atom less than the amide.

6. Physical Properties of Amines

  • Lower aliphatic amines are generally gases or volatile liquids.
  • Higher amines are usually liquids or solids.
  • Lower amines have a fishy smell.
  • Primary and secondary amines can form intermolecular hydrogen bonds.
  • Tertiary amines cannot form hydrogen bonds with each other because they have no N-H bond.
  • Lower amines are soluble in water due to hydrogen bonding with water.
  • Solubility generally decreases as the size of the hydrocarbon group increases.

7. Chemical Properties of Amines

1. Basic Nature of Amines

Amines are basic because nitrogen contains a lone pair of electrons that can accept a proton.

Reaction:

R-NH2 + H2O ⇌ R-NH3+ + OH−

2. Reaction with Acids

Amines react with acids to form ammonium salts.

Reaction:

R-NH2 + HCl → R-NH3+Cl−

3. Alkylation

Amines react with alkyl halides to form higher substituted amines and ultimately quaternary ammonium salts.

Example:

CH3NH2 + CH3I → (CH3)2NH + HI

4. Acylation

Primary and secondary amines react with acid chlorides or acid anhydrides to form amides.

Example:

CH3NH2 + CH3COCl → CH3CONHCH3 + HCl

Tertiary amines do not undergo this reaction because they do not have an N-H hydrogen.

5. Carbylamine Reaction

Primary amines, when heated with chloroform and alcoholic KOH, form foul-smelling isocyanides.

General reaction:

R-NH2 + CHCl3 + 3KOH → R-NC + 3KCl + 3H2O

Important: This reaction is given only by primary amines, both aliphatic and aromatic.

6. Reaction with Nitrous Acid

Nitrous acid is generally prepared in situ using sodium nitrite and hydrochloric acid.

Primary aliphatic amines

They form alcohols with the evolution of nitrogen gas.

R-NH2 + HNO2 → R-OH + N2 + H2O

Primary aromatic amines

At 273–278 K, they form diazonium salts.

C6H5NH2 + NaNO2 + 2HCl → C6H5N2+Cl− + NaCl + 2H2O

Secondary amines

They form N-nitrosoamines.

Tertiary amines

Their reactions depend on whether they are aliphatic or aromatic. Tertiary aromatic amines undergo electrophilic substitution, commonly at the para position.

7. Reaction with Benzene Sulphonyl Chloride

This reaction is used in the Hinsberg test to distinguish primary, secondary and tertiary amines.

  • Primary amines: Form sulphonamides that dissolve in alkali because they contain an acidic N-H hydrogen.
  • Secondary amines: Form sulphonamides that are insoluble in alkali.
  • Tertiary amines: Do not form sulphonamides under these conditions; they dissolve in dilute acid by forming salts.

8. Basic Strength of Amines

Basic strength depends on the availability of the lone pair of electrons on nitrogen.

  • Electron-releasing groups generally increase basicity.
  • Electron-withdrawing groups generally decrease basicity.
  • Solvation and steric effects also influence the basic strength in aqueous solution.

In aqueous solution:

The general order for simple methylamines is: (CH3)2NH > CH3NH2 > (CH3)3N > NH3

This order is not universal for all amines; the solvent and structure matter.

Aniline is less basic than ammonia because the lone pair on nitrogen is delocalised into the benzene ring by resonance.

9. Electrophilic Substitution Reactions of Aniline

The -NH2 group activates the benzene ring and directs incoming electrophiles to the ortho and para positions.

1. Bromination

Aniline reacts with bromine water to form a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromoaniline.

C6H5NH2 + 3Br2 → 2,4,6-C6H2Br3NH2 + 3HBr

2. Nitration

Direct nitration of aniline with concentrated nitric acid and sulphuric acid gives a mixture of products. Protonation of -NH2 to -NH3+ affects the orientation.

To obtain mainly the para product, the amino group is first protected by acetylation, followed by nitration and hydrolysis.

3. Sulphonation

Aniline reacts with concentrated sulphuric acid to form anilinium hydrogen sulphate. On heating, it gives sulphanilic acid (p-aminobenzenesulphonic acid).

10. Diazonium Salts

Diazonium salts contain the group -N2+ attached to an organic group. Aromatic diazonium salts are important intermediates in organic synthesis.

Preparation: Diazotisation

Aniline reacts with sodium nitrite and hydrochloric acid at 273–278 K to form benzene diazonium chloride.

C6H5NH2 + NaNO2 + 2HCl → C6H5N2+Cl− + NaCl + 2H2O

11. Reactions of Benzene Diazonium Chloride

1. Sandmeyer Reaction

The diazonium group is replaced by chlorine, bromine or cyanide using cuprous salts.

  • C6H5N2+Cl− + CuCl → C6H5Cl + N2
  • C6H5N2+Cl− + CuBr → C6H5Br + N2
  • C6H5N2+Cl− + CuCN → C6H5CN + N2

2. Gattermann Reaction

The diazonium group is replaced by chlorine or bromine using copper powder and the corresponding hydrogen halide.

3. Replacement by Iodine

Benzene diazonium chloride reacts with potassium iodide to form iodobenzene.

C6H5N2+Cl− + KI → C6H5I + KCl + N2

4. Replacement by Fluorine: Balz-Schiemann Reaction

Benzene diazonium tetrafluoroborate on heating gives fluorobenzene.

C6H5N2+BF4− → C6H5F + BF3 + N2

5. Replacement by -OH

On warming with water, benzene diazonium chloride gives phenol.

C6H5N2+Cl− + H2O → C6H5OH + HCl + N2

6. Replacement by -H

Reduction with hypophosphorous acid (H3PO2) replaces the diazonium group with hydrogen.

C6H5N2+Cl− + H3PO2 + H2O → C6H6 + H3PO3 + HCl + N2

7. Coupling Reaction

Diazonium salts react with activated aromatic compounds such as phenol and aniline to form brightly coloured azo compounds.

These compounds contain the linkage -N=N-.

12. Important Named Reactions

  • Gabriel Phthalimide Synthesis: Preparation of primary aliphatic amines.
  • Hoffmann Bromamide Degradation: Preparation of amines with one carbon less than the amide.
  • Carbylamine Reaction: Test for primary amines.
  • Hinsberg Test: Distinguishes primary, secondary and tertiary amines.
  • Sandmeyer Reaction: Replacement of diazonium group using cuprous salts.
  • Gattermann Reaction: Replacement of diazonium group using copper powder and HX.
  • Balz-Schiemann Reaction: Preparation of aryl fluorides.
  • Diazotisation: Conversion of primary aromatic amines into diazonium salts.
  • Azo Coupling: Formation of coloured azo compounds.

13. Important Differences

Primary, Secondary and Tertiary Amines

  • Primary: One organic group attached to nitrogen; R-NH2.
  • Secondary: Two organic groups attached to nitrogen; R2NH.
  • Tertiary: Three organic groups attached to nitrogen; R3N.

Aliphatic and Aromatic Amines

  • Aliphatic amines: Nitrogen is attached to an alkyl group.
  • Aromatic amines: Nitrogen is directly attached to an aromatic ring.

14. Important Formulae and Reagents

  • Reduction of nitro compounds: Sn/HCl, Fe/HCl or H2/Ni.
  • Reduction of nitriles: LiAlH4 or H2/Ni.
  • Reduction of amides: LiAlH4.
  • Hoffmann degradation: Br2/KOH.
  • Carbylamine reaction: CHCl3 + alcoholic KOH.
  • Diazotisation: NaNO2 + HCl, 273–278 K.
  • Sandmeyer reaction: CuCl, CuBr or CuCN.
  • Balz-Schiemann reaction: HBF4 followed by heating.

15. Important Short Questions and Answers

Q1. What are amines?

Amines are organic derivatives of ammonia in which one or more hydrogen atoms are replaced by alkyl or aryl groups.

Q2. Why are amines basic?

Amines are basic because nitrogen has a lone pair of electrons that can accept a proton.

Q3. What is the general formula of primary amines?

R-NH2.

Q4. Which test is used to identify primary amines?

Carbylamine test.

Q5. Which amine gives the carbylamine reaction?

Only primary amines, both aliphatic and aromatic.

Q6. What is aniline?

Aniline is an aromatic primary amine with formula C6H5NH2.

Q7. What is diazotisation?

The conversion of a primary aromatic amine into a diazonium salt using nitrous acid at 273–278 K is called diazotisation.

Q8. What is the formula of benzene diazonium chloride?

C6H5N2+Cl−.

Q9. Which reaction produces fluorobenzene from a diazonium salt?

Balz-Schiemann reaction.

Q10. Why is aniline less basic than methylamine?

In aniline, the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring by resonance, making it less available for accepting a proton.

16. Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs)

  1. Which is a primary amine?
    A. (CH3)2NH
    B. CH3NH2
    C. (CH3)3N
    D. None
    Answer: B. CH3NH2
  2. The formula of aniline is:
    A. C6H6
    B. C6H5NH2
    C. C6H5OH
    D. CH3NH2
    Answer: B. C6H5NH2
  3. Carbylamine reaction is given by:
    A. Primary amines
    B. Secondary amines
    C. Tertiary amines
    D. All amines
    Answer: A. Primary amines
  4. Hoffmann bromamide degradation gives an amine with:
    A. Same number of carbon atoms
    B. One carbon atom less
    C. One carbon atom more
    D. Two carbon atoms more
    Answer: B. One carbon atom less
  5. Diazotisation of aniline is carried out at:
    A. 273–278 K
    B. 300–310 K
    C. 350 K
    D. 400 K
    Answer: A. 273–278 K
  6. The Balz-Schiemann reaction is used to prepare:
    A. Chlorobenzene
    B. Bromobenzene
    C. Fluorobenzene
    D. Iodobenzene
    Answer: C. Fluorobenzene
  7. Which amine cannot form intermolecular hydrogen bonds with itself?
    A. Primary amine
    B. Secondary amine
    C. Tertiary amine
    D. All
    Answer: C. Tertiary amine
  8. Benzene diazonium chloride reacts with water on warming to form:
    A. Aniline
    B. Phenol
    C. Benzene
    D. Toluene
    Answer: B. Phenol

17. Chapter Summary

  • Amines are derivatives of ammonia.
  • Amines are classified as primary, secondary and tertiary.
  • Aniline is an aromatic primary amine.
  • Amines show basic properties due to the lone pair on nitrogen.
  • Gabriel synthesis prepares primary aliphatic amines.
  • Hoffmann bromamide degradation gives an amine with one carbon less.
  • Carbylamine reaction is a test for primary amines.
  • Diazotisation is carried out at 273–278 K.
  • Diazonium salts are useful intermediates in organic synthesis.
  • Sandmeyer and Balz-Schiemann reactions are important named reactions.

End of Chapter 9

Next Chapter: Chapter 10 – Biomolecules

Chapter 10: Biomolecules

Class 12 Chemistry Notes

1. Introduction

Biomolecules are chemical compounds present in living organisms. They are essential for the growth, development, maintenance and proper functioning of living organisms.

Major types of biomolecules:

  • Carbohydrates
  • Proteins
  • Vitamins
  • Nucleic acids
  • Enzymes
  • Hormones
  • Lipids

2. Carbohydrates

Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, or substances that produce such compounds on hydrolysis.

General formula: Cx(H2O)y (for many, but not all, carbohydrates).

Functions of Carbohydrates

  • They are an important source of energy.
  • They store energy in plants and animals.
  • They form structural components of cells.
  • They participate in cell recognition and communication.

3. Classification of Carbohydrates

A. Monosaccharides

Monosaccharides are the simplest carbohydrates which cannot be hydrolysed into smaller carbohydrate units.

Examples: Glucose, fructose, ribose and galactose.

B. Oligosaccharides

Oligosaccharides yield two to ten monosaccharide units on hydrolysis. Disaccharides are the most common examples.

Examples: Sucrose, maltose and lactose.

C. Polysaccharides

Polysaccharides are complex carbohydrates that yield a large number of monosaccharide units on hydrolysis.

Examples: Starch, cellulose and glycogen.

4. Monosaccharides

Glucose

Glucose is an aldohexose with molecular formula C6H12O6. It is commonly called blood sugar or dextrose.

Important properties:

  • It is a monosaccharide.
  • It contains six carbon atoms.
  • It contains an aldehyde group in its open-chain form.
  • It is soluble in water.
  • It is a reducing sugar.

Open-chain Structure of Glucose

The open-chain structure of glucose contains one aldehyde group (-CHO), five hydroxyl groups (-OH) and six carbon atoms.

Fischer projection:

       CHO
        |
       H-C-OH
        |
      HO-C-H
        |
       H-C-OH
        |
       H-C-OH
        |
      CH2OH

Evidence for the Structure of Glucose

  • Glucose reacts with HI on prolonged heating to give n-hexane, showing a straight chain of six carbon atoms.
  • It forms an oxime with hydroxylamine, indicating a carbonyl group.
  • It is oxidised by bromine water to gluconic acid, indicating an aldehyde group.
  • It reacts with acetic anhydride to form glucose pentaacetate, showing the presence of five hydroxyl groups.

Cyclic Structure of Glucose

Glucose mainly exists in cyclic hemiacetal forms in aqueous solution. The ring is formed by reaction between the aldehyde group at C-1 and the hydroxyl group at C-5.

Two anomeric forms:

  • Alpha-D-glucose (α-D-glucose)
  • Beta-D-glucose (β-D-glucose)

These forms differ in the orientation of the hydroxyl group at the anomeric carbon (C-1).

Mutarotation

The change in specific rotation of an optically active sugar solution due to interconversion of its anomers until equilibrium is reached is called mutarotation.

5. Fructose

Fructose is a ketohexose with molecular formula C6H12O6. It is naturally present in fruits and honey.

  • It contains a ketone group in its open-chain form.
  • It is a monosaccharide.
  • It is a reducing sugar.
  • It is sweeter than glucose.
  • It generally forms cyclic hemiketal structures.

Structure of Fructose

       CH2OH
          |
         C=O
          |
       HO-C-H
          |
        H-C-OH
          |
        H-C-OH
          |
       CH2OH

6. Disaccharides

Disaccharides are carbohydrates that yield two monosaccharide units on hydrolysis.

1. Sucrose

Formula: C12H22O11

  • It is commonly known as table sugar.
  • It is made up of glucose and fructose.
  • Its glycosidic linkage is α(1→2)β.
  • It is a non-reducing sugar.
  • On hydrolysis, it gives glucose and fructose.

Hydrolysis:

Sucrose + H2O → Glucose + Fructose

2. Maltose

Formula: C12H22O11

  • It is made up of two glucose units.
  • It contains an α(1→4) glycosidic linkage.
  • It is a reducing sugar.
  • It is obtained during the hydrolysis of starch.

Hydrolysis:

Maltose + H2O → Glucose + Glucose

3. Lactose

Formula: C12H22O11

  • It is commonly called milk sugar.
  • It is made up of glucose and galactose.
  • It contains a β(1→4) glycosidic linkage.
  • It is a reducing sugar.
  • It is present in milk.

Hydrolysis:

Lactose + H2O → Glucose + Galactose

7. Polysaccharides

1. Starch

Starch is the main storage polysaccharide of plants. It is made up of many α-D-glucose units.

  • It is a polymer of glucose.
  • It is stored in plants.
  • It is a non-reducing carbohydrate.
  • It gives a blue-black colour with iodine.

Two components of starch:

Amylose

  • It is a mostly unbranched polymer.
  • It has α(1→4) glycosidic linkages.
  • It is generally water-soluble.

Amylopectin

  • It is a branched polymer.
  • It contains α(1→4) linkages in the chains.
  • Branches are formed through α(1→6) linkages.

2. Cellulose

Cellulose is the main structural polysaccharide of plant cell walls.

  • It is made up of β-D-glucose units.
  • It contains β(1→4) glycosidic linkages.
  • It is an unbranched polymer.
  • It is insoluble in water.
  • Humans cannot digest cellulose because they lack cellulase.

3. Glycogen

Glycogen is the storage polysaccharide found in animals. It is mainly stored in the liver and muscles.

  • It is made up of α-D-glucose units.
  • It has α(1→4) linkages in the chains.
  • It has frequent α(1→6) branch points.
  • It is more highly branched than amylopectin.

8. Glycosidic Linkage

The oxygen bridge formed between two monosaccharide units through a condensation reaction is called a glycosidic linkage.

Examples:

  • Maltose: α(1→4)
  • Lactose: β(1→4)
  • Sucrose: α(1→2)β

9. Proteins

Proteins are high molecular mass biomolecules made up of α-amino acid units joined together by peptide bonds.

Functions of proteins:

  • Growth and repair of body tissues.
  • Formation of enzymes and hormones.
  • Transport of substances.
  • Immune protection.
  • Structural support.

10. Amino Acids

Amino acids are organic compounds containing both an amino group (-NH2) and a carboxyl group (-COOH).

General structure of an α-amino acid:

          H
          |
      H2N-C-COOH
          |
          R
  • The central carbon is called the α-carbon.
  • It is attached to an amino group, carboxyl group, hydrogen and R group.
  • The R group determines the identity and properties of the amino acid.

Classification of Amino Acids

1. Neutral Amino Acids

They contain one amino group and one carboxyl group.

Example: Glycine.

2. Acidic Amino Acids

They contain more carboxyl groups than amino groups.

Examples: Aspartic acid and glutamic acid.

3. Basic Amino Acids

They contain more amino groups or basic nitrogen-containing groups than carboxyl groups.

Examples: Lysine and arginine.

Essential and Non-essential Amino Acids

Essential Amino Acids

Amino acids that the human body cannot synthesise in sufficient amounts and must obtain from food are called essential amino acids.

Examples: Valine, leucine, isoleucine, lysine, methionine, threonine, phenylalanine, tryptophan and histidine.

Non-essential Amino Acids

Amino acids that the body can synthesise are called non-essential amino acids.

Examples: Glycine, alanine, serine and aspartic acid.

11. Zwitterion

In aqueous solution, amino acids commonly exist as dipolar ions containing both a positively charged ammonium group and a negatively charged carboxylate group. Such ions are called zwitterions.

Structure:

+H3N-CH(R)-COO−

12. Peptide Bond

The -CO-NH- linkage formed between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of another amino acid is called a peptide bond.

Formation:

Amino acid + Amino acid → Dipeptide + H2O

Types of Peptides

  • Dipeptide: Contains two amino acid units.
  • Tripeptide: Contains three amino acid units.
  • Oligopeptide: Contains a small number of amino acid units.
  • Polypeptide: Contains many amino acid units.

13. Structure of Proteins

1. Primary Structure

The specific sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain is called its primary structure.

2. Secondary Structure

The regular folding of a polypeptide chain due to hydrogen bonding is called secondary structure.

  • α-Helix
  • β-Pleated Sheet

3. Tertiary Structure

The overall three-dimensional folding of a polypeptide chain is called its tertiary structure.

4. Quaternary Structure

The arrangement of two or more polypeptide chains into a functional protein is called quaternary structure.

Example: Haemoglobin.

14. Fibrous and Globular Proteins

Fibrous Proteins

  • They generally have long, thread-like structures.
  • They are usually insoluble in water.
  • They provide structural support.
  • Examples: Keratin and collagen.

Globular Proteins

  • They have compact, spherical structures.
  • Many are soluble in water.
  • They perform biological functions.
  • Examples: Insulin and haemoglobin.

15. Denaturation of Proteins

The process in which a protein loses its natural biological activity and higher-order structure due to heat, change in pH or chemicals is called denaturation.

Examples:

  • Coagulation of egg white on boiling.
  • Loss of activity of enzymes due to high temperature.

Denaturation generally disrupts secondary, tertiary and quaternary structures, while the primary structure usually remains intact.

16. Enzymes

Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up biochemical reactions without being consumed in the process.

Characteristics:

  • Most enzymes are proteins.
  • They are highly specific in their action.
  • They work best at an optimum temperature and pH.
  • They lower the activation energy of reactions.
  • They are effective in small amounts.

Examples of Enzymes

  • Amylase: Breaks down starch.
  • Pepsin: Helps digest proteins in the stomach.
  • Lipase: Breaks down fats.
  • Maltase: Converts maltose into glucose.
  • Urease: Catalyses the breakdown of urea.

17. Vitamins

Vitamins are organic compounds required in small quantities for normal growth and proper functioning of the body.

Classification of Vitamins

A. Fat-Soluble Vitamins

Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble.

B. Water-Soluble Vitamins

Vitamin B-complex and Vitamin C are water-soluble.

18. Important Vitamins and Their Functions

Vitamin Function Deficiency Disease Sources
A Vision and healthy tissues Night blindness Carrots, milk, eggs
B1 Energy metabolism and nerve function Beri-beri Whole grains, legumes
B2 Energy metabolism Ariboflavinosis Milk, eggs
B3 Energy metabolism Pellagra Meat, peanuts
B6 Amino acid metabolism Anaemia and neurological problems Bananas, fish, grains
B9 DNA synthesis and cell division Megaloblastic anaemia Green leafy vegetables
B12 Red blood cell formation and nerve function Megaloblastic anaemia Animal foods, fortified foods
C Collagen formation and antioxidant function Scurvy Citrus fruits, amla
D Calcium absorption and bone health Rickets in children Sunlight, fortified foods
E Antioxidant function Rare deficiency; neurological and muscle problems Nuts, vegetable oils
K Blood clotting Excessive bleeding Green leafy vegetables

19. Nucleic Acids

Nucleic acids are biomolecules responsible for the storage, transmission and expression of genetic information.

Two major types:

  • DNA – Deoxyribonucleic Acid
  • RNA – Ribonucleic Acid

20. Components of Nucleic Acids

Nucleic acids are polymers of nucleotides. Each nucleotide consists of:

  • A nitrogenous base.
  • A pentose sugar.
  • A phosphate group.

Nitrogenous Bases

Purines

  • Adenine (A)
  • Guanine (G)

Pyrimidines

  • Cytosine (C)
  • Thymine (T) – mainly in DNA.
  • Uracil (U) – mainly in RNA.

21. DNA (Deoxyribonucleic Acid)

DNA is the genetic material in most living organisms. It stores hereditary information.

Characteristics:

  • It generally consists of two polynucleotide strands.
  • The strands form a double helix.
  • It contains deoxyribose sugar.
  • It contains bases A, G, C and T.
  • It is usually double-stranded.

Base Pairing in DNA

  • Adenine pairs with Thymine (A=T) through two hydrogen bonds.
  • Guanine pairs with Cytosine (G≡C) through three hydrogen bonds.

22. RNA (Ribonucleic Acid)

RNA plays important roles in protein synthesis and gene expression.

Characteristics:

  • It contains ribose sugar.
  • It contains bases A, G, C and U.
  • It is usually single-stranded.
  • Some RNA molecules can fold into complex structures.

Types of RNA

1. Messenger RNA (mRNA)

It carries genetic instructions from DNA to ribosomes for protein synthesis.

2. Transfer RNA (tRNA)

It carries amino acids to ribosomes during protein synthesis.

3. Ribosomal RNA (rRNA)

It forms a major structural and functional component of ribosomes.

23. Difference Between DNA and RNA

DNA RNA
Contains deoxyribose sugar Contains ribose sugar
Contains thymine Contains uracil instead of thymine
Usually double-stranded Usually single-stranded
Stores genetic information Plays important roles in gene expression and protein synthesis

24. Hormones

Hormones are chemical messengers produced by endocrine glands or specialised cells. They regulate various activities of the body.

Examples of Hormones

  • Insulin: Regulates blood glucose levels.
  • Thyroxine: Regulates metabolism.
  • Adrenaline: Helps the body respond to stress.
  • Growth hormone: Supports growth and development.
  • Estrogen: Important in female reproductive development.
  • Testosterone: Important in male reproductive development.

25. Lipids

Lipids are a broad group of biological substances that are generally insoluble in water but soluble in non-polar organic solvents.

Types of Lipids

  • Fats and oils
  • Phospholipids
  • Steroids
  • Waxes

Functions of Lipids

  • They store energy.
  • They form cell membranes.
  • They provide insulation and protection.
  • Some lipids act as hormones or signalling molecules.

26. Important Differences

Reducing and Non-Reducing Sugars

Reducing Sugars Non-Reducing Sugars
Have a free anomeric carbon or can form an open-chain carbonyl form. Have no free anomeric carbon available for ring opening.
Give positive Tollens' or Fehling's tests. Do not give these tests before hydrolysis.
Examples: Glucose, maltose, lactose. Example: Sucrose.

Starch and Cellulose

Starch Cellulose
Storage polysaccharide in plants. Structural polysaccharide in plant cell walls.
Made of α-D-glucose units. Made of β-D-glucose units.
Contains α-linkages. Contains β(1→4) linkages.
Can be digested by humans. Cannot be digested by humans.

27. Important Chemical Reactions

1. Hydrolysis of Sucrose

C12H22O11 + H2O → C6H12O6 + C6H12O6

Products: Glucose and fructose.

2. Hydrolysis of Maltose

C12H22O11 + H2O → 2C6H12O6

Products: Two glucose molecules.

3. Hydrolysis of Lactose

C12H22O11 + H2O → C6H12O6 + C6H12O6

Products: Glucose and galactose.

4. Oxidation of Glucose

Glucose + [O] → Gluconic acid

Bromine water oxidises the aldehyde group of glucose to a carboxylic acid group.

28. Important One-Line Questions

Q1. What are biomolecules?

Chemical compounds found in living organisms are called biomolecules.

Q2. What is the molecular formula of glucose?

C6H12O6.

Q3. Which sugar is known as blood sugar?

Glucose.

Q4. Which sugar is known as fruit sugar?

Fructose.

Q5. Which sugar is called milk sugar?

Lactose.

Q6. Which sugar is called table sugar?

Sucrose.

Q7. Which is the storage carbohydrate in plants?

Starch.

Q8. Which is the storage carbohydrate in animals?

Glycogen.

Q9. Which is the main structural carbohydrate in plants?

Cellulose.

Q10. What is the linkage between amino acids called?

Peptide bond.

Q11. What is a zwitterion?

An ion containing both positive and negative charges but having an overall neutral charge.

Q12. What is denaturation?

Loss of the natural structure and biological activity of a protein is called denaturation.

Q13. Which vitamin deficiency causes scurvy?

Vitamin C.

Q14. Which vitamin deficiency causes rickets?

Vitamin D.

Q15. Which vitamin is essential for blood clotting?

Vitamin K.

Q16. Which bases are present in DNA?

Adenine, guanine, cytosine and thymine.

Q17. Which base is found in RNA instead of thymine?

Uracil.

Q18. What is the full form of DNA?

Deoxyribonucleic Acid.

Q19. What is the full form of RNA?

Ribonucleic Acid.

Q20. Which enzyme breaks down starch?

Amylase.

29. Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs)

  1. The molecular formula of glucose is:
    A. C6H6
    B. C6H12O6
    C. C12H22O11
    D. CH4
    Answer: B. C6H12O6
  2. Which of the following is a non-reducing sugar?
    A. Glucose
    B. Maltose
    C. Lactose
    D. Sucrose
    Answer: D. Sucrose
  3. The storage carbohydrate in animals is:
    A. Starch
    B. Cellulose
    C. Glycogen
    D. Sucrose
    Answer: C. Glycogen
  4. Cellulose is made up of:
    A. α-D-glucose
    B. β-D-glucose
    C. Fructose
    D. Galactose
    Answer: B. β-D-glucose
  5. The linkage between amino acids is:
    A. Glycosidic bond
    B. Peptide bond
    C. Ionic bond
    D. Hydrogen bond
    Answer: B. Peptide bond
  6. Which vitamin deficiency causes night blindness?
    A. Vitamin A
    B. Vitamin B1
    C. Vitamin C
    D. Vitamin K
    Answer: A. Vitamin A
  7. Which vitamin is water-soluble?
    A. Vitamin A
    B. Vitamin D
    C. Vitamin E
    D. Vitamin C
    Answer: D. Vitamin C
  8. The sugar present in DNA is:
    A. Ribose
    B. Deoxyribose
    C. Glucose
    D. Fructose
    Answer: B. Deoxyribose
  9. Which nitrogenous base is present in RNA but not DNA?
    A. Adenine
    B. Guanine
    C. Uracil
    D. Cytosine
    Answer: C. Uracil
  10. Which enzyme helps digest proteins in the stomach?
    A. Amylase
    B. Pepsin
    C. Lipase
    D. Maltase
    Answer: B. Pepsin

30. Chapter Summary

  • Biomolecules are essential chemical compounds found in living organisms.
  • Carbohydrates are classified into monosaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides.
  • Glucose is an aldohexose, whereas fructose is a ketohexose.
  • Sucrose is a non-reducing sugar.
  • Maltose and lactose are reducing sugars.
  • Starch is the storage carbohydrate of plants.
  • Glycogen is the storage carbohydrate of animals.
  • Cellulose forms the structural framework of plant cell walls.
  • Proteins are polymers of amino acids.
  • Peptide bonds join amino acids.
  • Enzymes act as biological catalysts.
  • Vitamins are classified as fat-soluble and water-soluble.
  • DNA stores genetic information.
  • RNA plays important roles in protein synthesis.
  • Hormones regulate different activities of the body.
  • Lipids are important for energy storage and cell membranes.

End of Chapter 10
